Oh! Nothing came of me at all, and my life has simply gone by. I received this human body, so hard to get, and never once worshipped Shri Ram with an honest heart, in body, mind and word.
Childhood passed in ignorance; in those days my mind was four times as restless, and happy only with play and food. Then the fever of youth came on and I ate the forbidden food of women, so that the wind of lust filled my whole body and delirium set in.
My middle years, when youth had passed, were lost in farming, trade and every kind of scheme for making money; but because I had turned my back on Shri Ram, I never found happiness even in a dream — day and night I went on burning in the three fires of this world.
I never served with true devotion the devotees of Shri Ramchandra or the pure-minded saints, and I never listened with a thrill of joy to the deeds Shri Raghunath performed, or told them with a glad heart.
Now that old age has come and broken every limb and left me in distress, I fret like a snake that has lost its jewel; I beat my head and wring my hands in regret, but at this hour I cannot see one kind friend anywhere to put out this unbearable forest fire.
The people for whom I ruined both this world and the next (piling up sin after sin) are ashamed even to stand near me today. Tulsi, even now, remember that Shri Raghunath whose name, spoken only once, carried the king of the elephants across the ocean of this world.

My mind! You will have to wring your hands in regret. Think a little: this human body, which even the gods long for and cannot get, has come to you so easily — why are you throwing it away for nothing?
When you turn your back on Hari, all your efforts for happiness are as useless as churning water to get butter. (Happiness is in Hari; forget him and serve pleasures that have no happiness in them, and happiness will never come.) Understand this, leave the bad road and the company of bad people, walk the good road and keep the company of good people.
Go and see the devotees of Shri Ram, listen to the stories of Hari from them, repeat the name of Ram, sing the songs of Ram's greatness, and in your heart meditate on Lord Shri Ram with his bow and arrows in his hands, dressed in the clothes of a sage, his quiver tied at his waist.
Tulsidas, leave behind all the empty show of the world and bow your head at the lotus feet of Shri Ram. Don't be afraid — Shri Ram, the lord of Janaki, has taken as his own many low people just like you.

My mind! Look towards Madhav, if only a little! Listen, you wicked thing: just as a pauper checks on his money every moment, remember your master Shri Ram like that.
That Shri Ram is the home of beauty, of good character, of wisdom and of every fine quality. He is lovely, and he gives with a very open hand. He delights the saints, he destroys all sins, and he wipes out the poison of the senses' pleasures.
If you want to cross the ocean of this world without yoga, without sacrifices, without vows and without self-denial, then Tulsidas, never for a moment of day or night forget the lotus feet of Shri Hari.

Suniti, the mother of the devotee Dhruv, said to her son: My child, the four Vedas all say this — apart from thinking of the feet of Shri Raghunath, the soul has no resting place anywhere.
By thinking of those feet even Brahma and Lord Shiva gained their powers; by serving him, Shuka and Sanak and the other sages walk the world free while still alive, and even now they keep on remembering him.
Lakshmi is very restless and never stays still anywhere for long, but even she, having found the Lord's lotus feet, has become steady in thought, word and deed — that is, she stays always in his service with mind, speech and body.
He is an ocean of compassion and a wish-granting jewel for his devotees; all beauty lies in serving him. And every god and every lord of the demons has been bitten by those six snakes — lust, anger, greed, pride, delusion and envy.
My child, what your stepmother Suruchi said is true, hard as it was to hear. Tulsidas, so long as one keeps his face turned away from Shri Raghunath, troubles are never destroyed.

Foolish mind, listen to my advice: no one has ever found happiness by turning away from the feet of Hari. You wicked thing, understand this quickly (nothing is lost yet — go to him for shelter and everything can still be set right).
Look! Ever since the sun and the moon left the eyes and the mind of the Lord, they have been suffering greatly. Day and night they must go round and round the sky, and even there their strong enemy Rahu keeps chasing them.
The Ganga is called the river of the gods and is very holy, and her fame is spread through all three worlds — but from the day she left the Lord's feet until today, even she has never once been able to stop flowing.
Without the worship of Shri Raghunath, troubles do not end. The Vedas have removed every doubt about this truth. So, Tulsidas, give up every other hope and become the servant of Shri Ram.

My mind! You have never taken any rest. Forgetting your own nature, which is joy itself, you wander day and night wherever the senses drag you, among the pleasures of the world.
Though you have suffered unbearable trouble from the company of those pleasures, and are caught in a hard net, still, you fool, you are in the grip of "mine, mine" and will not let them go. So even after understanding everything, you go on with no understanding at all.
Over many births you have done all sorts of deeds and smeared yourself with their mud. Mind, without getting the water of clear understanding, this mud can never be washed off. That is what the Vedas and the Puranas say.
Your good lies in Hari, the highest master, the highest father, the highest teacher — but you never once held him joyfully in your heart (day and night you were busy gathering up the world's pleasures). Tulsidas, when can such a pond quench your thirst, when your whole life goes by in digging it?

Shri Hari! My mind will not give up its stubbornness. Lord, day and night I reason with it in every way, but it keeps doing whatever its own nature drives it to do.
It is like a young woman who feels the most unbearable pain at the time of childbirth (and thinks then that she will never go near her husband again), but the foolish woman forgets all that agony and goes back to the very husband who gave her that pain.
It is like a greedy dog that gets beaten with shoes wherever it goes, and still the low creature wanders down the same street again — the fool feels not the least shame.
(This is exactly how my mind is: even after being hurt by the pleasures of the world, it runs straight back to them.) I have grown tired of trying one remedy after another. But this mind is enormously strong and cannot be defeated. Tulsidas, it can only be brought under control when the Lord who moves us all stops it himself.

This mind is such a fool that it leaves the Ganga of devotion to Shri Ram and hopes to satisfy itself with drops of dew.
It is like a thirsty papiha bird, which drinks only from the clouds, that sees a puff of smoke and takes it for a rain cloud, but when it gets there it finds no coolness and no water, and the smoke blinds its eyes even more. (That is the state of this mind.)
It is like a foolish hawk that sees the shadow of its own body on a glass floor and, mad with hunger, forgets that its beak will break if it strikes, and swoops down on it at once. (In just this way my mind swoops down on the pleasures of the world.)
Storehouse of mercy! How much of this bad behaviour can I describe? You already know the state your servants are in. Master, take away the terrible suffering of Tulsidas, and keep your own promise — that you love whoever comes to you for shelter.

Day and night I have danced and danced, and died dancing! Hari, ever since you gave me the name "soul", it has never once come to rest.
In this dance of maya (the world's illusion) I have put on all kinds of costumes of desire and jewels of greed and delusion — among the living and the lifeless, in water, on land and in the sky, what disguise have I not worn!
Gods, demons, sages, serpents, human beings — is there anyone left to whom I have not held out my hands? And not one of them took away my terrible poverty, my faults and my sorrows.
My eyes, my feet, my hands, my good sense and my strength are all worn out. Every companion has parted from me. Now, Lord of the Raghus, this servant, shaken and frightened by the fear of this world, has come to you for shelter.
Lord! Those qualities that win you over and make you glad — I have forgotten them all. Now, my Lord, just let this Tulsidas lie at your door.

Madhav! There is no one as foolish as I am. The fish and the moth are dull creatures, yet even they cannot match me.
The moth, drawn by the lovely light, did not know the lamp was fire, and the fish, drawn by the food, did not know the iron was a hook; but I see plainly that the pleasures of the world are nothing but trouble, and still I will not let them go. (So I am a bigger fool than they are.)
I go on drifting in the endless river of great delusion. To get across it there is the boat of Shri Hari's lotus feet, and I leave that and grab at the foam again and again — at pleasures that break in a moment.
It is like a starving dog that takes an old dry bone in its mouth, and when the rubbing cuts the roof of its mouth it licks the blood that comes and is greatly satisfied. (It never understands that the blood is from its own body. That is exactly my state.)
I am terribly afraid of the bite of this worldly life, that deadliest of snakes — but (such is my foolishness that) instead of taking shelter with the Lord who rides Garuda, I look for safety in the shelter of a frog, the pleasures of the senses.
It is like shoals of water creatures that get herded together into a net and, out of greed, eat one another, never seeing the death that is coming for them all. (That is exactly my state.)
If Saraswati went on counting my sins for age after age, even she could not reach the end of them. And still my heart holds this one trust: that my Lord makes the fallen pure (so he will surely take even a fallen man like me as his own).

Shri Ram! Where have you forgotten that mercy of yours, the mercy that used to make you leave your own home and come running the moment the sad cry of a helpless person reached your ears?
When Gajendra the elephant looked at his own strength, accepted defeat in his heart and fixed his mind on your feet, you heard his cry of pain and left Garuda behind and reached him at once — you did not delay for a moment.
Prahlad lived in fear of Hiranyakashipu day and night, and you kept the promise he had made: you took a body that was part mighty lion and part man, and killed that demon. The Vedas are witness to this.
When Draupadi, the wife of Arjun (who was Nar come down to earth), saw her honour being taken from her and cried out in the royal court before all those kings, "Lord, save me!" — then, enemy of the demons, you showed her great mercy there: you piled up heaps of cloth to save her honour, and ground the pride of her enemies to dust.
Lord of the Raghus! Every one of these devotees you saved was being tormented by a single enemy. But here I am being given unbearable pain by many enemies at once. Why do you not take away this pain of worldly life from me?
Greed is my crocodile, anger is my Hiranyakashipu the demon king, and wicked lust is my Dushasan, the brother of Duryodhan — all of them are giving Tulsidas terrible suffering. Generous Ramchandra, destroy this terrible suffering of mine.

Hari! Why have you forgotten me? Lord, you know both your own greatness and my sins — then why do you not take care of me?
You make the fallen pure, you are the friend of the helpless, you give shelter to those who have no shelter — so say the four Vedas. Then am I not low, am I not frightened, am I not helpless? Or is this declaration of the Vedas simply false?
Once you seated me in the same row as a bird (the vulture Jatayu), a courtesan (Jivanti), an elephant and a hunter (Valmiki) — that is, you accepted me even as a sinner. Now, treasury of mercy, whom are you ashamed of, that you are tearing up the leaf-plate you had already served me on?
If this age of Kali were stronger than you and did not obey your orders, then, Hari, we would leave off trusting you and singing your virtues, we would drop all the bother of being angry with Kali and blaming it, and we would worship Kali instead.
But you can make an ordinary mosquito into a Brahma and a Brahma into a mosquito — such is your power. And having this power, you are still letting me go; then, Lord, what is left in my hands?
I have lost in every way, and I am not even afraid of falling into hell; but this is the greatest grief of Tulsidas — that even my Lord's name has not burnt up my sins.

Shri Ram! If Yamraj, the lord of death, dropped all his other work and thought about nothing but the accounts of my sins and faults, even then he would not be able to count them (because my sins have no limit).
(And while he is tangled up in my account,) whole crowds of sinners will slip away and run off, and that will worry him greatly. Seeing his own authority damaged because of me, he will praise me to you in the highest terms (to prove himself blameless in the Lord's court) — he will say that Tulsidas is your devotee, that he has committed no sin, and that by the power of worshipping you he has even freed other sinners from the bonds of sin.
Then you will smile and believe your devotee Yamraj, and you will take me for the finest of your devotees. The truth is, Lord of Kosala, one way or another you will have to take me as your own.

Lord! If you pay attention to the faults of this servant, then how will the great forests of my sins ever be cut down by the little nail of my merit? (How will my tiny store of good undo such heavy sin?)
Who could even describe the sins I have done in thought, word and body? Many a Shesh, many a Saraswati and all the Vedas would give up trying to add up the sins of a single moment.
(There is no hope of being saved from my sins on the strength of my merits.) But if the greatness of your own name and your own quality of making the fallen pure ever come to your mind, then you will surely break the teeth of the messengers of death and carry this Tulsidas across the ocean of this world, just as you carried across the brahmin Ajamil.

(You do not pay attention to the faults of your servants.) Ram! If you kept the faults of your servants in mind, why would you stubbornly take on the enmity of Indra, Duryodhan and Bali?
If you did not set aside chanting, sacrifice, yoga and vows and want love alone, why would you leave the gods and the great sages and go and live in the cowherds' homes in Vraj?
If you did not keep your devotees' promises wherever they were made, and did not praise the power of worship, how would fools like us ever get through the hard road of duty in this age of Kali?
Destroyer of trouble! If you had not burnt up the endless sins of Ajamil, who spoke the name Narayan only because he was calling his son, then the messengers of death would have hunted out bullocks like us and yoked us to the plough.
And if you had not put on this dress that the whole world knows — the one who makes the fallen pure — then wicked people like Tulsi would never have had a share in freedom, not even in a dream, for ages upon ages.

Shri Hari loves his servant so much that he forgets all his own greatness and puts himself under that devotee's control. This way of his has been so from the beginning of time.
The Supreme Being who has tied gods, demons, serpents and human beings in the strong rope of their deeds — that same unbroken Supreme Brahman was tied by Yashoda, out of love, by force, to a grinding mortar, and tied so well that he could not get free of it himself.
Brahma and Lord Shiva, caught in his maya, danced and danced and never found the end of him — and the cowherd women made that same one dance in their courtyard while they clapped out the beat.
It is a well-known teaching of the Vedas that the Lord feeds and sustains the whole universe, that he is the husband of Lakshmi and the master of all three worlds; and yet not a bit of the greatness of such a Lord worked before his devotee King Bali — out of love he had to become a brahmin and beg from him.
Just remembering his name frees souls from the heavy burden of birth and death in this world — and that same treasury of mercy took birth ten times over himself for the sake of his devotee Ambarish.
The one whom the self-controlled sages go on searching for through yoga, detachment, meditation, chanting and penance — that same Lord gave his love to monkeys and bears, lowly restless animals.
The guardians of the worlds, Yamraj, Time, the wind, the sun and the moon all obey his orders — and that same Lord, out of love, stands with a stick in his hand at Ugrasen's door like a gatekeeper.

It is Shri Ram's own way to lift up the poor and make them glad. The Vedas, the Puranas, Lord Shiva and Shukdev all sing of this. And the power of his name, the name of Ram, is there for anyone to see.
Dhruv, Prahlad, Vibhishan, Sugriv, a lifeless stone (Ahalya), birds (Jatayu and Kakbhushundi), the five Pandavas and Sudama — to every one of them the Lord gave beautiful fame in this world and a good destiny in the next. And which of them had ever been of any use to Ram?
The courtesan (Jivanti), the Kol and Kirat tribals (Guha the boatman and his people), and Valmiki, the first poet — who was worse than these? When did Ajamil ever perform a horse sacrifice? When did the great elephant Gajendra ever chant the Sama Veda?
Who is more of a cheat than Tulsi, more soiled, more empty of every spiritual practice, more thin and weak? But in the kingdom of that king who is the name of Ram, such is his mighty splendour that age after age even a coin of leather passes as money — meaning that by the power of the name even the lowest of the low have reached the Supreme Lord, and so will I.

Hear the gentle nature of Ram, the Lord of Sita — and if a man's heart does not fill with joy at it, if his body does not thrill, if his eyes do not fill with tears of love, then let that wretch go on swallowing dust; it serves him right.
From his childhood his father, his mother, his brothers, his guru, his servants, his ministers and his friends have all said the same thing: not one of us has ever, even in a dream, seen anger on the moon-like face of Shri Ramchandra.
His three brothers and the other boys of the city played with him, and he always saw their unfairness and how they cheated him — yet even when he had won he would accept defeat, just to make them happy, and he would coax them lovingly and give away his turn to them, and have others give away their turns too.
The moment his foot touched her, Ahalya the stone slab was freed from the burning of her curse, and he gave her a blessed destiny. But his heart felt no pride in it at all — instead he was truly sorry, thinking: why did my foot have to touch the wife of a sage?
He broke Shiva's bow and took away the pride of the kings. When Parashuram came raging at him for it, he forgave the offence and, more than that, made Lakshman ask his pardon, and he himself fell at Parashuram's feet. Such patience is not to be found anywhere else!
King Dasharath promised him the throne and then, ruled by Kaikeyi, sent him to the forest instead — and died of the shame of it. Yet even that cruel mother Kaikeyi you cared for as tenderly as a man watches over a wound in the softest part of his own body; that is, you always went along with what her heart wanted.
When Hanuman's service so overcame you that you felt yourself in his debt, you said to him: "Son of the Wind, come here. I have nothing at all to give you. I am your debtor, you are my creditor — if you like, have me sign a bond for it."
Sugriv and Vibhishan did not give up their own hidden double-dealing, yet you took them as your own. As for Bharat, you honour him always in the full assembly, and your heart is never satisfied, however long you go on praising him.
Whenever there is talk of the kindnesses and favours you have shown your devotees, you almost sink into the ground with embarrassment — praise of yourself is simply not to your taste. But let a man bow to you even once and come to you for shelter, and you keep telling his story, listening to it, and having others sing it too.
Turning over and over in my mind the many virtues of Shri Ram, who has such a tender heart, my heart has flooded with love. Tulsidas, with this joy of love you will reach the lotus feet of Shri Ram without any effort at all.

Lord, where can I go if I leave your feet? Who else in this world is called "the purifier of the fallen"? To whom else are the poor and the suffering so dear as they are to you?
To this day, which god has kept his word so stubbornly that he went looking for the lowest people, one by one, just to lift them up? Which god has saved a bird (Jatayu), animals (bears and monkeys), a hunter (Valmiki), a stone (Ahalya), unfeeling trees (the twin Arjun trees) and foreigners?
Gods, demons, sages, serpents, human beings — every poor one of them is caught in maya (the world's illusion). A man in chains cannot unlock anyone else's chains. So, Lord, what would this Tulsidas gain by handing himself over to them?

Lord Hari, you have been so kind: out of pure grace you gave me this human body, so hard to get that even the gods long for it, the one body in which anything can be achieved.
Not even a crore of mouths could tell of a single one of your kindnesses; and yet, Lord, I am asking for something more. You are so generous — be kind and give it to me.
My mind is a fish that will not leave the water of the senses even for a moment, and I am bearing terrible suffering because of it — again and again I have to be born, in body after body.
So, Ram, make your grace the fishing line, and make the mark on your own foot, the goad, the hook at the end of it, and stick on it the soft bait of the highest love. Then hook this fish of my mind, pull it out of that water of the senses, and take away my sorrow. For you it will be nothing but a game.
The Vedas are full of remedies, and there are gods beyond counting — but how many doors should this poor man go begging at? Tulsidas, the one who tied this soul in the rope of delusion is the very one who will set it free.

Lord Raghunath, my master, this is my one request: this soul puts its hope, its faith and its trust in other practices, other gods, other deeds — take that foolishness away from me.
Ram, I do not want a good rebirth, or a fine mind, or wealth, or powers and perfections, or any great reputation. All I want is that my love for your lotus feet grows day by day — a love that is pure and turns to no one else. That is all I ask.
Wherever my bad deeds drag me by force, into whatever kind of birth, there too, my Lord, do not let go of your grace for even a moment — just as a turtle never abandons her eggs.
Lord, all the love and trust and attachment that this body has in this world — to wife, to children, to family — let it all gather into one place and be for you alone.

I will give myself away entirely to Raghunath, the life of Janaki. My heart says this: now I will never leave the feet of Sita and Ram and go anywhere else.
Such certainty has come into my heart: turn my face away from the feet of my master Shri Ram, and I will not find happiness anywhere, not even in a dream. So this is what I will teach my mind, and everything that lives in this body — the senses and all the rest.
My ears will listen to nothing else, my tongue will talk of no one else, I will stop my eyes from looking elsewhere, and I will bow this head to the Lord alone.
Now I have tied myself to my Lord in love, and I will cut every other tie and every other love. In this world I, Tulsidas, will be called the servant of one master — and the whole weight of all my deeds will rest on that master too.

Until now my life has been wasted, but I will not let it be wasted any more. By the grace of Shri Ram the long night of worldly life is over, I have woken from the sleep of maya — and now that I am awake, I will not spread out that bedding again; I will not be caught in maya's snare a second time.
I have found the beautiful wish-granting jewel that is the name of Ram, and I will never let it slip from the hand of my heart — I will keep remembering Ram's name in my heart, and telling the beads of his name with my hand. The pure, dark, lovely form of Raghunath — I will make that my touchstone and rub the gold of my mind against it, to see whether my mind really stays fixed on Ram at all times or not.
As long as I was in the grip of my senses they made a fool of me, making me dance to their tune. But now I am free — I have won over my mind and my senses — and I will not let them make a joke of me again. Now I take a vow and set the bee of my mind on the lotus feet of Shri Ram: I will not let my mind go anywhere except to his feet.

Blessed is the one whom the great king Shri Ramchandra has honoured. He alone is great, a treasury of virtues, all-knowing, full of merit, brave, gentle and holy — no one is his equal.
Ahalya the stone, the Nishad, the monkeys, the bears, the demons, Shabari, Jatayu — all of them were completely without calmness, self-control, mercy, generosity or any such quality. But because they remembered the name of Ram, Shri Ram made them so utterly pure that today people cross the ocean of this world simply by singing their praises.
Valmiki the hunter — was there any sin he had left undone? When had Pingala the prostitute ever turned her mind to devotion? What Soma sacrifice had the sinner Ajamil ever performed? And where would Gajendra the elephant have performed a horse sacrifice?
Where was even a trace of purity in the Pandavas, the gopis, Vidur and Kubja? Yet you made every one of them pure; seeing their love, you in your form as Shri Krishna took them as your own, and today their lovely fame spreads through the world like the fame of Vishnu and Shiva.
Among the Kols, the Khasas, the Bhils, the foreigners and all such outcast people, is there one who has spoken the name of Ram and not risen, low as he was, to the very highest place? The Vedas have sung the glory of Shri Ram, who destroys the sorrow of the poor, the husband of Lakshmi, the temple of compassion, the one who makes the fallen pure.
Never mind anyone else — in all three worlds and all three ages there has been no one as dull-witted, as crooked, as thoroughly wicked as Tulsi. Yet to keep the honour of his own name, remembering his own vow to save the fallen, Shri Ram took even this man, bitten by the snake of the dark age of Kali, into his shelter.

Shri Ramchandra, the king of Kosala, is my highest God. His eyes are as lovely as lotus flowers, and his body is the most beautiful dark blue.
He is always radiant with Sita beside him; his beauty is that of countless Kamadevs. In his long arms he holds a bow and arrows, and at his waist he wears a fine quiver.
He wants no offering and no ritual worship — he wants one thing only: love. Remember him and he is pleased at once, and he makes you pure in every way.
He gives every happiness and burns every sorrow to ash. He is the friend of those in pain; he takes hold of our good qualities and takes away our bad ones — such an ocean of compassion is he.
In every land and at every time he is always complete and present; so the Vedas and Puranas say. He is the master of all, he lives in all, and he knows what is in every heart.
Who would leave such a master and worship one god after another for a crore of little wishes? Tulsidas, serve the one whom even Mahadev, the God of gods, serves.

Worship the great hero Raghunath, for whoever reaches him has everything he could reach. He fulfils every wish — everyone knows this.
Do this quickly; there is no sense in delaying. Take the teaching from a true guru and repeat the seed mantra "Ram", the very name that Lord Shiva repeats.
Here is how to make the offering: pour out the water of love, make the clarified butter out of simple, natural affection, burn the firewood of doubt in the fire of forgiveness, and sacrifice your sense of "mine".
Drive out your sins, bring your mind under control, kill off your pride and your lust, and draw to yourself the happiness and wealth that are contentment and true understanding. Whoever has worshipped this way has found Raghunath. Tulsidas too has set out on this road, and the Lord will see him through to the end.

Lord Hari, Murari, you are the one who takes sorrow away — then why do you not have mercy on me? You destroy the three kinds of burning — of the body, of fate, of the world around us — and doubt, grief, ignorance and fear as well. Then destroy my sorrow and my burning and my ignorance too.
On one side the sins born of this dark age of Kali have dulled my mind and dirtied my heart; and on top of that, Master, you do not look after me either. How is this servant of yours to get through his life?
Lord, you can do anything, and I can do nothing at all. You know this, and still you do not show me kindness — so it seems that I am simply unlucky.
Raghunath, I have wandered through birth after birth, but I have no master except you. Through pain and through pleasure, I have always taken shelter with you.
In my heart I understand this very well: there is no god as merciful as you. But, Lord Hari, this Tulsidas has nothing with which to please you — no practice, no merit. You will have to be pleased with nothing but my surrender.

Treasure of compassion, if not to you, then to whom should I cry about this heavy misery that the world has given me? My senses cling to the things they crave and are wild with wanting them.
They are forever tangled in comfort and wealth, in heaven and hell — but, Lord Hari, this wretched mind of mine has left you and joined their side as well.
God, I am poor and miserable. I heard how merciful your name is, and I set my heart on you. And after that, Raghuvir, steadfast one, if you show me no kindness, how can I not be in pain?
Certainly I am a house full of sins — but you, Murari, are the one who wipes out sorrow without weighing the offence. This is the hope I, Tulsidas, always hold on to, because you have already saved so many fallen and guilty people; surely now you will save me too.

Keshav, what can I say? Nothing can be said. Lord Hari, I look at this strange creation of yours, and all I can do is understand in my own heart that it is your play.
What an astonishing play it is: this picture of a world, painted by a painter with no form at all, painted on a wall of empty air, and painted without any colour — made by a mere thought. An ordinary picture washes away, but this one will not wash off no matter what you do. An ordinary picture is lifeless and has no fear of death, but this one is always afraid of dying. An ordinary picture is a pleasure to look at, but look at this terrible picture of a world and it brings you pain.
In the water that seems to shimmer in the sun's rays there lives a frightening crocodile. That crocodile has no mouth, yet whatever goes there to drink, living or lifeless, it swallows whole. The meaning is this: the world is like water in the sun's rays, made of nothing but a mistake. Just as the deer that runs after that shimmer finds no water and dies of thirst, so those who run after this deceiving world thinking it will make them happy are eaten by the mouthless crocodile — by formless Time itself.
Some call this world real, some call it false, and some say it is a mixture of the two. Tulsidas says all three are mistakes, and whoever is free of all three — whoever sees that everything is the Lord's play — is the one who can recognise who he truly is.

Keshav, my master, what is the reason, what is the offence, that made you decide I am worthless and drop me like a stranger you never knew?
If you think I am worthless, and if you only take to yourself those whose conduct is spotless and whose hearts are tender and saintly, then why did you save Ajamil, and Valmiki, and the courtesan? Were they some special relatives of yours?
Lord Hari, this soul's time, its deeds, its good destiny and its bad destiny are all in your hands alone. So, my Lord, destroy this sense of "mine" in me and find some way to keep me from forgetting you and wandering here and there.
Even if you let me go, I will still worship only you; I will never accept anyone else as my Lord. That is my unshakeable vow. Whether you send me to hell or to heaven, Raghunath, there too I will go on praying to you in thought, word and deed.
Lord, I know it is not right for me to be so bold with my master — but day and night this Tulsidas sees how hard you are with him, and it hurts him so much that he had to speak this way.

Madhav, why do you still not show me mercy? Your vow is to protect whoever comes to you for shelter, and my vow is to live only by gazing again and again at your lotus feet. When I cannot even hold on to life without seeing your feet, then why, protector of those who bow to you, do you not have mercy on me?
Before I was the poor one and you the merciful one, before I was the servant and you the master, I bore my sorrows without telling you about them — though as the one who lives in every heart, you knew them all.
But now you and I are related. You are the giver and I am the beggar; you make the fallen pure and I am the fallen one — the Vedas sing of this. Raghunath, you and I are tied together in so many ways; how then can you possibly abandon me?
You are my father, my mother, my guru, my brother, my friend, my master, my well-wisher in every way. So think of some way to keep me from falling into that dark well of seeing two where there is one — let me see only you everywhere and stay drowned in the highest joy.
Lotus-eyed Lord, listen: your boundless compassion is what frees us from the great fear of this ocean of birth and death. Lord, the darkness of Tulsidas's ignorance cannot be lifted by anything at all except the light of your knowledge, except the sight of you. So you are the one who must take it away.

Madhav, there is no one else in this world like me — empty of every good practice, full of sin, utterly wretched, and drowning in the pleasures of the senses.
And there is no other master like you — one who is kind for no reason at all, who gives up everything for the good of the poor and the suffering. For it is only to take away the sorrows of the helpless that you leave Vaikunth, leave your form of pure being and awareness and bliss, and come down to this earth in a human body. What greater giving up than that could there be? And even so I am shaking with grief and sorrow. Merciful one, what is the reason you feel no pity for me?
I accept that none of this is your fault; the whole offence is mine. You gave me this human body, this storehouse of understanding, and even after receiving it I have not, to this day, recognised a Lord like you.
The bamboo blames the sandal tree and the thorny karil bush blames the spring, but they blame them for nothing. The truth is that both are simply unlucky. There is no heartwood in bamboo, so how is the poor sandal tree to fill it with fragrance? The karil has no leaves, so how is the spring to make it green? In the same way, how can I, with no wisdom and no devotion, put the blame on you?
Lord Hari, I am hard in every way, and you are soft by nature. I have thought it through and settled it in my mind: my Lord, the iron chain of delusion around this Tulsidas will only fall away if you unlock it — otherwise never.

Madhav, how will this noose of delusion around me ever break? You may do a crore of outward practices, and still the knot inside, the knot of ignorance, will not come loose.
Look at the moon's reflection in a pan full of ghee: as long as the ghee is there, you may pile on firewood and light the fire and boil it for a hundred ages, and still the reflection will not be destroyed. In the same way, as long as delusion remains, this noose of coming and going will remain.
If a bird is living in the hollow of a tree, cutting down the tree will not kill it. In the same way, however many outward practices you perform, without true understanding this mind will never become pure and steady.
Beat the ground above a snake's hole in every way you can, and try every other trick from outside, and still the snake inside will not die. In the same way, you may scrub and scrub your body clean, and the mind that the senses have dirtied will never be pure within.
Tulsidas, without the mercy of the Lord and of the guru there is no clear understanding free of doubt — and without that understanding no one can cross this terrible ocean of the world.

Madhav, this maya of yours is so hard to cross that a man may wear himself out trying one way after another and die of it; until you show mercy, getting past it is simply impossible.
I listen, I think it over, I understand it, and I explain it to others — but the real secret of this maya of yours I cannot grasp. And until I truly taste that secret for myself, the great miseries of this world born of delusion will keep on hurting me.
The nectar of God is so sweet, so full of peace. If the mind could once taste that nectar somewhere, why would it go on wandering day and night after the lying mirage of the senses?
If a man has a flawless wish-granting jewel at home, why would he go around collecting bits of glass? Once a man has found the joy of God, why would he even glance at the pleasures of maya? It is like a man in a dream who falls into someone's power and begs him to let him go — but once he wakes, what is there to beg for, and from whom?
There are many practices — knowledge, devotion and the rest — and all of them are true; not one of them is false. But the one thing Tulsidas's heart trusts is this: ignorance can be destroyed only by the grace of Shri Hari. Grace is the highest practice of all, and it is already there for every soul — all we have to do is trust it completely.

Lord Hari, how can I blame you? The whole fault is mine. The things I do all day and all night are the very things by which freedom could never come, not even in a dream.
I know that the pleasures of the senses only bring ruin, that getting caught in them means falling into a dark well of ignorance — and still I cling to them and run after them like a dog, a goat or a donkey.
In my ignorance I do harm to other living beings and never think of my own good. Pride, envy, arrogance — the enemies of true understanding — are the very things I am always soaked and steeped in. Tell me, who is lower than a man like me?
In the Vedas and the Puranas I hear and I understand that Shri Ram lives and moves through the whole world — but this will not go into my foolish, sinful mind, just as the fragrance of sandal will not enter hollow bamboo that has no heartwood in it.
You who are the mine of compassion, I am an endless ocean of offences — and you live in every heart and know it all. So, rider of Garuda, this Tulsidas, bitten by the snake of worldly life, has fallen at your feet for shelter. Save him: one look at your mount Garuda and this snake of a world will flee in terror. Just come this way, once.

O Hari! How can I call myself happy? What I do is like an elephant's show-tusks, and You know this perfectly well. The meaning is this: just as an elephant has one set of tusks to display and another set to eat with, so I too show one thing and do something else entirely.
If I would only do myself what I tell others to do, I would cross this ocean of the world as easily as stepping over a puddle no deeper than a calf's hoof. But what can I do? My conduct is one thing and my talk is another. How then can I ever reach the joy of Your feet, or the highest state?
The peacock is lovely to look at, and it speaks in a sweet voice, as if its words were soaked in nectar; but its food is the poisonous snake! How hard-hearted it is! It does one thing and says another. (That is exactly my condition.)
O Raghuvir! The holy ones You love are those who love every living being, who never burn with envy at the sight of anyone, who are in love with Your lotus feet, whose minds are steady and calm, and who have completely let go of the difference between "mine" and "another's" — that is, they see only You in everyone. (Then how can I, who lack all these qualities, be dear to You?)
O Raghunath! It is true that I have endless faults and that I deserve nothing better than to stay in this world. But You are the treasure-house of compassion — so look for a moment at Your own goodness instead, and have mercy on Tulsidas!

O Hari! By what means will this delusion of mine be removed — this habit of taking the world as real, as forever pure, as a place of happiness? I see, I hear, I think it over, and still this mind of mine will not give up its old nature. (Believing the world to be real and full of joy, it falls again and again into the tangle of the senses.)
Devotion, knowledge, detachment and all the other practices are ways to quiet this mind. But this craving never leaves my heart: "Let someone call me good," or "Let someone give me something." (Even in the hearts of those who practise knowledge, devotion and detachment, the hunger for praise, wealth and honour usually stays alive.)
In that night — the night that is this world — all beings lie asleep, and only the one You have blessed stays awake. But when I look at my own doings and see they are the exact opposite, a heavy fear comes over me.
It is true that by fate, by the weight of past deeds, all a man's hopes are ruined, and worldly happiness was never written into his lot (because he did no good deeds before). Even so, by simply wishing for pleasures he suffers — like a painter with no hands who wants to serve his own ends with pictures that exist only in his mind, and gets nothing but the pain of broken hopes. (In the same way I want happiness without ever doing the good work of worship and practice.)
Hearing Your name Hrishikesh (Master of the senses), I would give my life for You. My heart trusts You completely. You simply must destroy the suffering that the senses bring to Tulsidas.

O Hari! Why do You not remove this heavy delusion of mine — this taking of the world as real and as a place of joy? This world is false, it has no true being, yet until Your grace comes it goes on looking exactly like the truth.
I know that these things — body, wealth, sons and the rest — are not real. And yet, my Lord, even knowing this I do not get free of the world. No one else has tied me: by my own stubborn attachment I am bound and helpless, like a parrot on a perch. (I have tied myself with my own ignorance.)
Imagine a man who in a dream catches all kinds of diseases, so bad that death itself seems to be coming, and outside doctors keep trying one remedy after another — but until he wakes up, his pain does not end. (In the same way, people caught in the delusion of maya (the world's illusion) suffer endless pain and try false remedies to cure it; but without true knowledge there is no escape from that pain.)
The Vedas, the guru, the saints and the scriptures all say with one voice that this visible world has no true being, and that once you imagine it to be real it becomes nothing but sorrow. Until a person lets it go and worships Shri Raghunath, who has the power to destroy this misery?
In their clear words the Vedas point out many ways to cross the ocean of this world; but O Tulsidas, until "I" and "mine" are gone — until pride and possessiveness are wiped out — no soul can ever find happiness.

O Hari! It is delusion, and nothing but too much of it, that even after seeing, hearing, speaking and understanding, the false belief does not leave me — taking an unreal world for real — nor does the doubt go away, the doubt of whether the one Supreme Being alone truly is, or whether there is something else besides.
(Someone may ask:) If the world is unreal, then why do we feel the three kinds of suffering? (If the world is unreal, its sufferings must be unreal too; yet the suffering certainly feels real.) (The answer is this:) The water of a mirage cannot be called real, but as long as the illusion lasts it looks completely real, and that very illusion causes real distress. In the same way, in this world it is delusion that makes us feel pain.
Think of a man asleep on a beautiful bed who dreams he is drowning in the sea and is terrified. Until he wakes up himself, ten million boats cannot carry him across. In the same way this soul, senseless in the sleep of ignorance, is drowning in the ocean of the world; without waking into the true knowledge of the Supreme Being, not even a thousand practices can free it from pain.
This world is terrifying, and only ignorance makes it look charming. Of course, the world can be a happy place for those who live with balance, contentment, compassion and clear judgement. O Tulsidas, the Vedas are saying it: this whole worldly show is unreal in every way, but without devotion to Raghunath and the company of holy people, who has the strength to destroy the dreadful fear of this world and set us free from this delusion?

O Hari! I never learned how to practise the cure for my ignorance. The disease was one thing and the medicine I took was another. What fault is that of the treatment?
Suppose a king in a dream is stained with the sin of killing a brahmin, and wanders here and there in torment because of that terrible crime. Until he wakes, a hundred million horse-sacrifices will not make him clean. In the same way, without true knowledge there is no release from the sins that ignorance breeds.
Out of ignorance a garland can look like a huge, terrifying snake; and (until that false snake-illusion goes) a man may strike at it with every weapon he has, with all his strength, until he is worn out, and still it will not die — if it were really a snake, weapons would have killed it. In the same way, this world that ignorance makes us see is not destroyed by outward practices, only by knowledge.
By his own delusion a man sees an ocean made out of sunlight — a mirage — and it looks utterly terrifying; and a man drowning in that false sea cannot get across by climbing into any real ship or boat. Exactly this is the case with the ocean of the world, which ignorance has produced.
Tulsidas says: until the world is uprooted completely, along with the sense of "I", then brothers, you may make ten million efforts and die trying, but you will never get across this ocean of the world.

O Raghunath! This much I have begun to understand: O Merciful One, O well-wisher of Your servants, without Your grace neither can delusion be removed nor can maya (the world's illusion) let go of me.
At night, just talking about a lamp in the house does not drive out the darkness. In the same way, however skilled a person may be at knowledge that is only words, he cannot cross the ocean of the world.
Imagine a poor, wretched man suffering the pangs of hunger because he has no food, and someone tries to end his misery by drawing pictures of the wish-fulfilling tree and the wish-fulfilling cow all over his house — that misery will never end. In just the same way, talk about the scriptures alone does not put an end to delusion.
A man may lecture day and night about all kinds of dishes with all six flavours; yet the happiness of a hunger that is actually satisfied by eating is known only to the one who said nothing at all and simply ate. (In the same way, dry lecturing achieves nothing; the work is accomplished by doing.)
Until the light of true knowledge shines in your own heart, and while the hope of sense-pleasures still lives in your mind, O Tulsidas, you will have to keep wandering through the births of this world, and happiness will not come to you even in a dream.

If our mind would let go of its disorders, then where would the sorrow of this world be, born of seeing two where there is one, and where would the delusion and the endless grief be? (All of this comes from the mind's own disorders.)
Enemy, friend, and the one who is neither — the mind alone has stubbornly invented all three. An enemy should be dropped like a snake, a friend should be grasped like gold, and the one who is neither should be ignored like a blade of grass. These are all nothing but ideas of the mind.
Just as food, clothes, cattle and all kinds of goods are held inside a precious jewel, so heaven, hell, all that moves and all that does not, and many worlds besides, are held inside this mind. The meaning is that with the price of one small jewel you can buy whatever you like to eat, to drink, to wear; in the same way, by the power of this mind a soul can travel to heaven, to hell and everywhere else.
Just as the puppet is already inside the wood and the cloth is already inside the thread, always there without anyone making them, so in this mind too all kinds of bodies lie hidden, and in their own time they appear.
When will the disorders of this mind be gone? When the heart is washed clean by the water of devotion to Shri Raghunath — then the Supreme Being, who alone is real, will be seen without any effort. But Tulsidas says: the truth of this world, which is the play of pure consciousness, will be understood only by going on trying to understand the Supreme Being.

O Raghunath! O patient One, who does good for me without ever growing tired of it — if I leave You, to whom else can I tell my terrible trouble?
O Lord! My heart is Your dwelling place, but these days a whole crowd of thieves has come and settled in it! Thieves have made their home in Your temple.
(I want to throw them out, but they are very hard-hearted.) They keep bullying me all the time. They pay no attention at all to my pleading and begging.
The chief of these thieves are seven: ignorance, delusion, greed, pride, arrogance, anger, and lust, the enemy of wisdom.
O Lord! They are causing havoc; they see that I have no one to protect me, and they trample me down.
I am alone and these rioting thieves are past counting. Not one person listens even to my cry.
O Lord! Even if I run away it is hard to be rid of them, because they come right after me. Now, Raghunath, You alone must protect me.
Tulsidas says: O Ram, what do I lose by this? It is Your own house that the thieves are robbing.
What worries me so much is this — that Your name should not be disgraced. (Even though I am called Your devotee, if robbers like lust and anger carry off the pure jewels of my heart, the disgrace will be Yours. So please look after this house of Yours Yourself.)

O my mind! If you want the power of God in your heart, then take my advice.
Remember the countless kindnesses God has done for you, from your time in the womb until now, and let go of your pride; serve Him carefully, with your whole attention.
Treat pleasure and pain, honour and insult, all the same; only then will your trouble end.
You wretch! Death has already taken hold of this body — do not blame anyone else for that.
Tulsidas says: without this understanding, Shri Ram is never found by putting on a false show of meditation; He is found only through true love.

I have realised that I have no love for the feet of Shri Hari; for not even in a dream does detachment rise in my mind. (Losing the taste for worldly pleasures is the very test of whether there is love for God's feet.)
Those who love the feet of Shri Ram have thrown away all sense-pleasures the way one throws away a disease.
Only when a person is bitten by the snake of lust does the bitter neem of sense-pleasure stop tasting bitter to him.
Thinking about this, my heart is in great confusion: what should I do? This very thought keeps adding fresh worry to my mind every day.
O Tulsidas! There is no other way; whenever this sorrow ends, it will end by the grace of Shri Ram alone.

O mind! Remember Ram, the beloved of Janaki, and remember Him with love. For apart from the feet of Shri Ramchandra, there is no refuge for you anywhere.
Chanting, austerity, pilgrimage, the practice of yoga, deep meditation — these are all methods; but in this age of Kali the minds of people are unsteady, and so not one of these methods has been left free of obstacles.
Today even good deeds do not destroy sins (because the mind is not in its right place). Like the demon Raktabij, these sins only keep multiplying. The meaning is that a confused mind takes sin for merit and merit for sin, and so even doing good deeds, it is sin that keeps growing.
O Tulsidas! This army of demons that is our sin will be destroyed only by Kalika in the form of the Lord's grace. (Now nothing but taking shelter in God's mercy will do the work.)

O lovely tongue! Why do you not say "Ram, Ram" over and over? For by remembering Ram's name, happiness and merit increase and sin and misfortune fall away.
By remembering Ram's name, without the least effort, the net of the bitter and terrible sins of this age of Kali is cut away, just as the mass of darkness is torn apart when the sun rises.
To leave Ram's name and take up yoga, sacrifice, chanting, austerity, detachment and pilgrimage is like twisting a rope out of grains of dust to tie down the great elephant that is this world; that is, just as it is impossible to tie an elephant with a rope of dust, it is impossible for the mind to settle in God through practices that have no Ram's name in them.
You have dropped the beautiful wish-fulfilling jewel that is Ram's name, and now you are eyeing the little red beads of sense-pleasure and craving them. It is this cheap greed of yours that makes Tulsi scold you.

The chanting of Ram's name brings the dawn of blessing and joy, and the sins and tricks and deceits of this age of Kali are wiped from sight.
Who has ever sown a thorn-tree seed and harvested mangoes? So do not waste this human birth, so hard to get, in idle chatter. (Idle chatter leads only to ruin; so chant Ram's name — that is where your good lies.)
Time, past deeds, the three qualities (goodness, passion and darkness) and one's own nature rule over every head — that is, under their power everyone has to suffer and to act. But the moment the talk of Shri Ram's name and its greatness begins, all of them are crushed; not a trace of their power is left. (So chant Ram's name.)
People are desperate to gain every power without doing anything for it; but when was that ever possible? Yes — the whole heap of this age's trade and goods and wealth gets used up in the city of the Name; that is, by the power of Ram's name the whole pile of Kali's sins is destroyed.
Put your faith and your love in the Name, and your heart becomes steady and perfectly at peace. Ram's name has purified even an enemy like Ravan and a fallen creature like Tulsi.

To have pure, selfless love for the lotus feet of Shri Ramchandra — that is the highest fruit of a life. The moment one takes Ram's name, every duty of dharma becomes easy.
It is true that yoga, sacrifice, discrimination, detachment and many other practices are taught in the Vedas; they sound very sweet and gentle when you hear about them, but they are very bitter and hard when you try to do them.
So, O Tulsidas, listen, and do not knowingly lose yourself in this confusion; just become the servant of that Lord who guards the honour of everyone.

Without loving a beloved like Shri Ram, this soul lives in vain; and this thing you take for happiness — just think for a moment: how much happiness is it really?
Wherever you were born, in whatever kind of body — on earth, in the regions below, in heaven — in each place you longed for some sense-pleasure, and your past deeds gave you exactly that. (But were you ever truly happy anywhere?)
Why are you caught in delusion, absorbed in stitching up a torn sky? The meaning is that just as it is impossible to sew the sky, it is impossible to find joy in the pleasures of the world. So, O Tulsi, if what you want is joy, why do you not sing the beautiful praises of Lord Ramchandra and drink that nectar? (Then you would become deathless, joy itself.)

O soul! Again and again I speak to you words that are good for you, loving, pure and true. You hear them, you turn them over in your mind, you even understand them — so why do you not take the easy and beautiful road? That is, why do you not go to Shri Ram for shelter?
Small or great, false or true, whoever lives wherever in this world — tell me, is there a single one among them who does not want his own good?
From Brahma down to the smallest insect, all are made happy by happiness and burned by sorrow; and like a cowherd with his cattle, the Supreme Being ties up these souls (with ignorance), unties them (with knowledge) and yokes them (to their deeds).
Look at the pleasures of the senses. They are like shifting a load from your head to your shoulder. That is, there is no happiness in sense-pleasure at all; understand this in your mind and accept it. You fool! Why do you keep bearing this pain?
Just think about it: who has ever churned the water of a mirage and got butter from it? That is, how can there be real happiness in the imaginary things of an unreal world? O Tulsi, go and take shelter with that Lord from whom everything is obtained.

O Lord! Knowing this nature of Yours, I lie at Your door and call out to You over and over: O Lord, the moment anyone tells You of his pain, his humility, his helplessness, You take away all his troubles.
When Indra, Kuber and the other guardians of the worlds were terrified of Ravan and torn apart by grief, then, O Merciful One, what was it that You heard, that You should shyly take on a human body?
This much I cannot understand: Vishvamitra, Ahalya and Janak were burning in the fire of anxiety — by what practice of theirs did they become cool again?
Guha the Nishad, the bird Jatayu, Shabari and the rest were not by nature devoted to Your lotus feet; but O Lord, the moment they came before You, even these bad trees bore excellent fruit! The meaning is that even sinners like the Nishad and Shabari crossed over by taking shelter in You.
Sugriv and Vibhishan were being eaten away by terrible sorrow because each had fallen out with his own brother. O Ram, what service of theirs so pleased You that You treated them as equal to Bharat?
Hanuman, by serving You and serving You, became just like You. O Ram, at the mere mention of his name You are completely delighted with everyone.
(Why did all this happen? You did it only because of their pain, their humility, their helplessness.) And so, O Lord, it is only because the world does not know this way of Yours — of what wins Your heart — that it wears itself out and dies among other practices. Whoever learns that You are pleased by the suffering, the humble and the helpless, and takes shelter in You, certainly crosses over; for by dropping all pretence and coming to You for shelter, even a creature like Tulsi crossed the ocean of this world.

Look! He gave you this human body that even the gods long for, and you did not love Him — Shri Ram, who loves you so dearly. He gave you birth in such a good family and a fine body, the very means of wealth, dharma, desire and moksha (freedom). Getting this, wise people reach the highest state of Lord Shiva or of Krishna. And then this land of Bharat, with the divine river Ganga close by — what a beautiful place it is! And good company too, of the best kind. Even after all this, you coward, because of your crooked thinking the wish-fulfilling vine of all these gifts is about to bear poisonous fruit — the fruit of birth and death! That is, having been given such beautiful means, you are misusing them through the fault of your own mind.
Understand even now. Listen with your whole heart to what is said about the highest good. That word brings blessing, and even in this world your own interest is served by it. If it is your own interest that appeals to you, then think: who is the one from whom that interest will be obtained, the one the Vedas sing of? (It is Shri Ram alone.) You wretch, look — stop playing with the snake of sense-pleasure and recognise that Master, for whose sake alone your father, your guru, your master, your body, your son, your servant, your friend all seem dear to you, because He is the Self, Ram, present in everything. You have not recognised that Lord, that highest friend who does good for you asking nothing in return.
That Lord Hari who wishes you well is not far away; He is right inside your heart. If you drop your pretence and remember Him, He keeps pouring out His grace always. The meaning is that the Supreme Being is certainly in the heart, but a curtain of deceit hangs between; that is why He is not seen face to face. Lift the curtain, and the lovely face of the Beloved is there! In His mercy He keeps the shade of His lotus hands over His devotees; He Himself protects them always. Whoever worships Him, He worships in return. He is the Lord of the world, the life of every soul. He who arranges everything for everyone, who gave Vishnu his Vishnu-hood, Brahma his Brahma-hood and Shiva his Shiva-hood — He is this sweet, joyful, blessing-filled form of Raghunath, the Lord of Janaki.
Though He is the greatest of masters and the ruler of all, He is wonderfully gentle, beautiful and simple. Look! The One whom even Shiva finds it hard to meditate upon stood up and pressed the boatman to His heart! And as He embraced him, His eyes filled with tears and His body went soft with love. The gods, the perfected ones, the sages and the poets all say that no one loves love the way Shri Raghunath does; love is dearer to Him than it is to anyone else. He made a bird (Jatayu), Shabari, a demon (Vibhishan), the bears (Jambavan and the others) and the monkeys (Hanuman and the others) more worthy of worship than Himself. (Now look at His gentleness.) Even after all that, whenever He remembers the service those people did for Him, He shrinks inwardly with shyness.
When you take into your heart this gentle nature of Lord Ram that I have described, then all your worries will vanish, and Lord Ramchandra will be glad in His heart too. Why — Shri Raghunath will be pleased the moment you fold your hands and bow your head. Tulsidas! In that very instant you will receive the fruit of your birth and your life; that is, Shri Ram will show Himself to you. Chant the name of Ram, bow to Ram, sing the whole treasury of His qualities, seat Shri Ram in your heart, and make your mind a bee that lives forever at the lotus feet of Shri Ramchandra, the Lord of the universe — then walk this earth with no fear at all.

O soul! From the moment you turned away from God, you began to treat the body as your home. Caught in maya (the world's illusion), you forgot your own true nature — being, awareness and bliss — and because of that one mistake you had to suffer terrible pain. You were handed the hardest, most unbearable sorrows, the round of birth and death. Not a trace of happiness was left to you, not even in dreams. The road ahead was packed with worldly troubles and grief, and still you walked it stubbornly, again and again. You wandered through countless kinds of bodies, you grew old, you bore one disaster after another, and you died. And even after all that — you fool! — you still did not recognise Shri Hari! Stop and think, you blind man: has anyone, anywhere, ever found peace by turning away from Shri Ram?
O soul! Your home is an ocean of joy — joy itself is what you are — so why have you forgotten that and why are you dying of thirst? You take the mirage of sense pleasures to be real water, you believe happiness is there, and you lose yourself in it. You bathe in that mirage and you drink from it; but in the water of that mirage there is not, and never was, and never will be, one drop of real water, one drop of real happiness. You wretch! You forgot the simple, direct experience of what you are, and now here you lie. You have let go of your own pure, deathless, unchanging nature, which is the highest happiness, and you suffer for nothing — like a king who dreams that he has lost his kingdom and been thrown into prison, and grieves for nothing. Even in the dream the king is still the king, but caught in delusion he imagines himself stripped of his kingdom and shut in a cell, and until he wakes he suffers for nothing. In exactly the same way the soul, in its confusion, forgets that it is being, awareness and bliss, believes itself tied down by maya in this world, and is miserable.
You yourself, out of ignorance, twisted the rope of your own deeds tight, and with your own hands you tied the hard knot of ignorance in it. That is why you lie bound and helpless, you unlucky man. And the fruit of it will be the suffering of lying in the womb again. Only the one lying in his mother's belly knows the heap of torments this world holds. In the womb the head is down and the feet are up. In that terrifying hour nobody even asks how you are. Surrounded by blood, filth, urine, waste, worms and slime, you sleep there. And when great pain runs through that tender body, you beat your head and cry.
And there, where the net of your own deeds had closed around you and you were suffering for it, Shri Hari still did not leave your side. In the womb the Lord fed you and kept you alive in a hundred ways, and then the supremely merciful Master gave you knowledge there as well. When Hari gave you knowledge and clear sight, you remembered the events of your many past lives, and you began to say: 'I take refuge in that Supreme Lord whose maya, woven of the three gunas (the three strands that make up all of nature), is so terribly hard to cross. That maya has taken every living being under its power and drained the joy out of their lives, and it puts on a fresh face every single day. May the Lord of Lakshmi, who in this misery of the womb has given me this clear understanding, save me from it now.'
Then, ashamed in every way in your heart that you had never worshipped Him in your past lives, you said that this time, once you were born into the world, you would do nothing but worship the Lord who carries the discus. You had barely fallen silent on that thought when the wind of birth drove you out, sinner that you are, and pushed by that fierce wind you bore every kind of agony as you were born. In that hour, in the fire of that terrible pain, your knowledge, your meditation, your detachment and your insight all burned away — the pain wiped everything from your mind. The agony left you frantic, and you were so weak you could not speak a single word. Nobody had any idea of the cruel suffering you were in; instead everyone around you sang for joy that a son had been born.
Then in childhood the great sufferings you went through were so many that counting them is impossible. Hunger, sickness and one huge trouble after another closed in on you, but your mother never really knew what was wrong. A mother does not know why her baby is crying, so again and again she does the very things that make the burning in your chest worse. (The child cries because his stomach hurts from indigestion, and the mother, thinking he is hungry, feeds him more, and the illness grows.) And as an infant, as a boy, as a young lad, the endless wrongs you did — who could even describe them? You heartless, wicked one! Who but you could bear to carry all of that?
In your youth you were caught in your craving for a young woman, and then you were drunk with ignorance and pride. In that drunkenness of youth you threw away the limits dharma sets, and you forgot every suffering that had come before, in the womb and in your childhood, and you began to sin. You forgot all those past torments. And the disasters waiting ahead of you because of the sins you commit now — does your heart not split open when you think of them? Over and over you did exactly the deeds that drop you back into the pit of the womb and back into the wheel of the world. For a body that will end as worms, ash or dung — buried, it rots into worms; burned, it becomes ash; eaten by animals, it becomes their dung — for that body you made yourself the enemy of the whole world. Another man's wife, another man's money, and hatred of others: these alone grew fresher and stronger in you every day.
Before you knew it old age arrived, which you had never once invited, not even in a dream; and what old age does to a person cannot be told. Look at it now, plainly, in your own body: the body is worn out; sickness and stabbing pain torment you; your head shakes; the strength of your senses is gone. Nobody likes to hear you speak, and even the dog that guards the house treats you with no respect — worse than a dog, in fact. A dog has its bread thrown to it from a distance, but at least it gets it on time; nobody looks after you even that much. What more is there to say — you cannot even get food and water. With old age ruining you like this, does detachment still not come to you? Even in this state you keep letting the waves of craving rise higher.
And these are only a few of the sufferings of one single life of yours; who could tell the whole story of all the many, many lives like it? You have to wander forever through the four kinds of birth — born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat, sprouting from the earth. Even now you will not stop and think! Even now, think it over, let your ignorance go, and worship Lord Shri Ram, who gives joy to his devotees. He is the ship that carries you across the ocean of this world that no one can cross alone; worship that Lord of the gods who holds the Sudarshan discus. He shows mercy with no reason at all, he is boundlessly generous, and he carries people over this endless maya. He is the Lord of moksha (freedom from birth and death), of the world, of Lakshmi and of these very breaths, and he is the one through whom freedom comes.
Devotion to Shri Raghunath is easy to reach and it brings happiness. It takes away the world's three kinds of burning, its grief and its fear. But that devotion does not come without the company of holy people; and holy people are met only when Raghunath shows his grace. When Raghunath, so kind to the helpless, shows his grace, then the company of saints comes to you. Just seeing them, touching them, being with them destroys whole heaps of sin down to the root; meeting them, you come to see happiness and sorrow with the same eye, humility and many other good qualities appear in you, and because you come to know God fully, pride, delusion, greed, grief and anger fall away on their own.
Serving such holy people makes the fear of duality run away — seeing God everywhere, a person becomes fearless — and the mind settles at the feet of Shri Raghunath. All the faults that rise out of the body drop off, and then love for one's own true self, for the Self, is born. Whoever comes to love his own true nature, whoever reaches the Self, lives in this world in a way that is simply extraordinary. Contentment, evenness, peace, and control over the mind and the senses become natural to him, and he no longer thinks of himself as a body — the idea that he is this body is gone. He becomes pure, free of the sickness of worldly life, always the same, settled forever in God. After that neither joy nor sorrow can touch him. Whoever comes to rest like that, for good, makes all three worlds holy.
When a person walks this road with his heart in it, why would God not help him? This is the road the Vedas and the saints have shown; walk it, and every kind of happiness will come. The seeker who walks this road gives up hoping for happiness from the things of the world, and by God's grace he receives the happiness that never ends. There are millions of things that could be said — who would go about saying them all? But as long as a person still sees two where there is only one, he cannot find true happiness even in a dream. True happiness is only in resting in the one undivided God, and that is what crossing the ocean of this world means. And nobody crosses that ocean without the grace of brahmins, of the gods, of the guru, of Hari and of the saints. Knowing this, Tulsidas too sings the praises of the Lord of Lakshmi, who takes away all fear.

If merciful Raghunath's grace is with you, what can other people's hatred ever gain against you? Not one hair of a devotee's head is ever harmed, however many millions of tricks anyone tries.
The low man who plots a saint's death dies that very death himself, wretch that he is. The story of Prahlad is famous in the Vedas — after hearing it, who could be so unlucky that he would not set his foot on the path of devotion?
Shri Hari rescued Gajendra, the king of elephants; he seated Vibhishan on a royal throne; he gave Dhruv a place so firm that it never moves; and Ambarish's story is something else altogether — the great sage Durvasa, remembering what came of the curse he laid on him, still melts with shame and could die of embarrassment.
Was there any wickedness Duryodhan could think of that he did not do to the Pandavas? The fool went on burning in his own arrogance. But by God's grace, good fortune, victory and fame insisted on belonging to the Pandavas alone.
Whoever digs a well for someone else will fall into it himself, wicked man. Whoever makes an enemy of the saints can never be happy, not even in a dream. For him even the wish-granting tree will bear nothing but poisoned fruit.
Who has two heads, that he would dare cross the line and touch a devotee of God? O Tulsidas! The man who has the strength of Shri Raghunath's arm behind him is always safe, and can never be afraid of anyone.

O Raghunath! O my Lord! Will you ever lay that lotus hand of yours on my head — the hand with which you once made fearless the suffering devotees who, helpless and with nowhere else to turn, called out your name?
The same lotus hand with which you broke Lord Shiva's unbending bow and cleared away King Janak's doubt; the same lotus hand with which you lifted up Guha the Nishad and held him to your heart with all the love of a brother.
O merciful one! The same lotus hand with which you made the funeral offering for Jatayu the vulture, as a son does for his father, and gave him your own highest home; the same hand with which, for the sake of your servant, you killed Bali and made Sugriv king of the whole clan of monkeys.
The same lotus hand with which you crowned the frightened Vibhishan when he came to you for shelter; the same hand with which you drew your bow and arrow, destroyed the demons, and gave the gods their freedom from fear.
And that lotus hand throws a cool, comforting shade that destroys sin, torment and maya — O Lord, it is the shade of that very hand of yours that this Tulsidas longs for, night and day.

O friend of the helpless! The world is burning with sin, with poverty, with sorrow, and with three unbearable kinds of suffering — what fate sends, what the body brings, and what comes from other creatures and the world around us. O God! This suffering man is crying out at your door, because every kind of happiness people had is gone.
The Vedas agree and the learned agree, and the Lord's own lips have said it, that a brahmin is my very own form; but today the minds of those brahmins have been swallowed by anger, craving, delusion, pride and hungry greed — they have dropped the calm and self-control that were natural to them and become ignorant, lustful, angry, arrogant and grasping.
In the same way the ruling class, the kshatriyas, have filled up with millions of crooked ways; every day they invent fresh ones — plundering as they please, injustice, cruelty, adultery, every kind of misconduct — and a clever godlessness that argues everything away has hunted out and destroyed good statecraft, real faith in God and the scriptures, love, and the honour of dharma and of the family line.
The world has thrown off the duties of varna and ashrama completely. The limits set by custom and the limits set by the Vedas are both gone. Nobody keeps to what society holds right, and nobody listens to what the scriptures command. The people have sunk low and give themselves to hypocrisy and sin. Everyone is dyed in his own colour now, doing exactly as he pleases.
Peace, truth and good ways have shrunk, bad ways have spread, and a thin coat of pretence has been painted over everything people do — wrongdoing and deceit keep growing. Good people suffer, goodness is in mourning, the wicked are enjoying themselves and wickedness is celebrating — false piety has taken over.
What was meant for the highest good has turned into self-interest — people pile up money now in the name of knowledge, devotion, charity and dharma. Spiritual practices, done carelessly, bear no fruit, and their powers no longer come. The earth, which is a wish-fulfilling cow, has fallen into the hands of the butcher that is Kali Yuga, and is in such distress that whatever is sown in her does not even sprout, and famine spreads everywhere.
How far can anyone describe what Kali Yuga does? It goes about doing harm for no reason at all. And even after all that it grinds its teeth and wrings its hands. Who knows what more it still has in mind.
O Lord! The gentler you are with it, the more you let it be and forgive it, the higher this low thing climbs on your head. Just be angry with it for a moment and scold it. One look at your raised finger and it will wilt like a tender pumpkin on the vine.
I would give my life for you — look at this and give your judgement, or there will soon be no joy and no blessing left on the earth. Do something that will let people say, in love and in great good fortune, that Shri Ram has looked on us with kind eyes. (The truly fortunate one is the one who loves Ram's feet, and that love comes only by Ram's grace.)
Hearing this plea of mine, Shri Ram looked at me with delight, and he smiled, and poured down such a rain of compassion that the whole ground was soaked — every corner of my heart was filled with peace. With Ram's rule established, every task came out right. Good signs began to show themselves, because King Ramchandra is the one who conquers the world: the moment he took his seat in my heart, the whole army of Kali Yuga ran away.
The all-powerful, all-knowing, merciful Master turned the losing army of goodness into a winning one, and his true devotees, as is their nature, praise him with reverence: our Lord has swept every torment away as easily as that.
And why would you not do it? It has always been your way to settle again what was laid waste and to give back what was lost — as you put Vibhishan and Sugriv on their thrones, as you settled the gods, who were terrified of Ravan, back in heaven again. O Tulsi! Whose sorrow has God not taken away, and to whom has he not held out his arm and said, do not be afraid?

Those unlucky people are living in this world as hell itself, the ones who turn their backs on the feet of the Lord who breaks the cycle of birth and death. Night and day their taste runs only to sin. Their minds stay unclean. The thinking of those wicked people stays dirty, and they have left the road the Vedas show.
They do not keep company with saints, they do not worship God, and their ears find nothing sweet in the story of Shri Ram. All they do is sleep on and on, senseless, in the night of 'mine' — my wife, my sons, my money, my house. Their minds never once wake out of that sleep of 'mine, mine'.
O Tulsidas!
