Those wretched people who push away the nectar of Shri Hari's name and stubbornly beg for the poison of worldly things and drink it down — always wanting money and sons and the rest — such people are like pigs and dogs and jackals: they are born into this world for nothing except to bring sorrow to their own mothers.

O Ramchandra, finest of the line of Raghu! How am I to make my plea to you? When I look at my heap of sins, and then think of your name, which means the one without sin, I am afraid.
To hurt when another hurts and to be glad when another is glad — that is the nature of the saints, and I have never once held it in my heart. Instead, seeing someone else's misfortune makes me perfectly happy, and hearing of someone else's good fortune sets me burning without any fire.
I go about preaching to people about devotion, detachment and knowledge, and cheating them in every way I can; and I sell your name, Ram — Shiva's whole treasure, the home of all joy — and with what I make I fill this belly of mine that is carrying me straight to hell.
In my heart I know my sins are as endless as the ocean; but when someone else says out loud that I have even a drop's worth of sin in me, I start fighting with him. That is to say: great sinner though I am, I want people to call me the holiest of men. Other people's faults, small as specks of dust, I blow up into Mount Meru, while their virtues, tall as mountains, I call worthless as dust and sneer at them. That is the kind of thing I do.
I dress myself up in one costume after another, and day and night, by whatever trick works, I take other people's money away from them. Not once, not for a single moment, do I hold my mind still and lovingly remember your lotus feet.
If you start weighing up the things I have done, then I will have to boil and burn in the cauldron of this world for millions of ages, and never once be free of birth and death. But if you will look at me with kindness just once, then, my Lord, that alone will carry this Tulsidas across this ocean of a world as easily as stepping over the puddle in a cow's hoofprint.

O Ram, treasure-house of mercy! I feel so ashamed — how am I to speak my plea to you? Everything I do turns out to be against dharma. So tell me, Lord: how did I ever come to please you?
Even though I know that everything, living and lifeless, is the very form of Shri Hari, I never once look at the world and see Hari in it. Instead I send these eyes of mine, like moths, straight into the flame of a beautiful woman, to burn there.
I understand this, and I explain it to others too, that ears are only worth having so that they can listen to your story; but with those very ears I am forever listening to other people's faults, filling my heart with them and tormenting myself.
With this tongue I could sing the praise of your qualities and reach the highest happiness without any effort at all; and instead I use it to croak like a frog, running other people down over and over, and I am throwing my life away.
I go around teaching everyone this, that they should make their hearts completely pure, because only then will Lord Shri Hari sit inside them; and meanwhile I keep a whole gang of scoundrels — pride, delusion, arrogance and the rest — living in my own heart.
This human body, so hard to get, the body in which devotees do the work that brings them to God's highest place — I am throwing it away for nothing. There are golden pots filled with nectar standing right there in my house, and I walk past them to go and dig a well in the sky.
The sins I have committed in thought, in deed and in word, I take the greatest care to hide. And if some good deed ever happened through me, because someone pushed me into it or because I was jealous of someone, I go about making sure the whole world hears of it.
Quarrelling with brahmins seems to be my own particular share in life. I go out of my way to make an enemy of everyone. And even with my mind as ruined as that, I sit among the saints and list off the brilliance of my own understanding, making myself out to be the wisest holy man there.
If I begged the four Vedas, and Sheshnag, and Sharada to describe my faults for me, even then, my Lord, those faults of mine would not be finished in a hundred ages! So how far could I get in describing them with this one mouth of mine?
If I really thought about the things I have done, would I even have the nerve to come to you for shelter? But Shri Ram's nature is so very gentle and his patience has no end, and that is the one thing I keep showing my mind to give it strength.
My Lord! This Tulsidas has not one single quality that could win you over, even in a dream. But, master, in the face of your grace this ocean of a world is no bigger than a cow's hoofprint. Knowing that, I let my heart be at peace — that by your grace, however crooked my ways are, I will cross this ocean of a world easily.

O Ram! O Raghunath! O my Lord, listen: my mind is set on doing wrong; it forgets your lotus feet and wanders here and there, day and night, after the things of the senses.
It does not obey what the Vedas say, and it is not afraid of anyone. It has been crushed in the oil-press of its own deeds, like a sesame seed, more times than can be counted, and now it has forgotten all that pain.
Where good people gather and God's story is told, that mind of mine will not go, not even by mistake, not even in a dream. But the people who are sunk in greed, delusion, arrogance, lust and anger — those are the ones it loves best.
Hearing someone praised it burns up with envy, and hearing someone's faults it is overjoyed. It is building a whole city of sins of its own, and still it cannot stand the sight of another man's little hamlet of them. It pays no attention at all to its own huge sins, but the moment it sees a tiny fault in someone else it starts running that person down.
Your name, Ram, is the fruit of every spiritual practice, the heart of the Vedas, and the boat for crossing the river of this world; and this wretched mind sells that name to other people for a few small coins and goes about making itself their slave.
And if the company of good people ever does bring me close to the path of God, my attachment to the things of the senses rises up and shoves my mind straight back into the pit of wicked worldly wanting.
I am already helpless, sinful and without sense, and I am thoroughly caught in a net of troubles; and on top of all that, O ocean of compassion, how am I to bear this unbearable shove from my own mind?
I have tried everything and I have lost; so let me say it now, in advance: this fear of Tulsidas, the terror of birth and death, will only go when you come and live in his heart.

Hero of the Raghus! Is there anyone you have ever refused shelter to, once the honour of your own name was at stake? Hari, you show mercy for no reason at all, and you take away the fear of this world of birth and death.
The Vedas say it, and the whole world knows it: Ajamil was a brahmin by birth but a storehouse of terrible sins. As he was being dragged off to the realm of Yama, he called out your name, "Narayan" — meaning only his son — and you stopped him from going there.
When the crocodile seized the elephant, that proud, helpless creature, he remembered you just once — and, my Lord, you came running to that place. You wiped away the unbearable pain in his heart, freed him from the crocodile, and gave him your own supreme home.
A hunter (Valmiki), a boatman of the forest tribe (Guha), a vulture (Jatayu), a woman of the streets (Pingala) — countless beings like them, all of them rooted in sin. Yet Ram, under the shelter of your name you destroyed every last one of their sorrows.
Great king, jewel of the line of Raghu! In what deed of mine am I any better than these people? And still I, Tulsidas, lie day and night in the terrible well of ignorance, suffering. (You have pulled everyone else out — now pull me out too.)

Ocean of mercy! Why does this poor servant of yours get no help at your door? Whenever and wherever the suffering have called out to you, you have taken away their sorrow right there.
The king of elephants, Prahlad, the Pandavas, Sugriv — you removed the pain their enemies gave them all. When Vibhishan came to you for shelter, shaking with fear of his brother Ravan, you lifted him up and held him to your heart as if he were Bharat. (So why does this not happen for me?)
Taking your name, I want to settle a village in my own heart, and to live in it I keep bringing in good people, little by little, from here and there — worship, wisdom, detachment from the world.
But hearing this, the wicked ones — lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy — grow angry and force their way in. They throw out those poor good men, worship and the rest, and instead, my Lord, they bring in low creatures to live in that village: wicked women, enemies, money and the like.
Persuading, bribing, punishing, dividing, waiting on them hand and foot, trying one thing after another — I am worn out. So today, Lord, I have opened my heart and laid this great misery before you, this fight I never asked for.
(Who else could I tell this to but you?) The gods are selfish, powerless, unworthy and hard-hearted. There is no pity in their minds. Where am I to go? Who but you takes away disaster? Who but you carries anyone across this ocean of the world?
Tulsi may be low, but he is yours and no one else's slave. Take him as your own and reach out your arm of devotion just once, so this village of your name may fill up and flourish — so that by the power of love for you, worship, knowledge and detachment grow in my heart, and lust and anger and the rest are destroyed.

Ram, I want to be your servant in every way, but here every corner has its own master. My mind and my senses have all set themselves up as my owners. This is the game the dark age of Kali plays.
Time, past deeds and the senses have surrounded me like buyers at a market. When I refuse to be sold into their hands, they tie me up and raise their price on me — they dangle whatever bait they can to bring me under their control.
Your name breaks every chain, and your colours are great to wear. When I told those buyers, "Brothers, I am already sold into the hands of Raghunath," they put on a show of false love and began asking me for a little space to live in my heart. (If I give them room, they look humble now, but once they are in they will slowly take the place over.)
Until now I have survived on the strength of your name, but this age of Kali has me pinned down. So take care of this poor slave, or soon no one will find a trace of him, however hard they search.
Lord, with the same easy play by which you settled the case of the bird (the owl) and the dog, just say this too, to this dark age: "Tulsi is mine." (Say that much and Kali will have no power over him at all.)

Ocean of mercy! This is why I keep my grief locked inside day and night: great king, a man who uncovers his own thigh shames only himself.
These companions of mine — lust, anger, greed — stay close beside me and want to kill me at the same time. That is how wicked they are! They cannot live without me, and by trickery they set my own chest on fire. They act like my own, and they destroy me.
Thinking that they live in my heart, I have lovingly satisfied every taste of theirs — I have taken my fill of every pleasure. And still these wicked, crooked ones have turned me into a magician's stick. (Just as a dancer is made to dance at the wave of a stick, they make me dance.)
Such closeness as this I have never seen or heard of anywhere, to this day. They do all the deeds themselves, and whatever wrong comes of it lands on my head.
They all look utterly unjust to me! And still I cannot let them go. I am caught in a terrible fix. Now take my hand yourself and pull me out. (Or these false friends of mine will not stop until they have killed me.)
I would give my life for you — please, just once, look at this strange plight your servant is in. The moment you look, Tulsi's sorrow will melt away on its own.

Hero of the Raghus, my master! With what face can I say anything to you? I swear by my master — when I think about my own conduct, shame closes my mouth and I fall silent.
Serve you, and you are won over; remember you, and you become a friend; come to you for shelter, and you appear in person. Even on such qualities as these, Lord of Sita, I give no thought at all.
You are the ocean of compassion, the friend of the helpless, the well-wisher of the suffering, the protector of everyone who comes to you. I have heard the roll of your titles, I know it — and I have still forgotten it.
I did not serve you, and I did not meditate on you. I never remembered you and loved your feet truly. Even after finding a master as great as you, I made a thorough mess of things with you.
You are the one who is kind to the poor, but I never took poverty on myself. (So nothing will come of you looking at me.) Now, Lord, look at your own self instead, and do whatever you can.

Where should I go? Who should I tell? There is no other place for me at all. This slave of yours has spent his whole life lying at your door.
Whatever I ruined by my own doing, Lord, I ruined because I was frightened out of my wits by suffering. But treasury of mercy, if even you look at my deeds before giving me my reward, how will I ever manage?
Best of the line of Raghu! Until you look at this creature with kindness, every day will be a bad day, every state a wretched state, every day full of sorrow and full of fault.
I go about with my back turned to you, I keep my face away from you — but that is because I am sightless, blind, an ignorant man, while you are the one who sees the whole universe! (How could you ever turn away from me?) There is no one like you but you; apart from you there is no one else who takes away the grief of the poor and the suffering.
Lord, I am bound and helpless and poor; you are free, you are the master. I could give my life for you! What prayer can a shadow make to the living man who speaks?
So look at yourself first, and then look at me — only then count this servant as true. The shelter of Ram's name is a mighty shelter. Whoever has taken shelter in Ram's name has been saved from the wheel of birth and death.
Ram, the way you live and move keeps shining in my heart, and when I think of your gentle nature I am filled with joy inside, knowing that now everything I do will come right. That is all — this Tulsi is yours; be kind to him in any way you like.

Ramchandra, you who are goodness itself! I worry about myself, and then again I don't — because every living being in this world is made for sorrow. (Everyone here is suffering.)
But does someone as great and able as you have a bond with me alone? (Perhaps that is it — ) you have countless people like me, but I have only you.
Lord, you know what is in every heart, and this is the shame that burns in mine, this is what I count as my loss: I am a bad servant, a wicked one, a servant who betrays the salt he eats, and yet I talk like a true servant. How could such pretence of mine stay hidden from you, who know everything?
But good or bad, every man and woman still calls me Ram's, don't they? When a servant or a dog goes wrong, it is the master's head the curses fall on. If I do wrong, people will call you bad for it.
I cannot even see a way to end this mess in my mind — a way for my lowness to go and for no one to speak ill of you. Now, friend of the helpless, do for me whatever seems right to you and whatever you can.
Just look for a moment at the roll of your titles! Surely I am one of those people. (You are the friend of the helpless — am I not helpless? You are the purifier of the fallen — am I not fallen? You are the protector of those who bow to you — have I not bowed? I must be at least one of these.) And even if my master lets go of this Tulsi, he will still lie there at his feet, taking shelter in him. (I cannot go anywhere away from you.)

O my mind! If you had not been ashamed to serve Shri Ram, you would not be passing from hand to hand like a false coin, though you are a true one. (Though you are a true part of God, forgetting him you wander as a creature from one birth into another.)
If you had not been lazy about repeating Raghunath's name with your tongue, you would not be swallowing dust today like a magician's miser.
O mind! If you had listened to me and earned the wealth of Ram's name, you would have gone and taken shelter before Raghunath, the Lord of Janaki, and been happy, and you would be honoured everywhere! Both this world and the next would have come right for you.
If you had loved Shri Ram, everyone would have loved you too; time, past deeds, family and all the other forces that drive a creature would never have been angry with you again. Every one of them would have turned in your favour.
If you had loved the name of Ram and set your whole heart on it, then travellers on both roads — the road of worldly good and the road of the highest good — would have trusted you. That is, you would have been happy in this world and the next alike.
If you had served the saints, and if you had listened to and understood the suffering of others and felt it as your own, then the filth of ten million births lying in the pond of your heart would have settled to the bottom and your inner self would have become clear.
For those who do not take Ram's name, the road through this world is endless and impossible to cross; but you would have crossed it without any effort at all. When even Ram's name said backwards has such power that it turned a hunter (Valmiki) into a sage, what will not happen from saying the name the right way round?
You fool! This human body of yours, which even the gods long for, would not have been wasted like this. You would have become the root of blessing, and the Creator himself would have turned in your favour.
O mind! If you had fixed your love and trust on the name of Ram, then, Tulsi, by Shri Ram's grace you would never have burned in your three kinds of suffering.

Whose good has Shri Ram not done, simply out of his own good nature? Age after age, this work of the Lord of Janaki has been famous throughout the world.
When Brahma and the other gods came pleading, telling him of the earth's suffering, then — to lift the earth's burden and to kill the demons — Shri Ramchandra appeared: the moon that opens the lily of the Sun dynasty, giving joy like nectar itself.
Vishvamitra would melt like a hailstone at the mere sight of Tadaka's fiery power. The Lord killed Tadaka and gave this enemy the reward a friend would get, showing the highest mercy in the form of anger. By granting the wicked Tadaka a good destination, he was merciful to her.
He went himself and took away the sin and torment of the stone (Ahalya, who had become one). Then, at the bow sacrifice, he pulled King Janak of Mithila out of the ocean of grief he was drowning in — by breaking the bow and fulfilling the king's vow.
Parashuram was a heap of anger and a rich man in pride and possessiveness; the moment you looked at him, you turned even him calm and even-minded. The angry man became peaceful, and the proud man came to see everything as equal.
Obeying the order of his mother Kaikeyi and his father, he went to the forest with a cheerful heart. Who else carries the weight of dharma like this, who else is so patient, who else has conquered both goodness and gentleness? No one at all.
Guha the low-born, poor boatman of the forest tribe — is there any creature he had not eaten? He had devoured every kind of living thing. Yet even he, because of his pure love, received the welcome of a friend from Raghunath.
Who else gives moksha to Shabari and to a vulture (Jatayu), and honours them while doing it? And who else removed the trouble of Sugriv, whose grief had no limit? (Only Shri Ram.)
Who else, when Vibhishan was food for death itself and thrown out by Ravan, would take him in and shelter him? Vibhishan sits as king in Ravan's own kingdom to this day. (All of this is Raghunath's grace.)
A foolish washerman of Ayodhya, with no trace of sense in him, that wretched man too reached the place where even the minds of sages grow weary trying to reach. (The great sages cannot even reason their way to that supreme home; the washerman simply went there.)
Has Brahma ever made anyone who cannot win freedom by taking Ram's name? It is this very name that Lord Shiva, the beloved of Parvati, remembers himself and spreads by teaching it to others.
Who has not been filled with joy on hearing the story of Ajamil? And who, taking Ram's name, has not gone to Hari's supreme home, even in this age of Kali?
Such is the greatness of Ram's name that it can turn even a bitter milkweed bush into the wish-granting tree. The Vedas and Puranas bear witness to this — and if you still cannot believe it, look at Tulsi. (See what I was, and see what a devotee of Ram I have become by the power of his name.)

Raghunath, I would give my life for you; your shelter is all I have. For this shameless, low, penniless, worthless man there is no master anywhere in the world but you, and no place to rest either.
There are plenty of fine masters, one in every house, but every one of them has only his own interest in view. I can find shelter nowhere except with Shri Ramchandra, the king of Kosala, the friend of a monkey (Sugriv) and the well-wisher of Vibhishan; in no other master's house can I find a footing.
You destroy the sorrows of those who depend on you and give joy to those who love you. For anyone who comes to you for shelter, your name alone is a cage of thunderbolt-hard steel — the moment they take your name they are safe. So now, ocean of mercy, make Tulsidas your servant! I want to be sold into your hands for no price at all.

Lord, who else is there who shows mercy to the helpless? You are the storehouse of gentleness, the crown of the wise, the beloved of those who take shelter, the guardian of all who depend on you.
Who is as able as you? You know everything, you are the master of all that moves and all that does not, and you are the swan that swims in the clear lake of Shiva's love. What other master, conquered by love, has made friends of a bird (Jatayu), a demon (Vibhishan), monkeys, a forest tribesman (Guha) and bears?
Lord, the whole web of maya (the world's illusion), and the faults, the virtues, the deeds and the fate of every creature, are all in your hands alone. This Tulsidas, good or bad, is yours. Turn your kind eyes on him for a moment and make him glad forever.

The name of Ram is the one thing I trust. My crooked mind is simply made this way: it cannot put its trust in anything else.
Studying the six schools of philosophy (Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Sankhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, Vedanta) and the Rig, Yajur, Atharva and Sama Vedas was never written into my fate at all, and my mind trembles at the very mention of fasts, pilgrimages and hard penance. Who wants to wear himself out in such practices until he dies, or waste his body away?
The path of ritual and sacrifice is hard in this age of Kali, and it depends on having money as well. As for knowledge, detachment, yoga, repeating the name and penance — trying to do those means facing lust, anger, greed and delusion.
In this world it is the ones who sing the many virtues of Raghunath who are always worthy in every way. For those who sit in the shade of the wish-granting tree of Ram's name, what is there to fear from thick black clouds (the darkness of ignorance) or from fierce sunlight (the dazzle of worldly pleasures)? Ignorance cannot take hold of them and drag them into pleasures, so sin and torment always stay far away from them.
Who knows who will go to hell, who will go to heaven, who will go to the supreme home? As for Tulsidas, simply living in this world as Ram's slave suits him very well indeed.

In this age of Kali, the name of Shri Ram is the wish-granting tree. It destroys poverty, famine, sorrow, fault, thick clouds (ignorance) and burning sunlight (the pursuit of pleasure).
The moment you take Ram's name, even a hostile fate and a hostile mind turn friendly. The great sage Valmiki sang the greatness of the name backwards, as "mara, mara", and Shiva taught the greatness of the name the right way round. Saying the name backwards over and over turned Valmiki from a hunter into a sage of God, and by saying it the right way round Shiva drank the deadly poison and came to be seen as God himself.
Whoever has the strength of this beautiful name of Ram has joy in this world and the next alike. Tulsi, once you have the strength of Ram's name, there is nothing to worry about in leaving this world and nothing to worry about in staying — so lost is such a person in the highest joy that living and dying become the same thing.

We should serve a master as beautiful as Shri Ram: the giver of joy, gentle, clever, brave, pure, and lovely as ten million gods of love.
Saraswati, Sheshnag and the saints keep describing his greatness. Scriptures like the Sama Veda sing of his qualities. Even Lord Shiva remembers his name with love, and longs to love him.
When he left for a far country — the forest — at his father's command, it did not trouble him in the least. Bow to him even once, and he is so overcome with shyness that he feels bound to you; Vibhishan is the famous proof of this, ruling to this day in Lanka on an unshakeable throne.
Working for him is very easy, because he never even looks at his servant's slips and mistakes. He stays awake in the heart of every devotee, through all four ages and all four watches of the day, sitting inside and keeping guard forever. He sees the wrong we do and still does not get angry with his servant! But let him hear one good thing about his servant and he is won over completely.
Worshipping him, even animals and birds, and even bodies made of darkness (the demons), became the crowning glory of all three worlds. Tulsi, the Creator is set against anyone who does not worship a Lord like this — joy-giving, gentle, beautiful, loving to his devotees, clever, the purifier of the fallen.

How can I put the blame on my master? Hari, my mind has left your love behind and wanders here and there, tangled up in its cravings.
I am very fond of being worshipped myself — I always want people to take me for a wise man and a devotee, and to honour me — but I have very little love for worshipping you. I am full of advice for other people, and I take no one's teaching myself. Such is my foolishness.
The sins I committed with real eagerness I keep hidden away in my heart. But whenever some good deed has come out of me by the influence of good company, without any love behind it, I go around telling the whole world about it and making sure they are grateful — so that nobody thinks me a sinner and everyone thinks me a very holy man.
Whenever some good deed gets done, I gather it up and store it like grains of corn left lying in a field. But, treasury of compassion, pride pushes its way into my heart and throws the whole store out. Pride grows and destroys the little good I have done.
And besides this, greed keeps my mind dancing on a rope of hope, the way a street magician ties a string round a monkey's neck and makes it dance as he pleases. And even so, out of sheer pride, I go about making fine speeches on the deep truth of detachment, like a great scholar.
For all this pretence, I still get called your servant. It is as if I had ground up my shame and drunk it. Raghunath, you are generous — be won over by this very shamelessness and cut Tulsi's bonds. Set me free from the chains of birth and death.

My Lord, the whole fault is mine. You are the ocean of gentleness, full of mercy, the protector of the protectorless, the one who feeds and cares for the poor and the suffering.
My clothes and my words look like a life given up to God, but my mind is a treasure-house of sins and failings. Ram, my mind is hollow when it comes to love for you and faith in you — there is not a trace of either in it; but for crooked deeds it is solid all the way through, packed with trickery and nothing else.
Like a rabbit who serves a jackal and expects to be famous as a lion, I love bad company and get irritated in the company of holy people. (The rabbit hopes for a lion's name on the strength of a jackal, and the jackal simply eats him — instead of fame he loses his life. In the same way, whoever falls into bad company hoping for fame not only never gets it, he loses his good qualities too, and has to go round and round in the wheel of death.)
Lord Shiva's teaching is just this: "Sing Ram's name with your tongue every day." In this age of Kali, even a name taken out of pride soaks up the ocean of sorrow the way the sage Agastya drank the sea — even a name taken out of pride takes away your worries about this world and the next.
That name of Ram is the root of joy and blessing. Shri Ram's name is so perfectly good for me that no other good thing can be compared with it. Hearing of the power of Ram's name, Tulsi too is deeply content, because this name is all he leans on.

O Hari! I have heard that you make the fallen pure. Well then — I am fallen and you are the purifier of the fallen; the two of us are a perfect match, we have come together. (What doubt is there now that I will be made clean?)
The Vedas bear witness that you carried across the ocean of this world the hunter (Valmiki), the courtesan (Pingala), Gajendra the elephant king and Ajamil, and many other lowly ones besides — who could ever count them all?
Those who took your name, knowingly or without knowing, have been shut out of both hell and heaven — that is, they cross the ocean of birth and death and are set free. (Knowing all this,) Tulsi too has come to take shelter with you; take him as your own as well.

If there were anywhere another master as able as you, then what small, wretched creature would put up with sheer disrespect and grow thin repeating your name night and day?
What I am begging from you — the nectar-water of your grace — is truly something rare. The chatak chick of my mind wants the joy-water that falls from the Swati star of love (the chatak bird will drink only the rain that falls under that one star).
If now and then, under the pull of time and past deeds, some bad desire rises in my mind (and my heart begins to turn away from you), it is like a fish that lives happily in the water and now and then leaps out, then in a panic dives straight back in. (Just as a fish cannot bear even a moment out of the water, my chatak-heart panics the instant it is parted from the water of your love, and struggles to get back to you alone.)
(But even saying this will not do, because) how can anyone tell how much deceit there is in Tulsidas's heart? Still, O darling son of Dasharath, in your kingdom people have reaped without ploughing or sowing. That is, without doing a single good deed, countless sinners have crossed over on your name alone — and so I too will cross over; that is my faith.

Who in this world is so generous that, without being served at all, he melts at the mere sight of the poor and the suffering? There is only one such — Shri Ramchandra; no one else is like him.
The supreme state that great wise sages do not reach even after long years of yoga and renunciation — that state Lord Raghunath gave to a vulture and even to Shabari, and he thought nothing much of it in his own mind.
The wealth that Ravan won by offering all ten of his heads to Lord Shiva — that same wealth Shri Ram handed over to Vibhishan, almost shy that it was so small a gift.
Tulsidas says: O my mind, if you want every happiness in every way, then worship Shri Ram. The Lord, the treasure-house of mercy, will fulfil all your desires.

O Shri Ram! Among true givers you alone are the crown. Whoever asked you once never had to dance about begging again — his every wish was filled.
Demons, gods, men, sages — they are all out for themselves. Nobody gives anything without taking something first. But O Lord of Kosala, you are such a merciful wishing-tree that you melt with kindness the moment someone bows to you once.
In your other incarnations too you kept the rule the Vedas lay down. For instance, though Sudama was your friend from childhood, you gave him riches only after you had taken his handful of flattened rice.
O Ram! Among Sugriv, Shabari, Vibhishan and Hanuman, which of them did you not fill so completely that nothing was left to ask for? O treasure of compassion, now this cruel she-demon called hope is tormenting Tulsi (free me from her grip, and bless me too by letting me see you).

Only Shri Raghunath knows the way of love. Shri Ram lets go of every other tie and keeps the tie of love alone.
King Dasharath gave up his body to keep faith with love and set up a fame that will never fade; yet you showed even more tenderness and more honour to Jatayu the vulture than to that loving father. (Dasharath did not die before Ram's eyes, but the dear vulture breathed his last in Ram's lap, and Ram with his own hands performed his funeral rites and set him free.)
When you saw your friend Sugriv aching for his lost wife, you forgot even Sita, dearer to you than your own life (you set aside the search for Janaki, killed Bali first and ended Sugriv's sorrow). On the battlefield your dear brother Lakshman lay unconscious, struck by the spear — yet (forgetting that grief) your heart began to worry about Vibhishan (thinking: if Lakshman does not live, what use is my fighting Ravan? And then the monkeys and bears will go home, but where will poor Vibhishan go?)
At home, in guru Vasishtha's ashram, at the houses of dear friends, or at your wife's family home — whenever and wherever you were a guest, you said the same thing: nowhere have I found the taste and the sweetness I found in Shabari's berries.
When the sages begin to describe your own true form — the Supreme Being beyond all qualities — you bow your head in embarrassment. But when the boatman and the monkeys call you "friend" and "brother", you take it as your glory. (You are delighted to be called the boatman's friend, and you count it greatness to be known as a brother of the monkeys.)
Brother, in all three worlds and all three ages there is no one else so bound by love as Raghunath. He even said to Hanuman, "I am in your debt" — who else is so grateful for service as he is?
O Tulsi, if after seeing such affection and such gentleness in Shri Ramchandra devotion has still not risen in your heart, then your mother wasted her youth for nothing in giving you birth.

O best of the Raghus! This is your greatness: you pay no regard to the rich and the important (those proud of money, learning or position), and instead you honour the poor and pour your grace on them.
The gods wore themselves out with every kind of practice, and you did not show yourself to them even in a dream; but you made brothers of a Nishad, of crafty bears and monkeys, and of a demon (Vibhishan) — because all of them were humble and had no pride.
You wandered through the Dandak forest mixing freely with the sages, but you never spoke of them afterwards; yet you always loved to praise, again and again and beautifully, the love of the vulture Jatayu and of Shabari. (Here too it is the same matter of humility and freedom from pride.)
On a dog's complaint you set the sannyasi on an elephant and had him driven out of the city; but the foolish washerman who slandered Sita falsely you treated as one of your own people, and fairly let him go on living in your city Ayodhya (because he was poor and lowly).
(So it is proved that) in this court, in Ram's kingdom, the custom of honouring the lowly has been kept from the beginning. But O merciful to the lowly — has no one, even to this day, reminded you of this lowly Tulsi?

Shri Ramchandra is the one who does such good to the lowly — he is very tender, a storehouse of compassion, and he helps others for no reason at all.
Ahalya, the wife of the sage Gautam, was helpless and poor, and because of her sin she had been turned into a stone. You went to her yourself, touched her with your holy foot, and freed her from that terrible curse.
Guha the Nishad lived by killing, his body was dark and heavy with tamas, and he roamed the forest like an animal; yet you gave no thought to his family or his caste, and, won over by love, you held him to your heart.
Jayant, Indra's son, had committed an offence too great to put into words (he came as a crow and struck Sita's foot with his beak); yet when he ran through all the worlds looking for shelter (terrified by your arrow) and at last came to you, broken with grief, you took away all his fear.
Jatayu was born a vulture, only a bird, and he lived on meat all his life. What great vow had he ever kept, that you should perform his last rites with your own hands as a son does for a father, and set everything right for him — that is, give him liberation?
Shabari was a foolish woman of low caste, outside both the world's rules and the Vedas. But merciful Raghunath saw the truth of her love, showed himself to her in kindness, and lifted her up.
When the monkey Sugriv, tormented by fear of his brother Bali, came crying to you for shelter, you could not bear your servant's terrible pain, and you killed Bali even though you had to take abuse for it.
Vibhishan was the brother of your enemy Ravan, and a demon by birth. What right had he to any worship? But when he came to you for shelter you went forward to receive him, spread your arms and held him to your heart.
Monkeys and bears are counted so lawless that even to say their name is thought to bring bad luck; yet O Lord, you made even them holy. The Vedas bear witness to this. It is all your greatness.
How much can I say? There are countless lowly ones whose troubles you have taken away; but somehow, on this Tulsidas, tied up in the sins of the Kali age, you have forgotten to pour your grace.

Devotion to Shri Raghunath is very hard. It is easy to speak of, but hard to do. Only the one who has managed to do it knows.
Whoever is skilled in an art finds it easy, and it gives him joy for ever. A small fish swims straight up against the current of the Ganga, while a huge elephant is swept away (because, unlike the fish, it does not know how to swim).
If sugar is mixed into dust, no one can separate it however hard they try; but a tiny ant, who knows its sweetness, gets it out and enjoys it without any trouble.
The yogi who takes everything he sees into his own belly (folding maya back into Brahman, dissolving the world of effects into God, its cause) and sleeps with the sleep of ignorance thrown off — that man, wholly free of duality, can directly taste the supreme joy of the Lord's highest state.
In that state there is no grief, no delusion, no fear, no excitement, no day or night, no place or time. (Only the Lord remains — pure being, awareness and bliss.) But O Tulsidas, until that state is reached, doubt is not pulled out by the root.

If there were love for the feet of Shri Ramchandra, why would I have to bear the three kinds of pain and sheer misery, night and day?
If this mind could find, even once in a dream by day or night, the nectar of contentment, why would it see the false mirage of the senses and run after it like a thirsty deer?
If we thought in our hearts of the greatness of the Lord, the husband of Lakshmi, and grew in love and worshipped him, why would we be wandering about today like a dog, showing our empty stomach at door after door?
The greedy who have become slaves of hope are slaves of everyone (whoever hopes for the pleasures of the senses has to serve them all); and those who have trusted God and conquered hope — they are God's true servants.
I am pleading with you because there is not one act of worship in me. (I only repeat your name.) O Lord, have mercy on Tulsidas for the sake of that name alone.

If Shri Ramchandra had tasted sweet to me, then the nine flavours of poetry (love, laughter, pity, courage, anger, fear, disgust, wonder and peace) and the six tastes of food (bitter, pungent, sweet, astringent, sour and salty) would all have gone flat and tasteless. (But Ram does not taste sweet to me, and so the pleasures of the senses seem sweet instead.)
I have taken body after body and learned this for myself, and I have heard it and seen it too: the pleasures of this world are thieves. (They lose us in maya and steal away the true wealth.) Though I know it well in my heart, my mind has never once, even in a dream, had its fill of them and turned away. (What lowness is this?)
Yet Tulsidas speaks these bold words to his master Shri Raghunath on the strength of one thing alone. (And that strength is this:) O Lord, for the honour of your own name, to how many have you not mercifully written a release (from the bonds of this world)? (Whoever took your name was handed the warrant of freedom — and that is why I speak like this too.)

My mind has never fastened on you the way it fastens on the things of the senses — with no pretence at all, naturally, and without a break.
The way I stare at another man's wife, and listen to the sinful gossip of house after house — in that way I never go to see holy people, and never listen to the praise of Shri Raghunath's qualities, clean as the waves of the Ganga.
Just as my nose is a slave to lovely scents and my tongue loves the six tastes, this nose never aches with longing for the garland that was offered to the Lord, and this tongue never longs for the food he has blessed.
Just as this low body wants to touch sandal paste, moon-faced young women, beautiful ornaments and soft clothes, it never once longs to touch the lotus feet of Shri Raghunath.
Just as I served bad gods and wicked masters in every way, with body, speech and heart, I never served Raghunath like that — Raghunath, who feels deeply grateful for the smallest service, and who grows shy with his own endless compassion when someone bows to him even once.
Just as these restless feet, driven by greed, have taken knocks at door after door, these wretched feet have never once, even in a dream, tired themselves out going to the holy retreats of Sita and Ram.
O Lord, in this way every part of me is turned away from your feet. With this mouth alone I have taken the shelter of your name — and only because Tulsi is sure of one thing: your form is made of mercy. (You are an ocean of grace, and by the power of the name you will surely take me as your own.)

O Lord, throw me into Yama's torture, send me straight into hell — because, O Ram, I am so wicked that I have turned my back on a master as pure and as kind as you, who does good for no reason at all.
In the womb you cared for me and fed me for ten months like a mother and father — what good you did me! To me, a fool, you gave clear understanding; to me, a wicked man, a gentle nature; to me, an offender, respect. And even so, instead of worshipping you, I go the opposite way.
I play tricks even on the Lord who lives inside me; I hide my sins from the one who moves in every heart and fills everything. (But blessed are you —) even towards such a stupid, low servant, O Ram, you never turned your heart away.
I fill my belly by calling myself your servant, while I have sold my heart to the pleasures of the senses; and still, O merciful one, you have shown a cheat like me nothing but honest, open kindness.
Though I know well, understand and hear of your kindness to me moment after moment, my heart, harder than a thunderbolt, has never once been pierced by love for the Lord of Janaki.
When I put my master's whole tenderness for his servant on one pan of the balance of my mind, and my own small treachery against him on the other, and weighed them — it was my side that came down heavier.
Even so, O Lord, you have gone on doing me good out of mercy, you do it now, and you will keep on doing it. For his part, Tulsi knows this: the Lord himself will look after this man who is weighed down by kindness he can never repay.

Will I ever live this way? Will I ever, by the grace of merciful Shri Raghunath, take on the nature of the saints?
I will stay content with whatever comes, and want nothing at all from anyone, man or god. I will keep myself busy always in doing good to others. With mind, speech and action I will keep the yamas and niyamas — not harming, truth, not stealing, chastity, not hoarding, cleanliness, contentment, self-discipline, the study of scripture, and surrender to God.
Even when my ears hear words that are harsh and hard to bear, I will not burn in the fire of anger they light. I will drop my pride, see everyone as the same, and keep my mind at peace. I will neither praise nor blame others (busy always in thinking of you, I will have no time left for praising or blaming anyone).
I will let go of worries about this body and bear pleasure and pain alike. O Lord, walking on this path, will Tulsidas ever come to an unshakeable love for Hari?

Apart from the name of Shri Ram, I can trust nothing else. In this Kali age, on all the trees of spiritual practice the only fruit I can see is hard labour — keep at those practices and all that comes to hand is toil, and no fruit at all.
Austerity, pilgrimage, fasting, charity, sacrifice — let each person do whatever appeals to him. But you only know about the fruit of these acts once you actually get it, even though the Vedas have served up plateful after plateful of fruits. The meaning: the Vedas praise these acts highly, but the Kali age will not let them succeed — so where will the fruit come from?
People do their chanting and their sacrifices by the rules of the scriptures, but the real work is not accomplished by them. In the practices for yogic powers there is no happiness, not even in a dream. (With hardly anyone left who knows how it is done,) that path too brings disease and separation (the body falls ill, and so one is parted from those one loves).
Lust, anger, pride, greed and delusion have joined together and all but stolen away knowledge and detachment. And once a man takes sannyas, his mind falls apart like an unbaked clay pot when water is poured into it.
The sages hold many different views (there are six schools), and looking at all the different paths in the Puranas one sees nothing but quarrelling everywhere. My guru told me that worshipping Ram is the best way, and to me too it looks best, like a straight royal road.
O Tulsi, whoever wants to wear himself out and die again and again, with no faith and no love, may go ahead and die; but to cross the ocean of this world, the name of Ram is the ship. Let whoever wants to reach the far shore climb aboard and cross.

Anyone who does not love Shri Ram and Janaki should be given up as you would give up ten million enemies, however dear that person may be to you.
(Look at these examples:) Prahlad gave up his father (Hiranyakashipu), Vibhishan his brother (Ravan), Bharat his mother (Kaikeyi), King Bali his guru (Shukracharya), and the gopis of Vraj their own husbands (seeing them as obstacles on the way to God) — and every one of them came to joy and blessing.
All the well-wishers, all the people truly worth honouring, are counted so only because of their connection with Shri Raghunath and their love for him — what more need I say? If the ointment you put in your eyes destroys the eyes themselves, what good is that ointment?
O Tulsidas, whoever brings you (by his company or his teaching) to love the feet of Shri Ramchandra — he is in every way your greatest friend, worthy of worship, and dearer than life itself. That is what I hold.

Anyone who has no love for Shri Ramchandra is living in this world for nothing, like a donkey, a dog or a pig.
Lust, anger, pride, greed, sleep, fear, hunger and thirst — every creature has these. But the reason the gods and the saints praise this human body is love for Raghunath, the Lord of Sita (only love for God makes a human life worth anything).
A man may be brave, clever, a good son who obeys his mother and father, marked with fine signs and full of great qualities, and may be counted among the best; but if he does not worship Hari he is like the indrayan fruit, which never gives up its bitterness (however lovely it looks from the outside).
Fame, high birth, good deeds, great wealth, gentleness and a beautiful face — if he has no love for Lord Shri Ramchandra, all these qualities are like vegetables cooked without salt.

You wretch! You never loved a master as beautiful as Shri Ramchandra, and never formed any bond with him. Yet after all this disrespect, he has still not let you go.
(Life after life) you tied new ties and new loves, all of them empty and without any sweetness, and they only burned up your body and took away your life.
Everyone wants good for himself and for his own people, but the root of both these goods is one alone — the beloved of Janaki.
He is the life of every living thing, the dearest of all to the heart, the joy inside joy itself — and you forgot Shri Ramchandra!
He has always done you good, and he will do you good in the days to come as well — oh, why did you play so many crooked tricks on such a beautiful master?
O Tulsi, if you understand even now, good can still come to you — for by fighting again and again even a coward becomes a hero.

O Ram, even if you give me up, I will not give you up. For if I leave your feet, whom else am I to love?
A master as beautiful as you, who gives such happiness, has never been heard of by my ears in all this world, never seen by my eyes, and my mind cannot even guess at one.
O Raghunath, I am a dull creature and you are God. You are the master of maya (maya is under your control), and I live under maya's control.
I am an ungrateful beggar and you are a most generous master; I am your bad son and you are the mother and father who does me good. The meaning: even when a son turns out badly, his parents still do him good, and in the same way you go on caring for me and keeping me always.
If anyone anywhere had so much as asked after me, this Tulsidas would have sold himself into their hands for nothing. (But apart from you, who takes in a low man like me? So I will never leave you.)

O Ram, you may turn away from me, but you are my only hope. (Do not be angry that I speak like this.) People in pain, and people out for themselves, talk like madmen. The meaning: to you, who always look with grace on your own people, I say "you may turn away"; and for myself I say, in pride, "you are my only hope" — these are surely a madman's words.
The cloud that gives away its water and protects every living thing — what does it lack? What could the cloud want, which saves lives by giving water? Yet it is the papiha that gets the praise, for keeping the unbreakable rule of love. The meaning: the cloud gives the chatak its Swati water without wanting anything in return, and the generosity is the cloud's; but because the bird will look nowhere else, the praise goes to the chatak.
The pure, life-giving water gains not the smallest thing from the fish; but for the fish, where is there any place apart from water where it could stay alive? The meaning: away from water it cannot live at all. In the same way, you gain nothing from me — but where am I to go if I leave you? You will have to keep me in your shelter, and the praise will come to me.
I would give my life for you. Look — it is under the shelter of the great that the small have always been saved, and everywhere false coins pass along with the true ones. The meaning: your real devotees are the true coins, and I, a fraud and a false coin, will still cross the ocean of this world because your name is stamped on me.
In your court everyone is blessed, good and bad alike, whether a person stands with you or against you (Vibhishan was turned towards you and Ravan away from you, and both were set free). O Ram, my only trust is in your name, that blesses whoever holds it.
O Lord, saying it out loud would spoil everything (the whole secret would come out), so it is better to keep what is in the mind inside the mind; and in any case, O treasure of mercy, you already know everything in Tulsi's mind.

Where should I go? Who should I tell? Who will listen to this poor man, who has none of the wealth that spiritual practice brings? For someone like me, with no means of any kind, you alone in all three worlds are the way.
The world is full of "lords of the universe" in house after house (everyone calls himself God), but for the one who has no support at all, singing of your countless good qualities is the only support. That is, by singing your praises alone he crosses the ocean of this world.
When the king of elephants had to be freed, who but you came running, leaving even Garuda behind? Who else has fed and cared for a storehouse of sins like me? Apart from you, what mother has ever given birth to such a one?
Even the cruel, the cowardly, the worthless sons not worth half a cowrie shell — people like me — you have made precious, you who performed the funeral rites for the vulture Jatayu.
I give myself to you! Tulsi's ruined case can be set right only if you set it right. If you are slow in lifting me up, then that delay will be a mother who gives birth to nothing but children called sorrow and sin. Meaning: if you do not have mercy and save me quickly, I will be surrounded by nothing but sins and sorrows.

My Lord, I give myself to you! Look my way just once and take me as your own. Son of Dasharath, you are the one who plants uprooted souls back into the ground.
There is no other all-powerful master like you, who protects everyone who comes to him for shelter. At the mere taking of your name even barren land grows a crop. Meaning: even those with not a trace of happiness in their fate gain devotion and wisdom by repeating your name, and reach the highest joy.
Your words and your deeds are driven deep into my mind (seeing your promise, made again and again, to rescue the helpless, and your deeds of rescue — Ajamil, the woman Ganika and other helpless ones — I have come to trust you completely). And I have also seen, heard and understood those people whom the world calls great.
Which of them lifted the curse from Ahalya, who had become a stone, and gave her peace? And which of them, as easily as play, won over a sage as full of rage as Parashuram? (Not one of them.)
Who kept the rules of the world and of the Vedas for the sake of his mother, his father and his brother? Who never once goes back on his word? And who fills a person with blessings the moment that person bows to him? (Only Shri Raghunath.)
Who, bound by love, gathered up the lowly and the wicked and made them his own? Who else would perform the funeral rites for a vulture and for Shabari, as for his own father and mother?
Who is the support of those who have no support anywhere? Who takes pity on the helpless? And who is the friend of monkeys, of a boatman, of a demon and of bears? (No one but Raghunath.)
Great King, every beggar, fool and low person you have blessed is sitting today in the gathering of saints.
This is your greatness told exactly as it is — not stretched by even a single letter. But, ocean of kindness, why is it taking so long for Tulsidas alone?

Ocean of mercy, look my way somehow. I have no other place, no other shelter anywhere; you are my one sure refuge.
My mind has gone duller than a thousand slabs of stone. Who else can I ask now to bring it to life? Who but you has ever set stones free?
Just as the great sage Vishvamitra completed his sacrifice undisturbed under your watch, I too want to offer a sacrifice of love at your feet. But when I see the wicked sins of this age of Kali, I am filled with fear. (Just as you guarded Vishvamitra's sacrifice from Marich, Tadaka and the rest) save me too from these sins and make me a lover of your lotus feet.
I am very afraid of Bali, the mighty king of those monkeys that are my crooked deeds. So, Lord of the helpless, just as you killed Bali and made Sugriv free from fear, I too want to live in the shade of your arms (save me from these hard deeds and take me as your own).
Just as Ravan struck Vibhishan, this great delusion is striking me. Master of Tulsi, I am burning up in the three kinds of suffering of this world — save me, save me!

My Lord, when I hear the story of your qualities, my heart fills with longing. But Ram, I do not know the devotion and the feeling that please you.
Because my deeds are not good, my nature is not good, and the times are not good either (this is the age of Kali); I have no master, no place of my own, no true wealth of spiritual practice, no fine body ready to serve you, no good mind turned toward the highest goal, and no good years spent in worship. In short, I do not have a single means of reaching God; I am without any support at all.
The one I beg water from, thirsty as I am, turns round and asks me to give him nectar to drink. Who can I tell my trouble to? I hardly have the courage to tell anyone.
Father, I give myself to you! You yourself find some good way out for me. Because the moment your kind eyes fall on someone, even a losing game turns into a winning throw. Meaning: by your grace even the greatest sinners become fit for Vaikunth, God's own world.
If you show it, even what cannot be seen comes into sight; and if you explain it, even what no one can grasp — your own true nature — becomes clear. Now show me that, and make me understand it.
Look, the support of your name is my water, and I who live in it am like a king of poor fish, like one enormous fish. If I am saying anything false about this in front of my Lord, let this tongue of mine burn.
Everything about my case has gone wrong; only one thing has come out well, and it is this: Tulsidas has told the whole matter to his merciful master. (Now the master himself will set right what has gone wrong.)

Shri Ram, you alone truly know the ways of love. I give myself to you! The Vedas honour your glory in this way: you take away the bigness of the big — their pride — and the smallness of the small — their misery.
You performed the funeral rites for the vulture Jatayu and you ate Shabari's berries; and this too is told again and again in the gathering of saints, that whoever you honour is honoured by both the world and the Vedas. Your love is held to be greater than yoga and greater than knowledge.
Merciful One, by your grace even in this hard age of Kali your devotees understand your greatness and hold it in their hearts. Tulsi has become a stranger to your love, because he is a slave to other things, to the senses; yet, Friend of the helpless, he sits at your door and will not move until your kind eyes fall on him.

Just repeating the name of Shri Ram puts out the burning in the mind. In this age of Kali all the other practices — yoga, sacrifices and the rest — have become as useless as a painted picture of the sun for driving away darkness.
Actions are soaked in sorrow and sin. Doing them now is like a tree that breaks into the loveliest flowers but never bears any fruit at all. Hypocrisy, greed and craving have thoroughly ruined worship. And knowledge, which is the way to moksha (freedom), has today become a way of filling the belly. (So all three — action, worship and knowledge — are in a bad state.)
Yoga does not come together, samadhi (deep absorption) is never free of pretence, and detachment and knowledge have shrunk to grand talk and fancy costumes. Nothing is done, only said. Millions of crooked paths full of deceit have opened up. What people say and how they live have both turned false. Everyone praises his own conduct.
(Only the glory of Ram's name has remained.) What does Lord Shiva teach a dying soul on the holy ground of Kashi, on the bank of the Ganga? He tells of the power of the name of Shri Ram. He tells it to others and he repeats it himself. The world has known this for ages, and the Vedas have gone on saying it.
Now you should fix your mind on the name of Ram alone, love the name of Ram alone, and take shelter in the name of Ram alone. Because this one practice is what takes away the soul's misery of being born and dying again and again. Tulsi, if you keep your faith and your firm love in Ram's name, then one day or another Shri Ram, out of his merciful nature, will surely have mercy on you.

Hari, I am not even ashamed to be called your servant! The way of living that pleases you is the very one I drop without a second thought. (I do not feel even a pang of regret at giving up the ways of the saints. And even so I set myself up as your servant.)
The Lord whom the sages worship after giving up every attachment, for whom they do their chanting, their tapasya and their sacrifices — how can a fool like me, a great wrongdoer and sinner, ever reach him?
God is utterly pure and my heart is full of sin and utterly filthy; the whole thing seems impossible to me. Why would a swan come to a pond where crows, vultures, herons and pigs live? Meaning: God will not come into my dirty heart, full of lust, anger, greed and delusion. He walks in the heart-temple of those sages who have made their hearts spotless through selfless action, detachment, devotion and knowledge.
The holy places where seekers of knowledge take shelter and put out the three hard burning sorrows of the world — even if I go there, pride, ignorance and greed will only torment me more, because a wife's jealousy of her rival does not leave her even in heaven; it goes along with her there too.
I go about teaching others, "Look, the saints are the only boat for crossing the river of this world" — and yet, Hari, I myself carry a great hatred toward them, and still I want my good from you.
(But even so, where can I go?) I have no other place, no other shelter, and so, unworthy as I am, I go on forcing a bond with you. Raghunath, greatest of all givers, this Tulsidas is singing your praises — take him as your own (not looking at his good or bad, but simply out of your merciful nature).

My Lord, how am I to make my plea to you? When I think about my own low behaviour and truly see it, my heart gives up and I am afraid (I no longer even have the courage to pray).
Hari, the very practice by which you take a man as your servant and show him mercy is the one I stubbornly keep dropping. And the wrong road, where a person is caught in a net of troubles and gets nothing but sorrow day and night, is the road I keep walking.
I know that by doing good to others in thought, word and deed I would cross the ocean of this world, but I do exactly the opposite: seeing others happy, I burn for no reason at all in the fire of envy.
The Vedas, the Puranas, all of them settle on this: hold firmly to the company of good people. But in my pride, my ignorance and my envy I never respect that company; I am forever hostile to the saints.
(The truth is) I always like exactly what keeps me sunk in the ocean of this world. So tell me yourself, my Lord, with what strength am I to put an end to the sorrows of this world?
Whenever your merciful nature melts toward me, that is when I will be saved — otherwise never. Because Tulsidas has no faith in anyone else, so why should he wear himself out and die struggling with other practices?

My Lord, you are my only hope, and that is why I came long ago to your shelter. Knowledge, detachment, devotion — I have none of these practices, not even in a dream (nothing by whose strength I could cross the ocean of this world).
Greed, ignorance, arrogance, lust and anger are the enemies that surround me day and night; they do not leave my body even for a moment. Joining hands with all of them, this mind of mine has taken the wrong road too. Now it will turn only if you turn it.
The saints and the Vedas cry out again and again that all the pleasures of this world are houses of sin and bring only grief. I know this, and still I love those pleasures so much — Hari, is this not your own doing? (Otherwise why would I act this way knowingly?)
(Whatever the case, if you wish) you can turn poison into nectar and fire into ice, and carry me across the ocean of this world with no ship at all. Search as long as you like, nowhere will anyone find a master as kind and as truly good for us as you. (And if I did not set my life right even after finding such a master, who could be a greater fool than me?)
Knowing just this in my heart, Raghunath, I have let go of everything else and fallen into your care. This net of troubles around Tulsidas will be cut only if you cut it!

O world of illusion, now I have seen you as you really are: you are plainly a house of deceit. But now I have God's strength with me, so you cannot bind me in your web of tricks any more. (The moment I took shelter in God's strength, this world made of his maya vanished completely, and so now I cannot fall into the world's false trap.)
You are beautiful only to look at; think about you and there is nothing there — in truth you do not exist at all. Look at a banana tree: no core ever comes out of it, however much you peel it, only one layer after another. That is exactly the state of this world.
For your sake I wandered through birth after birth and passed through countless kinds of life, and I never reached the end of you. You went on drowning me again and again in that river of mirages that is great delusion.
Listen, you wicked thing: play your millions of tricks and use all your force if you like, but a true devotee of God can never come under your power. Go and pitch your camp, with your whole army of sense-pleasures, in the heart where Shri Krishna, the son of Nanda, does not live. (What work do you have in a devotee's heart where God lives?)
Play your cheating games with the one who does not know your secret. Only the one who does not know the secret will die of fright at a rope he takes for a snake.
Listen, you fool, to what is good for you: if you want yourself and your whole family to stay safe, do not be stubborn. Leave the servants of Shri Raghunath, the Lord of Tulsidas, alone and run off to where pride and lust live. (Where Ram lives there is no pride and no lust; and where these are not, how can the world of maya remain?)

Brother, keep saying Ram, Ram, Ram, Ram as you go; otherwise you will be seized somewhere for the forced labour of this world, and then getting free will be extremely hard. (One can get free of a king's forced labour in a few days, but the world's wheel of birth and death keeps turning forever until true knowledge comes. If you keep repeating Ram, Ram, the enemies born of maya, the pleasures of the senses, will not be able to seize you for their labour — because Ram's maya has no hold over Ram's servant.)
Crooked Karmachand — the fate made by the sinful deeds of our past lives — has given us, free of cost and by the ordinary working of the world's wheel, such a miserable little cot: this dark, dull human body with no worship in it. Its bamboo frame is old (the ignorance and delusion that have no beginning), its whole fitting is out of order (the dark, pleasure-seeking turns of the mind, which make the body do wicked things and send a person down the wrong road), and though it is straight it has only three corners (it is set only on gaining wealth, pleasure and self-serving religion, with no thought at all of moksha).
Its bearers, who lift it and walk, are uneven and are drunk on lust (the five senses are what carry the body along; bearers should come in pairs, but five cannot pair off, so they are uneven, not matched, and all five senses are drunk on the enjoyment of their objects. When wicked deeds have already made body and mind dark and pleasure-bound, how are the senses to be pulled back from their objects?), and they do not draw in their feet and walk in step. (The senses each run after their own object.) So the cot goes now high, now low, and the jolts and jerks come, and in all this pulling this way and that there is great pain. (Sometimes into religious work out of a wish for heaven or fame, sometimes into the world's many businesses to get enjoyments, sometimes after women out of lust. And not even evenly — through sound, touch, form, taste and smell, each its own object, the senses go now up and now down, and the soul suffers terribly as a result.)
Thorns are spread on the road and sharp stones lie in it (poisonous creepers wind around and bushes catch and tangle, so one has to stop at place after place. For the senses, which forget God and run into the thick forest of worldly pleasures, the loss of those pleasures is the thorns, the pleasures one does not want are the stones, the attachment to home and family is the creeper that winds round, and desire is the tangle, so one must walk stopping at every step and suffering). And then, the further ahead we go, the further away our own home keeps moving. (The more the mind is caught in the world's enjoyments, the further away goes our own true home, which is reaching God.) And there is no one to show us the road either. (People sunk in pleasures never keep the company of saints, so who will show them the straight road to the highest good? The company they do keep points them the wrong way.)
The road is very hard (full of the thorny scrub of sense-pleasures and of hills and forests), there is no travelling money with us (no worship), and we have even forgotten the name of our own village (we do not take God's name even by mistake and we never think about what God truly is; so without God's grace it is simply impossible to reach that home, the highest state, by means of this body). So, Shri Ram, now be merciful and yourself take away this Tulsidas's fear of the world, of being born and dying again and again.

You did not love Shri Ramchandra with a natural love, though loving is his very nature. That is why you have become a creature of this world, caught in the wheel of birth and death. But even now, listen to this teaching.
Just as the face reflected in a mirror is not really inside the mirror, so this mother, father, son and wife, even while they serve you, are not your own. (It is only because you have merged yourself with the mirror of maya that they seem to be yours.)
(The world's ties are ties of self-interest.) Sesame seeds are laid with flowers again and again to make them fragrant, but once the oil is pressed out the cake is thrown away as useless — and that is exactly the state of relatives. (That is, as long as their purpose is served they stay with you and honour you, and after that no one even asks about you.) This earth is packed with such self-seeking people, whose minds are black though their bodies are white.
How many friends you have made, how many you are making now, and how many more you will make; but a friend like Shri Raghunath, who keeps his love the same forever, you will never find at all.
Listen! The One because of whom every relationship seems true — with him you have never got acquainted to this day! That is why you still have not understood this truth: what is real gain and what is real loss.
Of those who hold the unreal — this world — to be true and the true — God — to be unreal, which one has not destroyed his own real good and gone, is not going, and will not go? (In short, such foolish souls throw away this human life for nothing, without ever reaching God.)
The Vedas have said it, the learned say it, and I too am calling it out: Shri Raghunath, the Lord of Tulsi, is the only true well-wisher. Just look a moment with the eyes of your heart.

The only one who truly loves is Shri Ramchandra, the Lord of Kosala. There is no one as kind as Ram, who never forgets the love given to him.
Everyone connected with this body is out for himself, and the gods are shrewd in their dealings (they give you exactly as much as you serve them, and if anything goes wrong they make everything you have done count for nothing). Who else is there like Shri Raghunath, who does good to the suffering, the low and the helpless? (No one at all.)
(Now look at what lovers get.) A melody, the note of music, is heartless (it is music that traps the poor deer in the net and gets him killed). Fire treats everyone the same (and the poor moth has to fall into it and be burnt to ash). Water too is no hero at keeping love (the fish cannot live without it even for a moment, but water is such that it suffers nothing at all without the fish). The moon is sick all his life (his lover the chakor bird is so enchanted with him that it pecks at burning coals, but the moon feels not the least pity for it). The sun is lost in his own greatness (every single lotus bud opens at the sight of him, but he thinks it beneath him and dries it up in a moment). And the cloud is utterly cruel on the path of love (it does not only make the poor chatak bird long for it, it thunders and rains hailstones on it and strikes it with lightning).
(But what can be done?) Whoever a person's heart is tied to becomes the one who gives him happiness; he takes even pain for joy. But in my eyes there is no other master as simple and as good-natured as Shri Raghunath.
Who else signs off on your service the moment he hears of it and accepts it as service? And who else sees your offence and still pays it no mind? In whose court are the helpless honoured with such special love?
Who took a bird, Jatayu, and Shabari as his own father and mother? Who made monkeys like Sugriv his friends? Who met Guha the boatman and held him to his heart like his own brother Bharat? Tell me then, is there any other like him, who makes sinners pure? (There is none.)
Who makes the luckless lucky? Who keeps the frightened in his shelter? Whose glory is being sung in the Vedas, and whose songs are the poets and the learned singing? (Lord Ramchandra alone is such a friend of the helpless and lover of his devotees.)
Whoever took shelter in his name, however low and sinful he may have been, Shri Ram made his own at once, the way a man ties found money into the corner of his cloth without stopping to test whether the coins are true or false.
Even Tulsidas, whose mind is so dirty that those who merely hear of the things he has done in this age of Kali become sinners themselves — even him Shri Ram has accepted as his servant. That is how Shri Raghunath cares for the poor.

You fool! If you have no love for Shri Ramchandra, the Lord of Janaki, and no bond with Him, how will anything you want ever come true — in this world or the next? As things stand, the crooked age of Kali has cheated you halfway through, and both this life and the life beyond are ruined.
For people who have no love for God, the duties of caste and stage of life are found written only in books and Puranas. Nobody actually lives by them. Such empty outward show, with no real duty behind it, is like a body with no life in it — it is of no use at all.
We hear that all the famous practices laid down in the Vedas — sacrifices and the rest — can give all four things: wealth, dharma, desire and moksha. But without love for Shri Ram, knowing them and believing in them is like a pond or a river with no water in it. In short: every act done without love for God is wasted.
There are many roads to liberation and many kinds of practice. But Tulsi, take my word for it and simply repeat the name of Ram, day and night — that alone will save you.

Even now, if you would only look honestly at your own low deeds and at Shri Ram's deeds, which are full of mercy, you could still be saved. Where are you — a soul turned away from Ram, sunk in the pleasures of the senses — and where is the Lord of Kosala, Shri Ramchandra, an ocean of mercy that asks for no reason? And what do people call you? "A devotee of Ram." There is no difference between a devotee and the Lord. Is being called that the fruit of anything you have done?
Come, hold up the mirror of clear thinking and look at the face of your own mind. When has Shri Ram ever been pleased with you and shown you kindness, and when has He ever turned angry and abused you? Think it over and you will see plainly: Ram has only ever been kind, and whatever fault there is, is yours alone. If God started losing His temper and hurling abuse, how would any soul ever be rescued? So admit your defeat for what you have done — neither imagine that your own deeds earned you the name of devotee, nor lay the blame on Him, asking why He does not save you though you are His devotee.
And really, how long does it take Him to save anyone? He does not need even half a moment to set right a ruin built up over many lifetimes. Just say with love, "Merciful Lord, protect me" — and tell me, is there any sinner whom Shri Ramchandra has not turned into a truly good man?
After hearing the story of Valmiki and of Guha the boatman, and how Sugriv, Hanuman, Shabari and Jambavan the bear were welcomed and honoured — if a man still does not take shelter with Shri Ram, who on earth can teach such a fool anything?
What service had Sugriv ever done? What faithfulness in love had he shown? Once he had his kingdom he forgot Shri Ram's work altogether! Yet for his sake Ram killed his brother Bali like a hunter, taking the blame on Himself. When people hear of a killing done that way, nobody likes it — nobody except the devotees.
What worship had Vibhishan ever offered? And what did the Lord of the Raghus give him in return — the great empire of Lanka, and His own unshakable love. The truth is that Shri Ramchandra, the protector of the poor, holds His promise to guard whoever comes to Him as a matter of deep honour. He does not even look at the past deeds of the one who takes shelter with Him.
So keep repeating the name of the Lord of the Raghus and let no other talk begin, because He alone is the master who is beautiful, who gives joy, who is wise, who is able, who is an ocean of mercy, and who protects everyone who comes to Him.
Is there anyone who has sung the praises of Shri Ramchandra with tears in his eyes, with a voice choking with feeling, with a heart full of love and the hair on his body standing up — and whose suffering in this world, the round of birth and death, has not come to an end?
Stop torturing yourself with regret. Lord Ramchandra remembers every good turn, and He knows everything — inside and outside, past and future. Not one of your acts is hidden from Him. Tulsidas, your acquaintance with Ram is nothing new. Hold on to Him with firm trust.

If there is no love in you for Shri Ramchandra, who loves you above all, then what did you gain by taking a human body? Love for God alone, and nothing else, is the highest gain of a human life.
Clear-minded people take this body, throw away all the pleasures of the world as if they were poison, and become lovers of Shri Ram. You too received that rare body — and yet, you utterly wretched, unlucky man, all you did was stuff yourself with sin!
The world is not short of paths to joy and liberation — knowledge, detachment, yoga, repeating God's name, austerity, sacrifice and the rest. But without love for Shri Ram, every one of these practices is as empty as waves in a mirage-sea.
Looking at the world, listening to the Puranas and the Vedas, and learning from wise teachers, one thing is clear: to love and trust the lotus feet of Shri Ram is the mine from which all blessings come.
If even now you take this in and accept defeat in your heart — if you let go of your pride and take shelter with Him — you will be saved in a single moment. Remember Shri Ramchandra with love, your one true well-wisher. Accept this as the settled teaching of Tulsidas.

My Lord, Shri Ram, I would give my life for You. Be kind to me simply because kindness is Your nature.
