All the ways that give the joy of the highest truth, the joy of heaven and the good things of this world — self-control, restraint, austerity, sacrifice and the rest — the age of Kali has angrily wiped them all out, and set running in their place its own painful habits: pretence, deceit and slander.
Wherever this mind of mine looks for its own good, there fresh sorrows keep piling up day after day. The things I would like run away from me in fear, from far off, and the things my mind does not want come crowding in without end. That is to say: I struggle for happiness and endless sorrow is all that arrives.
My mind is drowning in worry, my body is wretched with disease, and my speech has turned false and foul — always untrue, harsh and ugly. And yet, my Lord, with all of this, the bond and the love between You and this Tulsidas stand exactly as they were. Blessed are You, who keep a bond of love unbroken even with a wretch like me.

My mind, why do you go running about trying one thing after another? As long as you turn your face away from Ram, the jewel of the line of Raghu, no amount of other effort will end your pain. A man turned away from God may try a million remedies, but his three kinds of suffering — of the body, of fate, of the world around him — cannot be destroyed. Shukdev, the greatest of sages, raised his arm and declared this.
Drop the old habit of your nature, the habit of turning away from Shri Ram, and think it through with a steady mind: can you ever get butter by churning water instead of milk? In the same way, staying lost in the pleasures of the senses will never bring you happiness. Understand this, let the confusion go, and worship the two feet of Shri Ramchandra — feet easily reached by service, feet that are a deep forest of every good quality, so that whoever serves them receives wisdom, detachment, peace and joy without any struggle.
Steady your mind and listen to the one settled conclusion of the scriptures, the Vedas, all the other books, the rishis, the sages, the gods and the saints — and it is this: give up every other hope and take shelter with God. Tulsidas, the bank of the Ganga may be close by, but an animal with no master still dies of thirst. In the same way, the highest joy of reaching God is there for the taking, and yet without taking shelter with Him it stays out of reach.

I have no love for the feet of the Lord of the Raghus, and that is why I am suffering one calamity after another. It is not only what I say — the Vedas and all the wise sages say the same. For why would a deer sitting in the lap of the moon, tasting nectar, ever be fooled by the water of a mirage? Once a soul has tasted the joy of loving Shri Ram's lotus feet, why would it go astray after the false pleasures of the world?
A parrot recites everything and understands nothing, and in the same way, listening to one Purana after another without understanding does not remove ignorance. The foolish parrot ties itself up with no snare at all — it grabs the perch with its own beak and hangs there. That silly bird hopes for something from the semal flower, but the moment it strikes at it there is no pulp in the fruit, nothing but cotton to eat, and then it is sorry. In just this way a man grips the perch of the senses and binds himself, hoping the pleasures of the world will make him happy, and spends his life gathering them — and the moment they leave him, he is miserable.
I have no spiritual practice to my name, and I have gained no powers. I do not know the rites of the Vedas, I do not know how to repeat God's name or how to do austerities, and I have never mastered my mind by controlling my breath. This Tulsidas has only one support: Lord Ramchandra, the storehouse of compassion. He alone will take away this terrible worldly misery, and free me from birth and death.

My mind, once this good chance — the years of a human life — has slipped past, you will be sorry. So while you have this rare human body, worship the lotus feet of the Lord with your acts, your words and your heart.
Even mighty kings like Sahasrabahu and Ravan could not escape powerful Time; they too had to die. Those who went about saying "mine, mine", carefully guarding their wealth and their houses, went from here at the end with empty hands — not one cowrie went with them.
Understand that your sons and your wife are looking after themselves, and do not pour your love into them. You wretch, when they are all going to leave you at the end anyway, why not let them go now? Why not drop this attachment and start loving God today?
Wake up, you fool, out of the sleep of ignorance! Love your master, the Lord of the Raghus, and throw out of your heart the false hope of finding happiness in the things of this world. There is no happiness in them — so where would you get it from? Tulsidas, just as a fire is not put out by pouring in more and more ghee but only blazes higher, so this craving of yours only grows the more you get. It can be put out by the water of contentment alone.

Foolish mind, why do you keep running here and there? Why have you left the nectar of Shri Hari's lotus feet and fixed your heart on the water of a mirage, the pleasures of the senses?
You have wandered through every kind of birth in this world — animals, birds, gods, human beings, demons and all the rest. In all these births you have had countless homes, wives, sons, brothers, and mothers and fathers who brought you into the world.
Every one of them taught you the same love of sense pleasure, the very thing that drags you again and again into hell after hell. Not one of them ever showed you the road that would cut your worldly bondage, free you from birth and death, bring you the highest good and give you moksha.
You have been cheated like this over and over, and even so, to this very day you are still working for those same pleasures! Again and again you suffer, and again your mind runs back to them. But you wicked creature, think for a moment — how can a fire of craving be quieted by pouring in the ghee of enjoyment? The more pleasures you get, the higher the fire of craving will blaze.
When you did not get what you wanted, you were in great pain; and when you did get it, and then lost it, misery came all the same — not even in a dream did happiness come. That is why the Vedas call this wealth of sense pleasure painful in both ways, like a fire lit by a ghost. Those who chase pleasures find no happiness in getting them and none in losing them.
Look — your life is draining away moment by moment, and you have thrown away this rare human body for nothing. So, Tulsidas, give up hoping for worldly happiness and worship Shri Hari alone. Be on your guard: the serpent of Time is swallowing the world, and who knows at what hour you too will be its meal.

You foolish soul, anyone would think you had been given a body plated with copper! That must be why you take this body — which cracks like an unbaked clay pot, which is gone in a moment like a bubble on water — for something that will never age or die, and lose yourself in pleasures. And you have forgotten God completely. You wretch, you do not even know that death is dancing over your head!
Who has not claimed land, a wife, money, a house, friends and sons as his own? But to this day, whose have they ever really been? Who did they go with at the hour of death? The love in all of them is nothing but pretence.
There were kings who conquered the whole world and locked up even Yama, the god of death, and made him their servant — and one day Time made a meal of them too. So what are you worth in that count?
Think it over: what is the real truth of it, and what have the Vedas declared for certain? Tulsi, even knowing all this, you still do not worship that Shri Ram on whom Lord Shiva himself has fixed his mind.

What did you gain by getting a human body, when not even in a dream were you of any use to another person, in thought, in word or in deed?
The pleasures of the senses come to you on their own, uninvited, whether you are in heaven or hell, at home or in the forest. And for that kind of happiness, my mind, you keep trying one scheme after another! However much you are explained to, you do not understand.
You fool, ignorance took hold of you and you did whatever you pleased — chasing other men's wives and making enemies of others. You went through terrible suffering, cruel pain and misery in the womb, and you have forgotten all of it. It never crossed your mind that these wilful, wicked acts will send you back to that same misery of life in the womb.
Fear, sleep, mating and eating are the same in every creature born into this world! But you were given a human body that even the gods find hard to get, and even with that you did not worship God — you lost it in pride and arrogance.
Those who have not destroyed the sense of "mine" and "yours", and who have not sunk their minds in Shri Ram with a pure heart — Tulsidas, once a chance like this human birth has slipped away from them, what will they get by being sorry afterwards? So wake up and start worshipping God now.

You took a human body — and what did you actually accomplish with it? Doing good to others is the very heart of the Vedas, and you never gave it a thought, not even by accident.
This world is a tree whose root is duality, the sense of separateness; its thorns are fear and its fruit is sorrow. Push at it and it will not move, because until the root of ignorance, that sense of separateness, is cut, it cannot be cleared. It falls only to the sharp axe of worshipping Shri Ram — and you never took up that worship and cut it down.
The name of Ram is a boat for crossing the ocean of doubt and ignorance, and you never used it to carry your own soul across. Birth after birth you have wandered through countless forms with no wisdom in you, and even now you are not tired of it.
When you saw others prospering easily, you let your mind burn in the fire of envy — "why doesn't his wealth go up in smoke?" — and you went on burning in that fire. You never quieted your heart with calm, self-control, kindness and care for the poor, and you never remembered God.
In thought, in act and in word you forgot your true master, teacher, father and friend — the Lord of the Raghus. Tulsidas, there is only one hope left now: He who carried Jatayu the vulture across will keep you too in His shelter.

My mind, put aside your pride and worship the lotus feet of the true guru, who is God in living form. Serve him, and you reach Shri Hari, who is joy itself.
Just as pratipada is the very first day of the fortnight, love is the first of all practices. Without love, meeting Shri Ram is a very distant thing — even though He is nearer than near, living fully in every heart.
Like the second day, the second practice is this: with a steady, unwavering mind, drop the sense of difference between God and the soul, and move about the whole earth free of anxiety, seeing all alike. In a heart with no delusion, no illusion and no arrogance, the Lord of the Raghus lives forever.
Like the third day, the third way is this: the Supreme Person, Mukund, the Lord of Lakshmi, is beyond the three qualities. So you must let go of nature, which is made of those three — purity, passion and darkness. Without doing that, the highest joy is hard to reach. As long as a person stays inside nature he remains a bound soul, tasting pleasure and pain; only by stepping out of nature and resting in his own true self, the Supreme Being, does he find the bliss of liberation.
Like the fourth day, the fourth practice for reaching God is this: give up the inner instrument — intellect, mind, thought and the sense of "I" taken together. While the body lasts this inner instrument will of course remain; giving it up means dropping your identification with it and becoming its witness, or offering it to God and using it only for His work. Do this, and clear wisdom will dawn; then you will reach the highest state, your own true self, generous and full of joy.
Like the fifth day, the fifth practice is this: do not let touch, taste, sound, smell and sight — the objects of the five senses — give you your orders and do not live under their command, because if they master you the soul falls into the dark, deep well of worldly life, into the wheel of birth and death.
Like the sixth day, the sixth way is this: to reach Shri Ram, the Lord of Janaki, you must conquer six enemies — lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy. Without the water of Shri Ram's mercy the fire of greed will not go out. His mercy is always on the soul; so feel that mercy and use it to kill greed and the rest.
Like the seventh day, the seventh practice is this: think hard about this body made of the seven elements — fluid, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow and seed — this impure, fragile, yet rare human body. It has only one good use: doing good to others.
Like the eighth day, the eighth way is this: Shri Ramchandra, who is beyond all change, is beyond the eightfold lifeless nature — earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and the sense of "I". So as long as all kinds of cravings are alive in your heart, how can you ever meet Him?
Like the ninth day, the ninth practice is this: whoever lives in this city of nine gates — this body with its nine openings — and does not work for his own soul's good will wander through birth after birth and meet every kind of terrible sorrow. So work for the good of your soul alone.
Like the tenth day, the tenth practice is this: whoever has not learned to restrain the ten senses, and has not brought them under control, finds all his practices come to nothing; and that man, a slave to his senses and without self-control, cannot reach God.
Like the eleventh day, the eleventh practice is this: master your mind and serve God alone. That is how the fast of ekadashi — the fast of seeking the highest truth — bears its greatest fruit, the end of birth and death: such a man reaches God.
On the twelfth day gifts are given, so the twelfth practice is this: give in such a way — with no selfish motive, only out of love for God — that no fear remains from any of the three worlds and God is reached. And the way to break that twelfth fast is to stay always busy doing good to others. After such giving and such breaking of the fast, sorrow never touches you again.
Like the thirteenth day, the thirteenth practice is this: go past the three states — waking, dreaming and deep sleep — and worship God. That is to say, worship Him constantly, asleep and awake. God cannot be grasped by mind, act or word, because, like water in ice, He fills everything, and, like the sights in a dream, He is Himself everything that is filled — and He is boundless and endless. Only the one He graciously makes to know Him can know Him, and His grace is felt through worship that never stops; so worship Him in all three states.
Like the fourteenth day, God, the keeper of the senses, is playing through all fourteen worlds as everything that moves and does not move. But until the soul's sense of separateness goes, the Lord of the Raghus does not cut the net of worldly life, does not set the soul free from birth and death. If you want release from this bondage, worship God knowing there is no difference.
Like the full moon, the fifteenth practice for reaching God, the highest and most complete of them all, is this: soaked in the sweetness of loving devotion, the devotee should come to know the sweetness of Shri Hari, the supreme and secret truth of God. That alone can make him see all things equally, and be peaceful, free of ego, full of understanding, and untouched by the pleasures of the senses.
Here Goswami Tulsidas is speaking of the full moon of the month of Phalgun — and this full moon is far greater than the full moon of any other month; on this joyful full-moon day of Holi, burn up in the bonfire the three kinds of suffering — of the body, of fate, of the world — and play the festival of colours with God, the festival of love. This is the state of highest joy. If you want that joy, then walk this road and take up these practices.
The Vedas, the Puranas and the learned all agree on one thing: singing of God's own deeds is the true song of Holi — so sing His praises with all your heart. Think over all these practices and cross the ocean of this world. And never again, not even by mistake, fall into the current of sense pleasures that carries a man to the realm of death.
Shri Hari alone destroys every doubt, takes away every sorrow, and is the treasure-house of joy. You may try as many methods as you like, but without the grace of the saints you cannot reach Him — so the grace of the saints is the greatest of all practices.
To cross the ocean of this world, the holy feet of the saints are the only boat. Tulsidas, climb into that boat — serve the feet of the saints — and Shri Ramchandra, who destroys all sorrow, will come to you without any effort at all.

If only this mind would fasten itself to the feet of Shri Ramchandra the same way it sinks — with no effort at all, all by itself — into the body, the house, sons, money and wife.
Then it would rise above the pairs of opposites (pleasure and pain and the rest), its pride would fall away, it would be lost in true knowledge, and it would turn from the pleasures of the senses the way the mind turns from all the sour things kept in a pot of brass, or of copper mixed with tin, because they have gone bitter. And then why would Shri Ramchandra, the Lord of Kosala, who is solid joy and the crown jewel of all who are wise, not be pleased with such a deserving devotee and give himself into his hands?
Whoever loves the Lord's lotus feet like this becomes a great soul: devoted to the good of every living being, with a heart that nothing can shake, steady in unbroken love and devotion and in the Lord's own ways. But O Tulsidas, this state comes only when the Master who killed Ravan (Shri Ram) is pleased and pours out his grace.

O my mind! If you want to take shelter under the Lord, who is the wish-granting tree, then let go of the rot of sense pleasures and sing the name of Shri Ram, which is the heart of everything — and do what I am telling you right now (nothing has been ruined yet).
Hold on tightly to these four: an even mind, contentment, clear and clean understanding, and the company of good people. And give up lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, liking and disliking completely — do not let even a trace of them stay.
With your ears, listen to the Lord's story. With your mouth, repeat the name of Ram. In your heart, hold Shri Hari in your thoughts. With your head, bow down, and with your hands, serve the Lord. With your eyes, look upon Ramchandra — the ocean of mercy, who fills all that moves and all that stands still, the great king, the beloved of Janaki.
This is devotion, this is renunciation, this is knowledge, and this is what pleases the Lord — so keep this beautiful vow. O Tulsidas, this is the very path Lord Shiva pointed out. Walk this blessed road and no fear will touch you, not even in a dream (a person reaches the Supreme and becomes fearless).

There is no one else like Shri Raghunath who takes away our troubles, no one else worth running to for shelter. Whose nature is so simple that he lets himself be ruled by his own servants? Who loves those who come to him for refuge like this, asking nothing in return?
Shri Raghunath treats even the smallest good quality in his servant as if it were Mount Sumeru, and though he sees ten million faults in him, he forgets them all. For he is deeply kind, he is the wish-fulfilling jewel of his devotees, it is his very name and nature to make people pure, and he lifts the fallen out of the ocean of this world.
Just remember him, and he is there — that easily. And when he hears that his servant is in pain, he comes running so fast (for fear of being late) that he does not even stop to hold his yellow robe in place. The Puranas, the Vedas and the scriptures stand witness to this, and Draupadi and Gajendra know it well.
Poets and wise, holy souls — those who have no greed, no delusion, no arrogance, no lust — sing his glory. O Tulsidas, let go of every hope (of this world and the next) and worship only that Lord of Kosala, the one who lifted up Ahalya.

There is no master like Shri Raghunath — worth worshipping, giving joy, keeping us under his shelter. He is the home of bliss, the destroyer of sorrows, the one who carries grief away, the beloved of Lakshmi; you can go on counting his qualities and never come to the end.
Even those who are miserable, low, outcast, dishonest, wicked, sinful and frightened, who can find shelter nowhere at all — even they, helpless, remember the name of Ram just once and reach that highest place where even the gods cannot go.
Sages who have given up everything hover at his lotus feet like bees, sages who do not even want moksha, that most beautiful of destinations. O foolish Tulsidas! Why do you not worship that Lord, full of compassion, who is always kind to those who have no one?

My Lord, how am I to speak my plea out loud to you? When I look at my own sins — endless kinds of them, done in three ways, by thought, by word and by deed — and I want to come and stand before you for shelter, shame pushes my head down.
I dress myself up as one of your devotees, as if I were building a pretty screen to hide behind, and I cover it over with fresh green leaves of deceit. I fix your name to it like a pole and smear it with the birdlime of sweet words — and then, like a fowler, I trap the birds of sense pleasure. (In people's eyes I walk around as a great devotee, with the sacred mark, the rosary, the beads, singing the praises of Ram's name and speaking sweetly — while inside I am thinking of nothing but pleasures and hunting for them.)
I am such a sinner that a hundred million sinners could be offered up for a single hair of mine — yet I still want my name counted first in the roll of saints, I still lay claim to being the greatest saint of all. I am crude and low, and yet I sit perched on a mountain of arrogance. That is why, fool that I am, I go about calling myself all-knowing and the best of devotees.
My Lord, I cannot say whether it is false or true, but some people say about me, "This one belongs to Ram" — and I too want to be called yours. So now, my Lord, for the honour of your own name, take this Tulsidas as your own (for if I am called yours and still stay wicked, what becomes of the honour of your name?). Please, no more putting it off.

My Lord, I have nobody else to lean on. O treasure-house of compassion, this is my honest promise in thought, word and deed: the only support I have is your sandals.
My mind is the home of anger, pride, ignorance and possessiveness; so there is no point even mentioning knowledge and wisdom to it. When I look into my heart and see so many plans born of desire and so many cravings of every kind, there is not even a sliver of hope left for moksha.
It is true that (though I do nothing right) my mind badly wants to go to heaven — but without the rites and duties the Vedas prescribe, heaven is very hard to reach. And serving the perfected ones, the gods, human beings and demons is just as hard. They will only be pleased if one does harsh yoga for them, gives them a share of the sacrifice and offers up one's very life. (I cannot do any of this either, so it is pointless for me to hope for kindness from them.)
And devotion is the hardest of all to reach for someone like me — because even Shiva, Shukdev and the sages who hover like bees at your lotus feet stay thirsty forever for that sweet nectar. (If even they are never satisfied drinking it, where does a low creature like me stand?) Yes, I do hear that your name makes the fallen pure and gives peace (moksha) — but the knots of pride are tied so tightly in my mind that it wanders off again. (So learned and clever am I, should I stoop to plain Ram's name? And through that pride I lose the name of Ram as well.)
Great King, looking at all of this, the only place I have earned is hell; by my deeds I deserve nothing but to lie in the pitch-dark well of this terrible world. And yet, even so, you are my strength. This Tulsidas remembers in his heart who Guha was, and Jatayu, and Gajendra, and Hanuman — and thinks nothing at all of that fear of the world, of birth and death. (If an outcast, an animal and a bird could be saved, why not me? Surely I will be.)

O jewel of the line of Raghu, where else is there for me to go (if I leave your feet)? You alone make sinners pure, you alone look after those who come for shelter, you alone give a home to those who have nobody. Who else wears that bold and beautiful name you wear? (No one.)
O Raghunath, even if you turn your anger on me, thinking over my offences in your heart, and refuse to listen to my plea, and turn your face away from me — even then I will speak without fear, O ocean of compassion, and I will say only this: how can you hear my words (hear this poor cry of mine) and not look my way? (How can the ocean of compassion hear the aching cry of a helpless man and stay still?)
(If you ask me what my heart wants, then listen.) What I want most of all is to go and live in your highest home. But my Lord, that wish of mine is surrounded and hemmed in by lust, anger, greed and delusion (they attack it and crush it down). Moksha is out of reach, and even heaven is hard to get, since it comes only as the fruit of good deeds (and I have done nothing good — so how can heaven be mine?). And as for Yama's city, hell, the power of your name will not even let me near it (Yama does not let one who says Ram's name come anywhere close to his city).
So now there is no place left for me anywhere. You tell me — where should I go? O Lord of Kosala, I am poor and helpless (if I had money I would have built myself a house somewhere), and I am frantic because I have no shelter. So my Lord, be kind and give this Tulsidas a place to live in that same village where Gajendra, Jatayu and the hunter (Valmiki) live.

O jewel of the line of Raghu, will you ever pour on me too the same grace whose power carried the hunter (Valmiki), Gajendra, the brahmin Ajamil and many other wicked people across the ocean of this world? My Lord, will you count me as one of those sinners too, and lift me up as well?
Birth after birth, in body after body, I have done wicked deeds of every kind. Will you keep my base behaviour out of your heart? O friend of the helpless, will you follow your own tender nature and your own qualities — that no one can defeat you, that you know what is in every heart, that you can do anything at all, that you protect those who come for shelter? (That is: looking at these qualities of yours rather than turning away in disgust from my sins, knowing what is in my mind, will you use your endless power to save me, who have come to you for shelter?)
There is a gang of villains living in my heart — ignorance, ego, conceit, lust and the rest. Will you destroy them root and branch, with all their family, and take away my unbearable pain? And will you give me your devotion, which is purer and greater than yoga, than chanting, than sacrifices and than deep knowledge, and fill my heart with the highest joy?
And if you look at this Tulsidas — the chief of the low, with not one spiritual practice to his name, crooked and filthy-minded — and feel a little afraid in your heart (that saving such a huge sinner might get you blamed as unfair), then my Lord, how will you spread that glorious name of yours which the Vedas celebrate, and that spotless fame? (If you care about the honour of your own name, then you must save me.)

Shri Raghunath is the one who takes our troubles away. You are so very kind, you look after everyone who comes to you for shelter, and you make sinners pure.
The cruel, the wicked, the lowborn, the poor, and even the most degraded outsider — the moment they remembered the name of Ram, you sent them to your own highest home.
Gajendra, Pingala the prostitute, Ajamil — who can count all the wicked people drunk on sense pleasures whom you have taken in? (Who knows how many sinners like these you gave your own home to.) O Tulsidas, the truth is this: whom has Ramchandra, the Lord of Janaki, not set free? (Whoever came for shelter was set free — so why not me?)

There is no one else like Lord Hari who carries away our troubles, who shows kindness so easily, who ferries us across the ocean of unbearable sorrow.
When the king of elephants saw his own strength failing and came to you for shelter, holding out a lotus flower as an offering, you heard his helpless words, took up your Sudarshan disc, left Garuda standing there and came at once, running on foot.
When wicked Dushasan began stripping Draupadi's sari off her in that crowded hall, all she said was, "Oh Lord, save me!" — and at once you piled up sari upon sari of every colour.
Knowing this love of yours for the helpless, gods and humans, sages and scholars serve your feet. Whom has the Lord who rescued King Nrig not made free of fear? (Whoever came to him for shelter, he set free of fear.)

Which other master anywhere (besides the Lord) has this way about him — that for the honour of his name he passes by the pure and pours his love on the worthless?
The demoness Putana smeared poison on her breasts and came to kill him (Lord Krishna), and yet the merciful Krishna, lord of the Yadavas, gave her the place a mother is given (he lifted her up and saved her).
The cowherd women were out of their minds with love, and you showed them such measureless kindness that even Brahma, the father of the world, took the dust of their feet and put it on his own head.
Shishupal made it a rule to curse you every single day, counting out his insults — and in the assembly of kings (at the Pandavas' royal sacrifice), with everyone watching, you took him up and merged him into yourself.
A foolish hunter mistook you for a deer, took aim at your foot and shot his arrow — and even him you sent to your own highest home in his own body, showing the world how kind you always are.
What is there to say about people who have done both good and bad deeds? (They had at least some claim on a good end.) But this Lord has taken in Tulsi, who is sin itself in plain sight — and that proves what he is like beyond all doubt.

This is simply how Shri Raghunath is: when he sees pure, undivided love in someone's heart, he loves even the lowest of people back.
(Listen to the proof.) Guha the boatman was of the lowest birth and a sinner; what respect did he have? But the Lord recognised his pure, undivided love and held him to his chest like a son.
Jatayu was a vulture, made by Brahma to live by killing; what kindness was there in him? Yet Raghunath poured the water of parting for him with his own hands, as if for his own father.
Shabari was dirty and unkempt by nature, of low birth, a storehouse of every fault; but seeing her pure and undivided love, you ate the fruit from her hand with great delight, praising the taste again and again.
When Vibhishan, a demon and an enemy, came to you for shelter, you stood up and held him to your heart as lovingly as you would hold Bharat — so lost in that love that you forgot your own body.
And what were the monkeys — handsome, well-behaved? They were creatures whose very name is thought to bring bad luck when spoken. Yet you made them your friends, brought them into your own home, and honoured them in every way.
(All this proves it:) Shri Ramchandra is kind by nature, gentle by nature, a friend to the poor, always giving. So Tulsi, drop your crookedness and your pretence, and worship no one but this Lord Shri Ram (always, with pure and undivided love).

Who should we worship, if not Lord Hari? There is no one like Shri Raghunath, no one else who feels such tenderness for the helpless who come to him.
(Listen to the proof.) Hiranyakashipu was Brahma's devotee in deed, thought and word; yet when he was tormenting his own son Prahlad, Brahma (though he knew the hour of his death) did not stop him — and so he went off to the land of death. (Had Brahma stopped him earlier, why would the poor man have died?)
The whole world knows that Ravan was a devotee of Lord Shiva, that he cut off his own heads again and again and offered them to Shiva. Yet when he began to make an enemy of Shri Raghunath, Shiva did not stop him, not even in a dream (though he knew that making an enemy of Shri Ram would get him killed).
(If this is how Brahma and Shiva are,) what is there to say about the other gods? They are friends only as long as it serves them. Not one of them ever protected a frightened soul who came for shelter.
Who does not hand out riches to someone who serves him? (They all do.) That is simply the way of the world. But O Tulsidas, only Shri Raghunath loves the helpless. (He takes them as his own the moment they come for shelter, without any service at all, and does not demand a perfect, complete ritual the way the gods do.)

My Lord, if there were anyone else (who would keep me under his shelter), why would I come crying to you again and again, pouring out my sorrow?
Who else (besides you) has any tenderness for the helpless? Whose name is "the purifier of the fallen"? And who gave his own highest home to that terrible sinner Ajamil (who said your name, Narayan, only because he was calling his son)? There is only you, and no one else.
Shiva, Brahma, Indra and many other guardians of the worlds were there; but when the king of elephants was drowning in a river of grief, not one of them saved him (you were the one who had to leave Garuda and run).
When Draupadi, the wife of Arjun (Nar himself in human form), was tormented by Dushasan in that hall full of kings and cried, "O Lord, save me!" — everyone there had the power to help, but not one of them gave her a cloth (you came down as cloth itself and saved that helpless woman's honour).
O ocean of compassion, how can I tell with one mouth the stories of the compassion that fills the ocean of compassion? O King of Kosala, what did you not do for your devotees when you came down in human form? (For the good of his devotees he did absolutely everything.)
If I disgust you so much, then hand me over to someone who is just like you — otherwise, why would this Tulsidas ever leave your feet for anything? What he means is this: I am staying right here at your feet, in your shelter.

O Hari, will you ever let me see those holy feet of yours, which destroy every sorrow and every sin of this dark age, and which are the source of all that is good?
Their colour is like fresh red lotuses, just opened, the beautiful ones that bloom in autumn. Lakshmi presses them with her lovely palms. Their beauty has no equal.
They are the father of the Ganga (the Ganga was born from them), they are dear to Shiva, who burned up the god of desire. They took the form of a cheating young monk and tricked King Bali. They freed Ahalya, the brahmin Gautam's wife, and King Nrig from their curses and gave them the highest joy, and they took away all the sorrow and terrible sin of the hunting boatman Guha.
The perfected ones, the gods and the whole company of sages bow to them always; they give joy and shelter to everyone; and a devotee who holds them in his heart even once is carried across himself and becomes someone who carries others across too.
O Raghunath, ocean of kindness, wise in every way, you take away the sorrow of all who come for shelter. This Tulsidas is dying now of thirst — the thirst of hoping to see those feet of yours. (Show him your lotus feet soon and save him.)

My Lord, since first light this morning I have been planted here at your door. I am whining and repeating my plea, I am begging and pleading. I want nothing else. One mouthful, one scrap, and my work is done. (One small glance of your grace and I will have everything I want.)
(If you ask why I do not work for it, why I beg and grovel, my answer is this:) in this dreadful dark age a terrible famine has fallen on all good spiritual effort. Every method, every practice, is spoiled; not one of them can be completed without something wrecking it. So I decided that begging from you was the right thing to do. People's deeds these days are base (day and night they sin for the sake of pleasure), yet their minds aim high (they want real happiness, though the real happiness of moksha never comes without the Lord's grace) — like scratching a leper's itch (it feels good while you scratch, but afterwards the wound opens and burns. In the same way, when the senses meet their pleasures it feels good at first, but the end of it is great suffering. Sense pleasures bring nothing but pain — understanding this, I have not put my heart into any of those efforts).
Afraid in my heart, I asked the kind company of holy people: tell me, will anyone give shelter even to a man like me, who has done nothing to earn it? And the saints answered with one voice: only one, the great king of Kosala, Shri Ramchandra, can take such people in.
O ocean of kindness, who but you can put an end to my helplessness and my poverty? O son of Dasharath, among all those who are known for giving, you are the greatest.
O protector of the poor, I am a beggar born hungry and destitute. So now give this Tulsi a bellyful of that lovely food, the nectar of devotion (give me such love for your feet that no other wish is left in me).

O King of Kosala, save me! Apart from your name I have no place to go and no one to lean on (your name is as far as I can run).
You understand your servants yourself, and you do more good for them than even their own mother and father could (even parents cannot give the joy of moksha). O Shri Ram, your name alone is my teacher, my god, my master, my friend and my helper.
My Lord, in your Ram-rajya not even the shadow of that filthy-minded age of Kali's trickery should be able to fall; yet this cowardly Kali age, out of that same rage, keeps striking and wounding me, who am already as good as dead. (It is not even afraid that I live inside your kingdom.)
The way a jackal kills a frog to get back at a lion, this age strikes me hard because it knows I am your servant. (Its quarrel is with you, since it cannot get into a heart that lives in your kingdom; but it has no power over you, so it torments a small servant like me.)
Even King Parikshit, who now lives in joy in the Lord's highest home, is full of regret in his heart when he hears of this age's cheating deeds, its countless injustices and all the obstacles it throws in the way of good people (regret that, having caught it, he let it go alive).
O ocean of kindness, turn one small glance of grace this way, so that the pain in this servant's heart may be stilled. O friend of the helpless, O Lord, I have come to your shelter to see your feet.
If you do not want to call that Kali age close and hold it back, or if you hear its cries of "Oh no, oh no!" and do not want to kill it — then I would give my life for you: just make one small sign to Hanuman, and at your signal he will look at it the way a lion looks into the face of a cow.
And when Hanuman's face turns red, his brows bend and his yellow eyes go red with anger — then, at the very memory of the son of the wind, brave Hanuman, all the swagger of this restless-minded Kali will vanish (it will forget every bit of its strength).
Hearing this plea of mine, Shri Raghunath smiled and explained to his younger brother Lakshman what I really meant (see how clever Tulsi is!). Lakshman laughed and said, "He is quite right." And just like that, everything I asked for was granted.
Shri Ramchandra gave this poor man his justice. Hearing it, drums of congratulation began to sound in the homes of the saints. Sorrow, worry, trickery and heaps of sin were all destroyed.
Seeing such rare, pure, illusion-free love and trust shown by the formless Lord to his servant, O Tulsidas, the sages began to call out, "Victory, victory to the Lord of boundless glory!"

Lord! I am poor and low, and day and night I keep watching the road for your mercy. Merciful to the helpless, I do not know — when will that mercy of yours come to me?
Goodness, wisdom, detachment, love for God — all the beautiful helps that come from a divine nature took one look at Kaliyug (this dark age) and ran away in fright. What is left behind is only heaps of sins and bad habits.
With so much injustice and wrongdoing, the earth has grown hotter than the sun (there is nothing left here to cool it — only burning). Where do I go now? I would give my life for you. I have no other place, no shelter anywhere. My mind is churning with distress.
Father! Not one person is mine — not even this body of mine (whose support can I lean on?). Everyone I see is hard-hearted and cruel. Dark rain-cloud Lord! This crop of Tulsi, grown tall and full of grain, is drying up — even now, become a cloud and water it (with the rain of your mercy).

Lord, I would give my life for you! Who else can I tell (my sorrow) to? Nowhere else is there a master like you — an ocean of goodness, one who does his servants good, a treasure-house of mercy.
Wherever my restless mind runs, pulled by greed and craving, hoping to find my good there, I come back disappointed — like an owl that sees the sun, wanders about and creeps back into a hollow in a tree (wherever I go, whoever I go to, the fire of sorrow is already waiting for me).
When I hear that time, one's nature and one's past deeds give strange and varied fruits, I am left beating my head, because for me all three are always the same: I go on burning in an unbearable, cruel fire.
Lord! Until now I thought of myself as having no master, so it was only right that I should be a vessel of sorrow — I had not yet become your servant. But protector of all who come to you, now I am called your servant and I am still suffering, and I cannot understand why.
Great King! Lotus-eyed One! I am drowning in the fever of my sins. Lord! Tulsidas can only get through if you yourself, somehow, in some way, carry him through.

Lord! Will you ever count me as your own? Ram! You take care of the poor, and you are king of kings. Will you ever think in your heart of the honour of your own name?
You are an ocean of gentleness, you are beautiful, you can do anything, you have all power, and you are a mine of every good quality. Lord! You have protected those who came to you for shelter, you are protecting them now, and you will go on protecting them. Will you also recognise the love of this (small, worthless) one who has come to you?
The Vedas and the Puranas say it, and the whole world knows it: you are kind to the lowly and you give them blessing every single day. I am forced to say this — I would give my life for you — it looks as though in my case you have forgotten your own habit.
Even though you are the friend of the poor, the sorrowful and the forsaken, are you afraid of what the world will say? (That if you take in such a sinner, someone may call you unjust.) Whatever happens, in the end Tulsidas will surely be blessed, because you are the one who breaks the fear of everyone who takes shelter in you.

O mind! Will you ever attach yourself to Shri Raghunath? You crooked thing! When will you give up the wrong road, bad ways, foolish thinking, bad desires and all your trickery?
Caught by a huge ignorance, you take poison (the pleasures of the senses) to be nectar, and you treat nectar (the remembrance of God) as if it were fire that burns you! When will you drop this upside-down habit and this love of the senses, and love the feet of Shri Ram?
When will you dip the sweet letters of Ram's name and the tender meaning inside them — sweets, both of them — in the syrup of love for Shri Raghunath? That is to say: will you ever repeat the name of Shri Ram with a heart full of love and with its meaning alive in you? If you please your master this way, singing his qualities again and again, you will get whatever you ask for.
Do this, and you will lie down for ever on the soft bed of happiness (moksha, freedom), and the great burning in your mind (born of ignorance) will run away for good. Tulsidas! By the mercy of Shri Ram, the yoga of loving devotion to Shri Ram will take root and be fulfilled in your heart.

Only that person will put his trust in someone else who has either found somewhere another master the equal of Shri Ramchandra, or who has some strength of his own — his own practices and efforts to rely on (I have found no such master, and I have no strength of my own of any kind).
Or else someone drunk on ignorance, desire and pride, so that he cannot see this terrible dark age for what it is; or someone who has heard of the nature of Lord Ramchandra — who is the well-wisher of people worn out by every kind of effort and wandering, and who loves the lowly and those who come to him — and yet has not kept it in mind. (I, at least, keep my master's merciful nature in my thoughts always.)
I know my own (tiny) strength very well, and I have never heard of any master besides Shri Raghunath with such fame (for taking in great sinners who come to him). A stone (Ahalya), a tribal woman, a bird (Jatayu), a deer (Marich), a demon (Vibhishan) — which of them had good deeds to show? (Yet the Lord lifted every one of them up.)
For me, the name of Ram alone has become the wish-fulfilling tree, and even that came through the mercy of the merciful Shri Ramchandra. (In this too, nothing is my own doing.) So now Tulsi is as happy and free of worry as a child living in the kingdom of his own mother and father.

Let anyone who trusts in someone else do so. For me, in this dark age, the one name of Ram is the wish-fulfilling tree, and the fruit it has borne is my own blessing. That is to say: it is from Ram's name alone that I have received this love of God.
It is true that ritual action, worship and knowledge — these teachings of the Vedas — are all true in every way. But I am like a man blinded in the monsoon: wherever I look, I see only green and green. (I see only the one name of Ram.)
I went about licking leaf-plates like a dog (plates other people had eaten from), and my stomach was never filled. Today, remembering the name, I see the juice of nectar served out before me. (I have tasted many pleasures fit for the gods, and nowhere was I satisfied. Nowhere did I find full, unending bliss. Now, the moment I remember the name of Shri Ram, I see a whole platter of freedom set before me — moksha, the bliss of Brahman, is already mine by right. Just as I can eat from a served plate whenever I want, so freedom is mine whenever I want it. But what I am actually drinking is the sweet juice of love for Shri Ram — the very thing that even freed souls long for.)
For me, the name of Ram gives both my own good and the highest good (freedom, which is my own good, and love of God, which is the highest good — I have got both from the name of Shri Ram). This is not one of those doubtful arguments — "is it an elephant or a man?" — (because I already have it in hand). I have heard that it was by the power of this very name that an army of monkeys built a bridge of stones and crossed the ocean.
Wherever a person puts his love and his trust, there his work has been done (and by that same rule) my mother and father are these two syllables — "Ra" and "m." It is in front of them that I plant myself and refuse to move, like a stubborn child throwing a fit.
If I am hiding even a little of the truth in what I say, Lord Shiva is my witness — let my tongue burn or rot and fall out. (This is not a poet's fancy or an exaggeration; it is a plain account of how things are.) This much I have understood: my good can come from the one name of Ram and from nothing else.

Ram! It is your name alone that brings me blessing. I raise my hand and call this out aloud to everyone travelling with me — in worldly life and in the life of the spirit (to my family and to fellow seekers) — I am announcing it.
My mother and father gave me birth and then let me go. Even the Creator made me unlucky and rather badly shaped. And yet some people call me "Ram's" (his servant) — with what possible reason do they say it? (It is the glory of Ram's name, nothing else.)
Before I took shelter in the name of Ram, I went from door to door with hungry eyes, begging to fill my stomach. Looking at me, even sorrow felt sorry (that was the state I was in). By the mercy of Shri Ram, the very trees that were thorny acacia and bitter beleric for me before are now giving me mangoes. (Where the world once looked full of suffering, today everything looks like Sita and Ram, and so that same world has become full of joy.)
Holy people listen to the scriptures, turn them over in their minds, and by many practices make both this world and the next good for themselves; but Tulsi has only one support, the one name of Ram. The knot is always a single knot, however many times the thread is wound around it (in the same way, however many practices there may be, the base of all of them is the one name of Ram).

There is one to whom even Shri Ram himself is not dearer than Ram's name (if someone said to him, "you can have Ram, but you must give up Ram's name," he would not agree even to that; he says, if meeting Shri Ram means giving up Ram's name, then I do not need to meet Shri Ram — I want his name always. How much Ram loves a lover of his name like this, only Ram knows; Goswami Tulsidas says that one who is drunk on Ram's name in this way) will be blessed in this terrible dark age at the beginning, in the middle and at the end — in all three.
Understanding the greatness of the name, pride, greed, ignorance, anger and lust shrink back in shame and do not come near. For good people who keep repeating Ram's name, even the fiercest heat gives shade instead (even the greatest sorrow turns into happiness).
If somebody says that by the power of the name a lotus grew out of a stone, take that as true too (because by the power of Ram's name even the impossible becomes possible). This is the name that made Shabari, a tribal woman, blessed beyond measure and full of goodness and holiness simply by hearing it and remembering it (what can such a name not do?).
Valmiki and Ajamil had nothing at all in the way of spiritual practice, yet even they, through the glory of Ram's name said backwards and muddled, won jewels in exchange for worthless red seeds (they gained the supreme jewel, God himself).
The power of the name is greater even than Shri Raghunath himself (because Shri Ram is won over by this very name). This name of Ram turned rough village people into polished citizens (turned coarse men into utterly holy souls). Repeating it, even wretched creatures like Tulsidas became good with the drums beating (after that, what more is there to say?).

If I say I belong to anyone but Ram, let this tongue of mine rot away. Life of Janaki! Birth after birth in this world, I have lived on the scraps left over from your plate.
In all three worlds and in all three times (on earth, in the world below and in heaven; in the past, the present and the future) I have not seen anywhere another true friend, another lover without a reason, equal to you. If I am playing false with you, then let me be a worm in a horrible hell for ages upon ages.
What does it matter if this dark age has joined forces and made my mind into a water-bug in a whirlpool? That is to say: just as a water-bug lives in the water and yet keeps floating on top of it and cannot sink, so, although Kaliyug has thrown me into the river of worldly life, by your glory I will not be swept away in this flood of the senses — I will keep floating right on top. The pleasures of the senses will have no hold on me. Tulsidas stays calm always on this one strength, that he belongs to a very great house (he is a slave of Shri Ram's court. What can cheap little things like Kaliyug do to him?).

Who else is there (besides Shri Ramchandra) who does good for no reason at all? Whose name is known for filling the poor with plenty, so that his devotees keep gazing at the slightest movement of his (merciful) eyebrow?
Small or great, all that the Creator has made wants to get something for itself (nobody does another's good without something in it for himself). Tell me, which other merciful master (besides Shri Ram) would look right feeding and caring for a tribal woman, monkeys and bears?
Whose is the name that wipes away sins and faults even when it is said lazily or in anger? (Only the name of Shri Ram is such a name.) The one who, in his foolishness, has always turned against his own master — even that low servant like Tulsi has been made his own (what greater kindness for no reason could there be than this?).

Lord! Who else do I have, who else will I tell (the things in my heart, if not you)? What my heart wants is like a beggar wanting to be king (I am utterly without any spiritual practice, and yet I want the joy of loving God, which is beyond even freedom itself. In such a state, apart from someone as merciful as you) who can I tell this longing to and feel lighter? (Who else will hear me out and grant it?)
I have borne the punishments of death, the torments of hell, and terrible suffering in countless kinds of bodies, and I will bear them again. (I do not care about that in the least.) Lord! I have no craving for wealth, for duty, for pleasure, not even for freedom — though these are hard for me to get, you could give them to me easily if you wished.
Ram! (What my heart wants is something quite different.) I want to stay as a toy in your hand — a bird, an animal, a tree, a pebble, a stone. Tied to you like that, I am happy even in hell, and without that tie I would go on burning in sorrow even if I got freedom. (I do not want freedom; keep me in hell if you like, but keep me as a toy in your own hand. Whether that toy is alive or a lifeless tree or stone, in that I find the highest joy.)
There is just this one wish in this servant's heart — that he may always hold on to your sandal (stay lying at your shelter). Either give me your word (that you will fulfil this wish of mine), or settle it in your own heart that you will carry through this vow of Tulsi.

Where will I find another friend of the poor (like you)? Lord! Apart from you, who else grieves at another person's (a devotee's) grief? Then to whom do I carry my tale of helplessness and weep?
Wherever I let my mind wander, in some places I find masters who have no mercy, and in others I find masters who are merciful but not able (not equal to the task). Hearing and seeing this, I simply keep quiet — why lose my good name in front of such people by saying anything? (My secret would come out, and nothing would come of it anyway.)
My deeds are so low that I could drown in the water in a cow's hoofprint (drown in a handful of water), and yet I talk big and measure the depth of the ocean. (It is all talk and talk, and not a grain of doing.) My mind is thoroughly greedy and a slave of desire, and yet with my mouth I go about calling myself your servant.
Lord! You know all of Tulsi's thoughts (the bad and the good), and still I want to tell you some of mine. Now do something, in whatever way you can, so that I leave off this pretending and lie at your door with a clean heart, doing nothing but singing your qualities.

My mind's longing is itself an odd sort of thing. It wants the fruit of such good deeds as even the minds of sages find hard to reach; yet since it does only sinful things, its longing is never fulfilled (to do wrong and expect the fruit of the very highest right — how can that happen?).
Even though I am born in Bharat, the land where deeds count, I am born in Kaliyug, and there is the company of low people, ignorance, a mind drunk on pride and ten million wicked deeds — with all this, how can the highest state and peace ever be reached?
By serving holy people and the guru, and by listening to the Vedas and the Puranas, the highest peace becomes as certain as recognising a melody the moment the fiddle is played. Tulsi! The nature of Lord Ramchandra is surely like the wish-fulfilling tree (whatever is asked of him is given), but along with that it is also like a face reflected in a mirror. (Just as whatever face you make, good or bad, is exactly what the mirror shows you, so the Lord too gives fruit according to the feeling you bring.)

This beautiful (human) life has gone by for nothing. Not the least bit of the highest good came into my hands. Day by day, only my wrongdoing kept growing.
Childhood went by in playing and eating, youth was carried off by women, and old age went by uselessly too, since it was full of disease, of separation (from wife and children), of grief and of hard toil.
Because of attachment, anger, jealousy and delusion, the company of holy people never appealed to me, and (having no such company) I neither spoke nor heard the string of Shri Raghunath's qualities, nor did love for Shri Ram's feet ever grow in me.
Now, hearing of the unbearable terrors of this world, my heart is burning in the fire of regret. Now let the Lord think over the way of his own good name and do for this Tulsi whatever he can.

Life after life has gone by like this (all wasted). Leaving aside a master like Raghunath, the very life of my life, I went on serving at the feet of others!
Those foolish creatures who are crooked, cowardly and wicked, and who are nothing but smeared with the sins of this dark age — my mouth has gone dry praising them, and I have held them to be greater even than God.
Running after happiness, I made ten million attempts one after another and my feet never once ached (day and night I wandered here and there in the pleasures of the senses). My heart stayed dirty like a puddle on the road, and never once turned clear or still.
To get rid of this wretchedness I thought up countless plans in my mind. But Tulsi! Until you recognise the wish-granting jewel (Shri Raghunath), the worry in your heart cannot end (only knowing God and his true friendship will destroy your worries).

O creature! If you have not truly known Shri Raghunath, the Lord of Janaki, then all your actions and all your duties will only give you hard labour. (Nothing real will come of them.) This is exactly what wise people have said. (All actions and all duties find their fulfilment in truly knowing Shri Ramchandra.)
The Vedas and the Puranas say that all the gods, the perfected ones, the great sages and the masters of yoga take your worship and in return give you (perishable, worldly) pleasures — and even that much they do only after working out their own profit and loss.
Apart from you, whose is the name that destroys whole heaps of sins even when it is remembered by mistake? Ajamil the brahmin, Valmiki the hunter, Gajraj the king of elephants, Jatayu the vulture — ten million such wicked ones were taken in by whom? (You alone accepted them and gave them your own highest home.)
He forgets his servants' offences, huge as Mount Sumeru, and keeps in his heart their merits, small as specks of dust. Tulsidas! You fool! Why don't you drop every other hope and worship him alone?

O tongue! Why don't you sing the qualities of Shri Ram? Day and night you speak ill of other people — why are you tying yourself down for nothing?
You live in the beautiful, holy temple of a human mouth — why do you shame it? (Why not leave off talk of the senses and speak the name of Shri Ram?) You live right beside the moon, and yet you leave nectar and run after the water of a mirage. (Why not drink the nectar that is Shri Ram's name?)
Talk of the world's pleasures is like moonlight for the night-lily that is this dark age (it makes it bloom), and you listen to that talk fondly, with your ears wide open. O tongue! Stop that talk of the senses and sing the beautiful glory of Shri Hari, so the stain on the ears is washed away (the ears have been stained by listening endlessly to talk of the senses; that stain will go only by hearing the story of God).
Take the gold of a clear mind and the fine jewels of good reasoning, string them carefully into a necklace, and place that necklace around King Ramchandra — the sun to the lotus of the solar line, the one who gives joy to all who take shelter in him. (With a pure mind and sound reasoning, settle the matter and sing the name and qualities of Shri Hari.)
Leave off arguing and leave off chasing taste; worship Shri Hari and fix yourself on his sweet deeds. If you do this, Tulsidas will cross the ocean of this world (be free of birth and death), and you too will win a spotless fame in all three worlds.

Lord! If this creature could see his own good coming to him through you, then why would he go on fighting like a headless trunk while his head is still on his shoulders? (He has no trust in God's mercy, and so, with his head still on — with God still over him — he takes himself to be headless, forgets God, and like a blind man fights with everyone for a little happiness. But with no head — with no support from God — he will neither win by fighting nor find any blessing.)
Seeing my own faults and seeing and hearing of your qualities, which even the gods find hard to reach, Ram, my mind and my thinking come to a halt. I shrink back: how can someone with such filthy deeds as mine come before you, who are truth, awareness and solid bliss? Merciful One! Who but you can understand Tulsi's behaviour, his words and the secret of him? (You know everything about this poor creature; lift him up with your merciful gaze alone.)

Whoever Shri Hari has pressed firmly to his heart — that person is well-behaved, pure, a knower of the Vedas, and full of all learning and every good quality (when God shows his mercy to someone, all good qualities come into him on their own, to add to their own honour).
Hearing how the sons of Pandu were born and what they did, even the path of right conduct took fright; yet by Shri Hari's mercy those same men came to be honoured in all three worlds, and people were carried across simply by hearing their holy story again and again.
King Nriga never fell short by even a little in keeping the duties the Vedas lay down, and yet through no fault of his own he became a lizard lying in a well; you took him by the hand, pulled him out and set him free. (You released him from the body of a lizard and sent him to the divine world.)
The (Brahmastra of Ashvatthama), powerful enough to burn up the whole universe, did not burn the king (Parikshit) in his mother's womb; and the demon (Namuchi), unaging and undying, whom even the thunderbolt could not kill, was killed by foam.
In the conduct of Ajamil the brahmin and of Indra, what was there that did not go wrong? And yet you helped them greatly and took away the burning in their hearts.
The courtesan (Pingala) and the god of love — what sin is there in this world that they did not commit? And yet the Lord treated their life as pure and gave them a place in the temple of his own heart.
What kind of conduct it is that pleases the Lord, I cannot work out. Tulsidas simply stands and stands, watching the road for the mercy of Shri Raghunath.

Lord Ram! Whoever you are pleased with — that one is truly good, that one is truly pure. The courtesan Pingala, the vulture Jatayu, the hunter Valmiki — they all went to your highest home, Vaikunth. When did they ever go to Prayag to do hard penance, or burn themselves to death in a fire of cow-dung cakes?
King Nriga never once strayed from the path the Vedas lay down, and yet the whole world knows how much he suffered (he was born as a lizard and lay rotting in a well for thousands of years!). And that elephant — at what holy place was he ever initiated? Yet the moment he remembered you, you left your mount Garuda behind and came running with your Sudarshan disc in your hand.
You passed over the high families of gods, sages and brahmins, and were born in Gokul in the house of a cowherd, Nanda. You turned away from the wealth and splendour of Duryodhan, lord of the Kauravas, and went instead to the house of poor Vidur and ate his simple meal of greens.
God is very good to the devotees who love him and no one else. You explained something of this way of single-hearted love to Arjun. Tulsidas says: Shri Ram belongs to simple, natural, spotless love. Every other practice is like the slickness water leaves on the skin! (After a bath the body feels smooth for a little while, but once it dries it is rough again, just as it was. In the same way, when other practices fulfil a desire they give a moment's happiness, but it vanishes the instant the next desire is born.)

You have given the highest state to so many wicked people — so why will you not simply insist on giving that highest place to a wicked man like me? However badly a sinner says your name, the moment you hear it you go out to meet him with great love and gather him into your lap. So why not do the same for me?
Yamraj's messengers took Ajamil to be a mine of sins. They flared up at him, terrified him and tormented him — but you snatched him out of their hands (just because, as he was dying, he called out "Narayan", and that only by accident). The messengers went back empty-handed, wringing their hands and grinding their teeth in rage.
Gautam's wife Ahalya, the king of elephants, the vulture Jatayu, the trees Yamalarjun, the monkey Sugriv — my Lord knows perfectly well what sort they were. Yet when each of them needed you, you got up and left even the gathering of holy people and went to help them.
Even today it is people like that who are welcomed most at your door, and who knows how many sinners are made pure there every day. And with all this going on, why has no one listened to me yet? Am I not sinful enough? Put together every wicked person who ever lived, who lives now and who ever will — all of them together would not even balance the small weight against me.
Until now I have been staring at your ways, watching and waiting for you to lift me up too. But you have not turned your eyes this way at all. So now, enough — Tulsidas will make a doll of your name and carry it around, because I cannot bear to be laughed at any more.
When street performers get nothing for their show, they make a cloth doll, hang it on a bamboo pole and go about saying, "Look how stingy this man is." People feel ashamed and give them something after all. I will carry a doll about in just the same way. And when people ask, I will tell them: this is Shri Ramchandra, the great king of Ayodhya! Then you will feel the shame of it, and then you will take me as your own.

Great king Ramchandra! There is no friend like you for doing good to the helpless, and there is no one as helpless as I am. In all the world there is no greater master of crookedness than me — and my Lord, there is no one like you for destroying crookedness.
In thought, word and deed I am soaked in sin — and you, Merciful One, are the one who gives sinners the highest state. I have no one of my own, and you, my Lord, are the one who does good to those who have no one. This thought never leaves my mind.
I am full of sorrow, and you are the one who takes sorrow away — the Vedas and Puranas sing your glory for it. I am afraid of this world of birth and death, and you are the one who destroys all fear. With so much between you and me, what reason can there be for you not to show me mercy?
Shri Ram! You are the home of joy and the one who ends all weariness, and I am worn out and miserable with the three kinds of struggle in this world (from my own body, from fate, and from the world around me). Turn these things over in your mind, remember who you are, and just take Tulsidas into your shelter.

Knowing this, I have pulled my mind back from everywhere else and fixed it on your feet: that there is no one else like you, my Lord, who does good without wanting anything in return. This is what the Vedas and the Puranas sing.
Wherever I was born, in whatever form of life, I had plenty of fathers and mothers, sons and wives, brothers and relatives. But every one of them loved me for what they could get out of it; their hearts were full of tricks and deceit. So not one of them ever taught me to worship Shri Hari. (They all taught me to stay tangled in the world; not one told me to turn to God.)
Having taken a body, whose feet did I not bow my head at, hoping it would do me good — gods, sages, humans, demons, serpents, kinnars? I put my head at everyone's feet and flattered them all. But Hari, I was burning with the three kinds of pain, the fruit of my own sins, and not one of them took pity and cooled me. (Not one could give me freedom and end the world's fever.)
I tried so many things to find happiness, but because I had turned my face away from God's feet, all I ever got was sorrow. Now I see the net of troubles spread out across the world, and I am as worn out by all my efforts as a boat is when there is no water under it.
My Lord, understand how I came to be like this: I forgot my master, who is the treasure-house of all happiness. Hari, stop counting my faults now and have mercy on Tulsidas, who has come to your shelter.

Hari! This is how I lost all understanding: I left you, seated in the lotus of my own heart, and went wandering desperately outside, trying this and that to be happy.
It is like the utterly foolish deer that carries beautiful musk in its own body and does not know the secret of it, and goes searching over hills and trees and creepers, over the ground and into holes, wondering where this wonderful scent is coming from. (That is exactly my state. My master, who is happiness itself, lives in my heart, and I go looking for him outside.)
The pond is brimming with clear water, but a little moss and grass has spread over the top. So I, wretched as I am, take it for something foul and leave that clean water, and instead I am burning up my own heart, thinking I can quench my thirst that way. (The lake of my heart is full of the endless cool water of the Supreme Being, who is truth, awareness and joy. But the moss of ignorance has covered it, so I run after worldly pleasures, which are a mirage, hoping they will end my thirst for the highest happiness — and so I burn in the three fires.)
As it is, the three terrible pains are spreading through my body; on top of that, this unbearable poverty of mine torments me, for I have nothing in the way of spiritual wealth. What a huge fool I am! In my own house — my own heart — stands the wish-fulfilling tree of God's name, which gives whatever is asked of it, and I have left it and set my heart on a garden of thorn trees, the pleasures of the senses. (What can a garden of thorn trees give except the thorns of sorrow?)
There is no store of wisdom like you and there is no fool like me — the Puranas have said so. Think about that, my Lord, and do for this Tulsidas whatever seems right to you.

This foolish mind of mine has cheated me over and over. Listen, you who are all compassion — because of it I have been born again and again in this world and gone about weeping in my misery.
Cool, sweet, deathless, natural happiness — the joy of God — is closer to me than anything (the very nature of the soul is truth, awareness and pure joy). Yet caught in the tangle of this mind I forgot it, as if it were somewhere far away. Blinded by delusion I worked hard in a hundred ways, and all I did, fool that I am, was churn water (I churned the water of sense-pleasure hoping to get the butter of supreme joy out of it).
In my heart I knew that action is mud — the moment you fall into it, dirt spreads over you from every side — and still I mixed my mind into it. Crooked as I am, I try to wash off filth with filth to quench my thirst. I am thirsty, and I am so wretched that I leave the holy Ganga and go about in distress, squeezing the empty sky again and again. (I wander after the sense-pleasures that bring pain, hoping to find true happiness there.)
My Lord, I have not hidden a single fault of mine from you, so have mercy on Tulsidas now. The whole night has gone by with me still spreading out my bedding, and my Lord, I never once slept my fill. (My whole life has gone in trying out ways to be happy; I never found you, never had every wish fulfilled, never slept the sound sleep of true understanding. Have mercy now.)

Small and great, bad and good, fat and thin — Shri Ram, all of them get through only because you carry them through. The world knows it and the Vedas say it plainly. And yet, though I hear this and think about it, my mind is so lost in delusion and so restless that it never settles and never makes up its mind.
If this mind were in my control it would stay steady and unchanging (for the soul always wants the happiness of God alone), so why would it have to put up with the joys and griefs and troubles of this world? (If the mind were turned to God and firm in its purpose) whoever wanted a thing would get it, and no one would be left with any craving at all (the soul would reach God and have nothing more to want).
But it is not like that. In this world a creature's actions, time, nature, virtues and faults all come out of your maya (the power that makes the world look real), and that maya stands stunned with fear, watching the movement of your eyebrows and dancing as you make her dance. She lets Shiva, Brahma, the guardians of the directions, the great yogis and the great sages go free only when you set them free, and she seizes them only when you hand them over.
This whole gathering of maya is a kingdom on a chessboard; none of it is real, it is all made of wood — there is no true king, no true minister. Great King, the rules of this game of chess are written by you, and there were no such rules before. Tulsidas says: my Lord, winning or losing this game is in your hands alone! Saraswati has said this in many forms and through many mouths (every wise voice has said the same thing — that bondage and freedom are in God's hands alone).

Tongue! Say the name of Ram, know what the name of Ram really is, and trust it with love. Saying that one name will cool the three fevers in your heart. Give yourself to the name of Ram, and speak of nothing but the name of Ram. Taking shelter in the name this way carries off the sins, sorrows and troubles of this crooked age of Kali.
It is the power of Ram's name that makes Ganesh the first to be worshipped. Ganesh said so himself about what he did; he hid nothing. This name of Ram is the bridge over the ocean of this world (devotees climb onto it and cross that ocean easily). In Kashi, Lord Shiva himself, with Parvati beside him, says the name of Ram to give freedom to the souls who die there.
Valmiki the hunter had sins beyond counting, but he said the name backwards — "mara, mara" — and became such a man that sages and even the gods worshipped him. It was on the strength of this same name of Ram that the sage Agastya stopped the Vindhya mountain and drank the ocean dry. Afterwards that ocean, beaten in its own heart by its fear of that brahmin Agastya, turned salt.
The glory of Ram's name has no limit. Shesha, Shukdev, the Vedas and the learned have described it again and again, each as far as his own mind could reach. For Tulsidas, loving the name of Ram is the wish-granting cow and the wish-granting tree (this very name has given him the rare place he longed for). What more can be said — this name of Ram is the sun itself, come to drive away the darkness of ignorance.

Shri Ram! Raghunath, you who are goodness itself — save me, save me. I heard of your great name and came to your shelter. Friend of the helpless, you are the one who destroys helplessness, poverty, sorrow, sin, terrible suffering, unbearable fear, and every wrong we have done.
Again and again good people — saints, cows and brahmins — have been caught in the net of this world by time and by their own past deeds, and cried out in their distress, and wicked kings have become a weight on the earth. And again and again you have taken a body and come down, destroyed the wicked, lifted that weight off the earth, and set the sages, the gods, the saints and the whole order of dharma back on their feet.
The Vedas and the world are both witnesses to this. When Ravan left no one with any honour, and the gods were lying in his prison, dying there — then, God, it was you who gave those lords of the worlds, Indra, Kuber and the rest, your shelter, took away their sorrow, and made each of them master of his own world again. And Lord Ram, in your rule dharma stood on all four of its legs (truth, self-discipline, mercy and giving all flourished).
Merciful One! As easily as play, you carried Ahalya, the boatman Nishad, Jatayu, the monkeys, the Bhils, the bears and the demons across, and gave them the power to carry others across too. (You lifted them up, and more — whoever kept their company or followed them was lifted up as well.) You who saved the king of elephants, you ocean of gentleness — Tulsi sees you slackening a little where he is concerned, and he is so ashamed of himself that he wants to melt away for it. So be kind and lift him up quickly too.

I have looked carefully at every master there is in this world and I know exactly what they are. A small thing pleases them and a small thing makes them burn with anger. They have no skill in keeping up a friendship and they know nothing of right conduct. Everything they do is bad, because time, past deeds and maya have them in their grip.
My Lord, great demons and monsters, fooled into thinking they were strong, turned into huge fools and climbed onto everyone's heads, and they even defeated the guardians of the worlds. Their masters, the gods, first melted at their hard penances and handed them any boon they asked for, and then turned against them and had their houses burned to ashes! Not one of them felt any shame at ruining his own servants — they came praying to you to do it.
Shri Ram! You alone truly know your watchful servants, because you alone are truly able, you are the home of every good quality and you are utterly pure. You are merciful to all, your face is always glad, you never change and you are always the same. You know the secret of every single heart.
Merciful One! There is no one like you for taking care of beggars who come for shelter, and there is no beggar like me. Lord, every dharma there is lives in mercy — so show mercy to this helpless man. And my Lord, you are the wish-granting tree; it is in the shade of this tree that I want to stay. I give myself to you — this Tulsi is in great distress because of the crooked ways of the age of Kali. Be kind and save him quickly.

My Lord, if I could find some other master anywhere, or any other place to take shelter, I would not annoy you by calling out to you again and again. Great king Ramchandra, it is you who have fed and raised lazy, luckless people like me. So, Merciful One, you alone are my king, and Ayodhya alone is the city where I live.
I have never lovingly served the guardians of the directions, or the Sun, or Ganesh, or Parvati, and I have never worshipped Brahma, Shiva or Vishnu with any faith. All my getting and keeping comes from the name of Ram alone. (It is the name that has given me what I did not have and kept safe what I have.) It is my one rule, my one love, the one thing I am given to completely. Trusting it is like nectar to me, and every other way is poison.
Lord of those who have no one! My companions — the thieves and the watchmen alike — are all in your hands, so who else can I tell about them?
