(If you drive off the thieves, desire and anger and greed and delusion, and wake up the watchmen, discernment and detachment, then my true wealth, my love for the name of Ram, will be saved.) Great King, think for a moment: have you ever been slow in your own work, or in the work of the gods, or in the work of the poor and suffering? Then why is there so much delay in my case alone?
I heard how you are — that you make the fallen pure, that you love those who come to you — and so I came to trust you and love you. But when I see how badly this age of Kali behaves, I am afraid (afraid it will turn me away from you and trap me in the pleasures of the senses). Raghunath, I would give my life for you; everything will be well with me if only you say, or have someone say to me, "Tulsi! You are mine. Don't lose heart and don't be afraid."

Shri Ram! Only Lord Shiva, Hanuman, Lakshman and Bharat have truly understood your nature, your qualities, the greatness of your goodness and your power. That is why the wish-granting tree of love for you stands so beautifully in the lovely garden-plot of their hearts, and on it the sweet flowers and fruits of the highest joy bloom and ripen. (Whoever comes to know the greatness of God's qualities and goodness has his heart filled with love for God; and wherever that love fills the heart, the highest joy comes to live.)
It is simply your nature to take Shiva as your master, Hanuman as your friend, and Lakshman and Bharat as your brothers — and all of them take you as their master, and are always careful in their love, and always a little afraid (afraid that their love might lose some of its purity or its single-heartedness). If master and servant go on loving each other this way, and always keep the rules of love, then their hold on one another can never come loose, and their love reaches its farthest limit.
Shukdev, Sanak and his brothers, Prahlad, Narad and the other devotees all say that the great devotion to Shri Raghunath — the pure, single-hearted kind — comes only to one who has turned right away from pleasure. (And only one who truly knows God turns away from pleasure like that.) So there is no devotion without true knowledge of God; and that knowledge, my Lord, is in your hands (no practice can produce it; it comes only from God's mercy). Understanding this, wise people come and fall at your feet, leaving every other practice behind and taking shelter in you.
The six schools of philosophy do not agree, the Puranas do not all say the same thing, and the Vedas go on forever saying "not this, not this." Then what is there to say about everyone else? (With things as they are, what way is there to truly know you except taking shelter in you?) For me, then, holding on to the one name of Ram seems the good and right thing, and it is the thing that can save me — because even people like Tulsidas have crossed the ocean of this world by it.

My dear father! With my own hands I have ruined everything I ever did. I would give my life for you — just once, put right the case of this greedy liar. Because everything came right for everyone you were ever good to (so be kind, and today set my ruined life right too).
My body is sick, my mind is filthy with ugly cravings, and my tongue is worn out with running other people down and telling lies. (The body, mind and speech through which any spiritual practice is done are all three unfit for it — and yet) the rule of all such practice is that nothing is achieved unless you practise it. So now, treasure-house of mercy, only your mercy is strange and wonderful enough to put my ruined case right. (Only your mercy can save a man with no practice to his name.)
You make sinners pure, you are the well-wisher of the sorrowing and of those who have no one, the support of those with no support, the friend of the helpless, and kind by your very nature. But I am not even one of those things (my pride never let me admit that I was fallen, sorrowing, helpless, without anyone, without support — so why would you have mercy on me on any of those grounds?). I never had the sense to fight my real enemies — desire, anger, greed, delusion — and I never defeated them. So I am burning in the three fires, from my body, from the world and from fate; I am reaping just what I sowed. Who else is there to blame?
On the outside I am dressed up as a simple, harmless holy man, but in sinning I have outdone the age of Kali itself. To my mind, anything about God and the next world tastes flat, and it is dyed through with the colours of this world (it stays tangled in whether it will get its pleasures or not). Great King, all the days I have spent till now in this wretched company have gone to waste — but now, somehow, I have caught hold of the support of your name.
Shri Ram! You know well what power your name has (who knows how many people like me it has already carried across). For me, the Creator has made no other way at all except your name. I have millions of evil deeds that could turn you against me, but the one thing I have that could win you over is my shamelessness. (Be pleased with my very shamelessness, and have mercy.)

Shri Ram! Keep me in your shelter, because you have always taken in people like me. Everyone knows there is no one as kind as you in the three worlds and in all three times — past, present and future. My Lord, who else is there but you to protect those who come to you in pain?
It was you who fed and raised lazy, luckless, sinful people, who looked after them and kept them happy — and even then, my Lord, you never felt the debt was settled. Master, you are the one with all the power; and whatever I am, good or bad, I am yours. When I see the ways of this age of Kali my heart turns over with disgust (I am afraid this wicked age will turn my mind away from your feet).
I give myself to you — why can't you say, just once, angrily or gladly, smiling or annoyed, however you like, only this much: "Tulsi! You are mine"? Just that much, great king Ramchandra, and I swear on you, that very moment all my sorrow would be pulled up by the root and every happiness would turn my way.

Shri Ram! Your name is my mother and father, my family and relatives, my beloved, my teacher, my master, my friend, and the one who does me good for no reason at all. And the love I have for your name, which turns to nothing else, is the one wealth of mine that can never be taken away.
Lord Shiva churned the bottomless ocean of curd that is your hundred crore deeds, and out of it he drew the butter that is the name of Ram. Leaning on your name and trusting it is the final fruit of all four fruits — wealth, dharma, desire and freedom. Drop all pretence and remember this name: it is the greatest offering there is.
Your name gets us everything we need in this world and gives us the highest good, freedom itself. There is nothing that does us as much good as the name of Shri Ram. Tulsi says this straight from his heart, and so it will surely be proved true. The name of Shri Ram, the beloved of Janaki, is the very awareness inside our awareness.

Shri Ram, for holy people your name is the wish-granting tree. The moment they remember it, it takes away the three kinds of suffering (of the body, of the world around them, and of fate) and fulfils every desire, leaving a person with nothing left to want. Your name is a lake holding all the lotuses of merit (whoever takes shelter in the name of Ram receives the fruit of every good deed).
It is gain beyond gain, joy beyond joy, and for your devotees it is everything they have. (No holy person has any gain, joy or wealth greater than this.) It makes the fallen pure, and it frightens even fear itself (the terrible fear of Death's messengers, who frighten everyone else). It is within easy reach of all — low or high, king or beggar, anyone can repeat it. It gives happiness to everyone and rests a person like his own home.
The Vedas, the Puranas and Lord Shiva have cried out again and again that to love the name of Ram is the fruit of all four fruits of life (wealth, dharma, desire and moksha). As I see it, a man who has no love and no faith in a name like Shri Ram's should be counted a donkey (like a donkey, all he carries through life is the load of his pride in being human).
Father and mother, friend and well-wisher, brother, guru and master — not one of them is equal to the name of Shri Ram. That name is a master of the finest nature and the deepest wisdom, like the moon that pours out nectar. (The moment you take shelter in it, it removes every burning sorrow, and by giving you the nectar of moksha it makes you happy forever.) Merciful One, I would give my life for you: give this Tulsidas that great strength, so that this poor man's love for your name holds firm to the very end.

Shri Ram, I cannot keep quiet, and once I have spoken there is no sweetness left in it. The truth is this: even after finding the shelter of a master as great as you, I — your servant, good or bad — am suffering unbearable pain because of time and my own past deeds.
I think about it (about how a hunter, a boatman and others came to be so great), but nowhere can I find the secret of where all these people got their greatness from. (What is heard is that you yourself saw how poor and low they were and made them your own, and that is how they all became great and worthy of worship.) When I hear and understand a glory like yours and then look at my own condition, hope drains out of me and my heart begins to burn with panic. (You are the one who lifts up the poor and the fallen — then why have you still not accepted me, poor as I am, who have come to your shelter? Thinking this, a burning starts in my heart, and that is why I blurt out whatever comes to me.)
(And who else can I say it to? Because) I have no friend, no true servant, no good wife, and no master. You alone are my mother and my father — Tulsi is telling the plain truth. My own matter is a small one; even if it is spoiled it can still be put right. But — it amazes me — I swear by you, what I want to protect is your good name (may your name as the saviour of the fallen and the lover of all who come for shelter never be shamed).

Friend of the helpless, if you push this poor man away from your shelter, he will find shelter nowhere else. Almost everyone wants good for himself, but someone who does good for his servants is very rare. Shri Ram, it is your feet alone that do good to everyone (under the shelter of your feet, good and bad alike find their welfare).
A slab of stone (Ahalya), animals (monkeys and bears), a bird (Jatayu), a forest tribesman (the Kol), a demon (Vibhishan) — Treasury of Mercy, you turned them all from glass into gold (they were caught in the senses, and you set them free). The ground of the Dandak forest became holy the moment your feet touched it, and trees that had been torn up and left dry began to flower and bear fruit again.
Your name, which makes the fallen pure, brings good even to those who have turned their backs on you (even people who worship you as an enemy cross over). My Lord, there is no one but you in this world who destroys unbearable sorrows and sins. You are an ocean of gentleness, and so even rough, ragged words spoken to you look fitting (what more can I say?). You alone — only one like you — can take away Tulsi's sorrow, and that is why I have come to your shelter.

Treasury of Mercy, though I knew you and recognised you, I have forgotten you, and pride has made me so shameless that I turn around and lay the blame on you (saying that though you are an ocean of gentleness, you do not make me your own). Great yogis struggle hard just to form a bond of love with you; somehow a little of that love had formed in me too, and unlucky as I am, I broke even that.
In all fourteen worlds there is no other storehouse of sins like me — I have searched hard, as far as my understanding goes. Just as a dog that follows a cart sometimes leaves the cart and runs off here and there, and then falls in behind it again, in one moment I drop the grandeur of maya (the world's illusion) and its attachments, and the very next moment I am lost in it again.
I swear by you ten million times: there is no one to match me in betraying his master. So drive me away from your door — this liar, this greedy man, this cheat — or else I will muddy your nectar-like water the way a sow does (if I call myself your devotee and go on doing evil, a stain will fall on your spotless name).
So either mend me properly and keep me in your shelter, or else simply kill this low man. Now you alone must weigh these two choices; I will not beg you any more. Tulsi has drawn a line and spoken the plain truth over and over. If you delay too, then I will sink the boat that is the glory of your name. (People will see my ruin and lose their faith in your name.)

If the matter you set right is spoiled again by my own spoiling of it, then — I would give my life for you — leave the Vedas aside, what will the world say? (Whatever the Vedas may say, the world will say that Tulsi himself is God, because he ruined what Ram had made.) If my Lord's coldness and the force of this servant's sins ever come together, then, Friend of the helpless, this poor man will burn to death in his sorrow. (I am a great sinner already, but if you also turn cold to me, my end will be terrible.)
I have laid a thunderbolt on my own chest (I am ready to bear the pain, yet I do not give up my sins), because the Kali age has me pinned down. That is why I am suffering. (And why only me?) Anyone who is not his own master will have to suffer. But Merciful One, bound by your own beautiful record of vows, you will have to protect me. (If not now, then) at the last hour, when you see the state I am in, this coldness of yours will not be able to hold (your merciful nature will not be able to watch my pain, and then you will have to come running to save me).
Those who perform the rituals, the righteous, holy men, servants, those who have given up the world and those who chase pleasures — all of them will find some place or other according to the good they have done. But if you turn your face away, who will give shelter to a coward, a bad son, a cruel, helpless, fallen creature like me? (No one at all.)
Merciful One, in time everyone's condition changes, everyone's days turn for the better; but apart from you, no one will ever want me (if I leave your shelter, I will find no place anywhere). Shri Ram, I swear by you and say it in word, deed and thought: this Tulsi will only get through if my Lord carries him through.

When the master turns cold, even his closest servant is ruined — so what is there to say about me? I am being swept away in sorrow, and openly, for all to see. When there is no place for me even in this world, what hope can I have for the next? Shri Ram, I would give my life for you: I have already sold myself into the hands of your name alone (this world and the next will both be made for me by that name).
Deeds, habit, time, desire, anger, greed and delusion — these great crocodiles — and a terrible poverty (of having nothing to help myself with) have caught hold of me with all their force. Great King, there are ten million warriors ready to bind me, but there is only one — you — to free me from the bonds. So my Lord, save me, save me! I am burning in the three fires of sin (with the rain of nectar that is your gracious glance, cool these fires).
My Lord, (whose door else should I go to?) Everyone's delight and understanding, everyone's love and trust, rest at your door alone. (It is by the authority you give them that the gods hand out something from your own treasury to their servants, but they cannot give freedom. And worship offered to any of them is worship of you, because you are the root of everything.) I am like a man once burned by hot milk, who now blows on buttermilk before drinking it. What this means is that worshipping others instead of you never once gave me the highest joy or a divine peace, so now I walk very carefully. I have worn myself out calling on the gods for happiness, and I have lost my caste, my community and my good conduct along the way. So now I am greedy only for the leftovers from your plate. I do not want to bathe in milk. What this means is: I have no wish for the riches of heaven; I only want to lie at your feet.
I do not want my welfare anywhere else, taking shelter with others and walking smoothly along an easy road; and here in your shelter, even without any honour, I am perfectly well. Trusting your wonderful record of vows, I lie here with no fear and no worry. Tulsi has understood this and told his own mind again and again, and he has said it to his Lord too and set his worry down: his living is in your hands alone.

Shri Ram, by anything I make or do, my good end will not come even in ten million ages; but if you wish it, it can happen in a quarter of a moment. Treasury of Mercy, what can I say — you yourself are the wisest of all. In exchange for a life that was like a priceless jewel, I took a handful of cheap berries (the human life that should have been spent in reaching you, I threw away on the pleasures of the senses).
(Because of that) my mind grew dirty, and in this Kali age my bad deeds grew even stronger, and new sins piled up day after day. My tongue never repeated your name; I babbled nonsense all my life. I kept walking crooked on bad roads. Not even by mistake did any good ever come to anyone through me. Why, even as a child at play I never once got a good throw (I never played a game that had anything to do with God).
Yes — if ever some good deed got done, by copying someone else (to put on a show of devotion), out of pretence, or through the company of holy people, I went around beating a drum about it; and the sins I committed (longing for them in my heart) I kept hidden. I always fed and pampered my likings, my dislikes and my anger, and my mind along with my senses. I always stayed under the control of liking, disliking and anger, and of my mind and my senses. It was these I was devoted to, these I loved.
Looking back at what I have been, what I am, and what I am likely to be, I have understood this much: I have never done one good thing. And yet the world is saying, "Tulsi belongs to Ram" — and I too have faith in you and love for you. Now whether it is false or true, my master Raghunath, I am lying here depending on you alone.

My Lord, I cannot speak, and I cannot keep from speaking either. I would give my life for you. (Even though) there is great comfort in telling your poverty to someone greater than you, (still) — where is my Lord's immense greatness and where is my small meanness; where is my Lord's purity and where is the weight of my sins.
Weighing these two sides, my mind shrinks back in shame (it has no courage to speak, and my feet start going backwards); but then it hears of my master's beautiful goodness (however poor, low or dirty the one who comes to your shelter may be, you accept him with honour) and it comes forward again. My Lord, simply by singing the stories of your qualities, and by folding their hands and bowing their heads, even the lowest people have been made rich beyond measure by you (that is the clever way of your love).
In this court, pride destroys a man completely, and it is poverty and humility that win a person his care and keeping. There was no one as mighty as Ravan, and no one as poor and weak as Vibhishan; and in this story it becomes perfectly clear how helpless you are before love. (To poor Vibhishan, who came for shelter, you gave the kingdom of Lanka and the gift of undivided devotion to you, and Ravan you destroyed completely.)
Here, in your court, cleverness counts for as much as a thousand acts of foolishness. Here all the dirt is washed away simply by admitting your fault in a simple, honest spirit. If you keep remembering every day what happened to Jatayu, Ahalya and Shabari, your love for your master will never grow less. (Those poor souls were simple and free of pride and came for shelter, and so the Lord accepted them easily and fulfilled them.)
Your name, like the wish-granting tree, fulfils every desire. The moment the name is remembered, the sins and deceits of the Kali age wear away. Treasury of Compassion, Tulsi asks for only this one gift: that he may stay sunk forever, like a fish, in the Ganga water of devotion to Shri Ram, the Lord of Sita.

My Lord, please understand exactly what is in the heart of this servant of yours. My understanding is like a good and faithful wife: she has taken trust in you as her husband, has vowed to love him alone with a pure love, and takes her delight in doing what is right.
Because I was in the grip of sin and merit, I have had to live among all kinds of people, and in that I have tested the ways of others and my own ways too. My Lord, I have no worry and no fear about my own good or bad. (If, even after coming to your shelter, I still worried about good and bad and stayed afraid, what kind of surrender would that be? The moment I came to my master's shelter I became free of worry and free of fear.) I swear by Sita's Lord and say this is the plain truth.
(If I say anything made up it will not work at all, because) you are the master of knowledge and of speech. You know what is outside and what is inside. How can what is on my lips and what is in my heart ever be hidden from you? Tulsi is yours, and you are the one who does good to Tulsi. If there is any cheating hidden in what I say, let me become a fly in ghee. What this means is: as a fly that falls into ghee dies at once, in the same way let me be utterly destroyed.

Listen, my mind — hear me out just once. After that, do whatever you like. Look with all four of your eyes (the two outside, and the two inside, which are the mind and the understanding) and tell me: in all three worlds and all three times, is there anyone anywhere who does you as much good as God does?
Living in this house that is the body, you have tasted new loves again and again (through countless births, with countless relatives), and you have also tested their false, cheating love. In the end the secret of everyone's love came out. What is this crowd of friends (the relatives that worldly pleasure throws up)? It is a trade in double-dealing, a business of give and take. As long as someone needs something from you, he falls at your feet (but once his work is done he does not even ask after you).
The gods are very clever too — have you understood them properly or not? They take ten million times over first, and only then do they give back one time's worth. As for rituals and religious duty, without Shri Ram to rest on they are nothing but hard labour. (Those who leave God aside, care nothing for the Lord and trust only in their own good deeds — those good deeds cannot stand.) Doing them is like pouring offerings into ashes, or rain falling on barren salt ground — it comes to nothing.
There is no other master so full of gentle goodness as Shri Ramchandra, the Lord of Sita — good in the beginning, good in the middle and good at the end, always doing good to everyone, his fame spreading everywhere in the world and in the Vedas. You wicked mind, you sit there as if you had forgotten him — how do you manage to rest in peace at all?
He is the life of every living thing, the greatest well-wisher of your very breath, dearer than anyone, the one who makes the lowest pure — and you are treating him with contempt. Tulsi! Remember in your heart the play that the merciful Shri Ram, the king of Kosala, arranged for you at Chitrakoot (when he appeared before your own eyes as two beautiful young warrior princes riding on horses).

My Lord, I keep my body clean, in my mind too there is a taste (for loving you), and with my mouth I say that I am the servant of Sita's Lord; but I cannot understand what bad luck it is that keeps the highest bond and love with my Lord from forming in me.
I ask for water and I get fire; and in the same way nectar turns to poison for me (instead of peace I get the burning of restlessness, and good deeds, which are nectar, breed the poison of pride). Everything the holy ones have said about the crooked ways of the Kali age is true. I have no knowledge at all of sun or of night (that is, I cannot truly tell knowledge from ignorance).
Thinking me blind, the Kali age tells me to smear my eyes with the ghee of a forest lioness; and when I hear this corrupt cure and begin working out how I might get hold of her ghee (in the forest of ignorance lives the lioness of craving; the pleasures of the senses are her ghee, and she will eat you the moment you go near. How can a creature trapped in those pleasures ever get the eyes of knowledge?) — then it carries off the strength of understanding from my heart.
(With the strength of my understanding gone, the cure the Kali age prescribed — enjoying the senses — starts looking good to me, and I throw myself into it. It is this obstacle that keeps me from forming the highest bond and love with you.) I have something to say to you, but I hesitate to say it, afraid my words may fall flat again (and come back empty). So I would give my life for you: call this Kali age close to you and hold it back, so that it gives up its designs on dull creatures like Tulsi.

Treasury of Mercy, the more I want to come near you, the further away I drift. Shri Ram, you are always the same through all four ages, and I too have been yours all along, even though I am full of sins and faults.
Finding its chance while I was away from you, this low Kali age cheated me with its tricks right in the middle of the road (it was through ignorance that it got its hold on my life). I was pure gold, and it turned me to base metal (it turned what was solid, unending joy into a creature caught in sorrow). It made a beggar out of a king, and a fool out of one who knew.
Since then I have wandered (through countless births) over countless mountains and through countless jungles, and burned without any fire (in the forest fire of sorrow that ignorance lights). But when I went to Chitrakoot (and began worshipping you there with love), then by your grace I saw through all the crooked moves of this Kali age — and yet now I am afraid of my own fear.
With folded hands I stand before my Lord, bow my head and say: a thief who has been recognised usually goes on to kill the person (the Kali age is that recognised thief, and it is watching for its chance). Hearing this, Tulsi has made his plea to his master and set his worry down (now do whatever you yourself think best).

Shri Ram, from today I have taken a vow to hold fast to the truth, and I have thrown myself down at your door. Until you say "You are mine", I will not get up from here as long as I live — and I have already sworn this by you.
(Do not think that a few shoves from the police will make me get up.) The messengers of Death grew tired of shoving me; they tried to force me away from the gate of hell, but no amount of their pushing could move me from there (I did so many sins that whole lifetimes were spent in hell). Taking birth again and again in this world, I bore the unbearable pain of the womb, and only then did I come out of there, turning my back on hell.
The thing I have set my heart on and planted myself for, I will take before I leave, because you are merciful — (seeing me stand my ground, in the end) you will have to give me that thing. I would give my life for you. (Since you have to give it anyway, give it now) — do not delay, because shame is eating me up. (People will say that so many days have passed with him sitting in protest at the door of such a merciful master. So just say this much at once: "Tulsi is mine." The moment I hear it, I will end my sit-in.)
I am full of offences, and if because of that you feel shy about saying it openly in front of everyone, then please accept Tulsi as your own quietly, in your heart — because I am terrified at the sight of this Kali age.

When my mind turns around (towards you) — only then will I take it that you have made me your own. When this mind, which clings to the pleasures of the senses by its own easy nature, loves you in that very same way, with all its pretence dropped (until that happens, how am I to believe you have accepted me as your servant?).
The way that mind of mine loves a son, trusts a friend and fears the king's punishment — in that very way, when it looks to my master alone for everything it wants, and will not be turned from its one hold on you from any side, like the chatak bird (depending on one Lord only).
When great honour does not thrill it, when being slighted does not burn it to death, when it keeps the heart level through loss and gain, joy and sorrow, good and bad, and gives up the crooked ways of the Kali age completely (only then will I believe that my Lord is making me his own).
And when my mind is overwhelmed with joy the moment it hears my Lord's qualities praised, and a stream of loving tears flows from my eyes — only then will Tulsidas believe that he has become Shri Ram's. Then, seeing that love that has no other in it, joy will rise and fill my heart. (My Lord, accept me quickly and bring me to such a state.)

Shri Ram, will you ever be as dear to me as water is dear to a fish, as a happy life is dear to a living creature, as its jewel is dear to a snake, and as wealth is dear to a man eaten up by greed?
Or the way a young lover naturally finds a clever young woman dear — in that very way, Mine of Compassion, plant in my heart just one longing: for a pure love for you and for no one else.
The Vedas say that my Lord gives whatever the heart asks for, and that he is very clever at it (without being told, he knows what is in your heart and fulfils it). Treasury of Kindness, I would give my life for you: give this poor Tulsidas too the gift of the very thing his heart longs for.

Hero of the Raghus! Will you ever be kind and look my way too? Treasure of mercy! Good or bad, whatever I am, I am your servant. Will you take this to heart and put an end to my endless faults? (Will your mercy wipe out all my sins and make me your own?)
Until now, in birth after birth, this mind of mine has defeated me (I keep losing to it and falling into the pleasures of the senses). This time, will you let me win against it? (Will it come under my control and hold on to your feet alone?) Then I will surely have a master — and you too, if you are not frightened off by how small and low I am, will be called the Lord of the forlorn (if you pay no attention to my lowness and take me as your own, your name as protector of the helpless will be proved true).
It is my fear of my own self that makes me plead with you like this. You are the one who wishes me well above all. But Lord, who else can this Tulsidas go and tell his sorrow to? For you alone are my master, my guru, my mother, my father — you are everything to me.

Shri Ram! Whatever I am, good or bad, I am still your servant — so do not throw me away. Lord of Kosala, you are an ocean of mercy, the one who cares for all who come to you for shelter. Just stay true to that way of yours, that love for those who take refuge in you.
I have already been ruined by others (by lust, anger and the rest); do not ruin this ruined man any further by keeping him out of your shelter. You have always mended everyone in every way — now mend me too.
The world will laugh at you for taking me in — why are you afraid of that fear? (This has always been your way.) With the same gentleness and the same simple heart that made you a friend of the monkeys and of the boatman, treat me that way too.
I may be a wrongdoer, but I am still yours. So do not forget Tulsi. Even a broken arm is tied in a sling around one's own neck, and when a ruined eye hurts, one still tries to get it healed. (In the same way, though I am as useless as a broken arm and a blind eye, I am still yours — so how can you let me go?)

Shri Ram! Do not turn your heart against me, do not turn your merciful eyes away from me (do not judge me guilty and grow angry, and do not withdraw your kind look). Listen, my Lord: in this world and the next there is no one but you who can do me any good.
Seeing me without any virtue, worthless, lazy, low, poor and good for nothing, the friends who came to me for their own gain dropped me the way a charm is thrown away once the fever has broken, and never once, not even by mistake, turned around to look at me again. (The moment their gain was over they left me so completely that they never even remembered me.)
Seeing me without devotion, outside the path the Vedas teach, and hemmed in by the sins of Kaliyug — Lord, even the gods gave me up. And they did me no wrong by it, because I have wronged every one of them.
I simply shelter behind your name and fill my belly with it, and even so I am called your servant, and the whole world has come to know it. Now you decide: which is greater, the world or the Vedas? (By the rule of the Vedas I am no servant of yours; but when the world holds me to be your servant and says so, then you too should accept it.)
If any good ever comes to Tulsi, it will come through you alone. (Since you will have to save me in the end, it is better to do it soon.) I would give my life for you — if you delay, this poor man will only go on getting worse day by day. (And then mending him will cost far more.) So make me your own, and make me your own quickly.

My Lord! Apart from you, who else can I tell? Who else wishes me well? Friend of the helpless, who else is kind by his very nature to a servant, to a friend, to a suffering man, to one with no one of his own?
By your glance alone, so many sinners have crossed this ocean of the world without any boat or raft. Ram, whether out of mercy or out of anger, in true feeling or by mistake, or with nothing more than a sidelong look, you had once turned your eyes towards them.
Whichever of these looks pleases you, look at me with that one, and look soon (that is all — the moment you look, my work is done). The thing is this: make Tulsidas your own now, do not delay, because the end of this life has come very near.

My God! Where shall I go? Where is there a place or a shelter for a sorrowing, helpless man like me? Who is a master as kind as you, who gives refuge to one who comes to him with no strength for any spiritual practice at all?
The other masters of this world, apart from you, take in only servants who are rich, who are full of good qualities, and who serve them well. (I am not rich, I have no good quality in me, and I do not serve well either.) To feed and care for low, penniless men like me, men with nothing to give, without virtues and full of laziness — that becomes only Shri Raghunath, who never tires of doing good.
What can my mouth say, Lord? You are wise yourself, and you know everything that is in my heart. For a man with a mind as soiled as Tulsi's, in all three worlds (heaven, earth and the world below) and in all three times, you alone are the support.

My Lord! I went from door to door, baring my teeth in a grin and falling at people's feet, telling everyone how wretched I was. This world has such kind-hearted people in it, people able to put down the sorrows and the faults of all ten directions — yet not one of them even spoke a word to me.
My mother and father threw me away the way a cruel creature, a mother snake, abandons the young born from her own body. Why should I be angry, and who is there to blame? All of it came out of my own bad luck. (I am so low that) people hold back from touching even my shadow.
Seeing me so miserable, holy people said: do not worry in your heart. Wretched, sinful creatures like you — even the birds and the beasts — Shri Raghunath never turned away when they came to him for shelter; he kept them in his care and stood by them to the very end. (So go to him for shelter too.)
From that moment this Tulsi became yours, and from that moment he has lived in great happiness, even though he has no real love for you and no real trust in you. (If he had that love and that trust, there would be no limit at all to his joy.) Lord, when I see that the glory of your name and your gentleness have done me good, unworthy as I am, I feel ashamed deep inside (because I have not done one single thing that deserves your mercy, and still the Lord is this kind to an ungrateful man like me), and I praise your love for all who come to you for shelter.

What have I not done? Where have I not gone? What place is left for me to go to? Before whom have I not bowed my head? But Shri Ram, until I became your servant, I was born in this world again and again, and in all ten directions I found nothing but sorrow (not even in a dream did happiness come to me).
Even as your own servant, in my confusion I hoped the pleasures of the senses would make me happy; ruled by that hope I went about offering myself, making myself known, before masters with unclean hearts, and again and again, at door after door, I told my tale of poverty with my mouth wide open — and not even dust fell into it. (Nowhere did I get so much as a glimpse of happiness or peace.)
Without food and without clothes I ran here and there like a madman. I threw away honour and respect, which are dearer than life itself, and moment after moment I opened up this empty belly of mine and showed it to wicked men.
My Lord! Greed for the pleasures of the senses made me crave and crave, and nothing at all ever came into my hands. I am telling you the truth: is there any dance that low greed has not made shameless me dance?
I set my ears, my eyes and my mind each on its own path, but everywhere I only fell further down. (I tried every king and great lord as well. Nowhere, in nothing, through anyone, did I find happiness or peace; and then) I beat my head and gave up in my heart — I lost all hope. That is why, in my helplessness, I have come and taken shelter at your feet, because it is here that I can see my own good.
Son of Dasharath! You alone are able. In all three worlds it is your fame that is sung. Tulsi is bowing at your feet — look his way, I would give my life for you. It is the roll of your own titles that called me, holding out your arm and your word. (When your names — saviour of the fallen, lover of those who take refuge in you — are watching over me, how can I not be saved?)

Great king Shri Ramchandra! Apart from you, who is my true well-wisher? I say this to everyone, and to my master too: hear it, weigh it, and if anyone else is greater, then draw a longer line beside mine.
All the friends and well-wishers we find through the tie of body and soul are stitched together with false, unreal threads. (Every bond of this world is made of illusion.) Think it over and these "friends" are like the heart of a banana tree. (Peel a banana tree and nothing but peel comes off it; in the same way every bond of this world is hollow, born of nothing but ignorance.) They look lovely only the way a worthless piece of glass looks fine when it is set here and there among gems and gold.
Dear father! This letter of pleading, this Vinaya Patrika written by a poor man, please read it yourself. (Do not have someone else read it to you.) Tulsi has written in it only the true things of his heart; so first, out of your own merciful nature, mark it "approved". Ask the council of elders afterwards.

Son of the Wind, Hanuman! Shatrughna! Dear Bharat! Dear Lakshman! When your own moment comes, when you get the chance, remember this poor Tulsi. I would give my life for you. If you are kind enough to do this, the one hope of this utterly weak servant will be fulfilled (Shri Raghunath will mark my letter "approved").
In the royal court everyone speaks well of true holy men — what is so special in that? But if you put in a word for this poor man who has no refuge, then he will find shelter with the Lord; you will earn merit, and beautiful fame will spread; your master will be pleased with you (because he is naturally glad with those who are kind to the wretched), and both your own good and the highest good will be served.
So watch for the moment, and as soon as you get the chance, set right the case of this fallen Tulsi. Explain to merciful Raghunath, who loves all who come to him for shelter, just how far the love of this helpless man goes.

The divine court of Lord Ram is in session. The Lord is seated with Shri Janaki, the mother of the world, on a wondrous throne set with jewels. Hanuman, drowned in love, is pressing the Lord's feet, gazing at him with eyes that can see nothing else. Bharat, Lakshman and Shatrughna are each busy in the service that is theirs to do. At that very moment Tulsidas's Vinaya Patrika arrived. Everyone there remembered Tulsidas's prayer. Hanuman, the son of the Wind, who loves the devotees, and Bharat quietly said to Lakshman that this was a very good moment and that Tulsidas's matter should be raised now. Seeing which way they leaned, Lakshman placed the Vinaya Patrika before the Lord.
Seeing the mind and the wish of Hanuman and Bharat, Lakshman said to the Lord: My Lord! Even in Kaliyug, one servant of yours has kept his love and his trust in your name to the end. (See, this true letter of pleading from him has come as well.)
Hearing this, the whole assembly spoke with one voice: yes, this is completely true, we know his ways too. Lord Ram, who lifts up the poor, is very merciful to him. Before the eyes of all, the Master has taken that poor man by the arm and made him his own.
Hearing them all, Shri Ram smiled and said: yes, it is true, news of him has reached me too. (Janak's daughter must have spoken of him many times, for Goswami Tulsidas had already made his prayer to her.) And that was that — with his own hand Raghunath marked the Vinaya Patrika of helpless Tulsi "approved". And when my own case was settled, I too, filled with the deepest joy, laid my head at the Lord's feet (and took shelter there for ever).
When Tulsidas came to live at Asi Ghat, one night Kaliyug took on a body, came to him and began to torment him. Goswami Tulsidas turned his mind to Hanuman. Hanuman told him to compose verses of humble pleading; so Goswami wrote the Vinaya Patrika and offered it at the Lord's feet. Shri Ram signed it with his own hand and made Tulsidas free of all fear.
On Saturday, the third day of the dark half of Shravan, in the year Samvat 1680, at Asi Ghat, Goswami Tulsidas left his body with the words "Ram, Ram" on his lips.
May this be an offering at the feet of Shri Sita and Ram.
